## Cross-Border E-Commerce Stock Planning in China
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/cross-border-ecommerce-stock-planning-china
Published: 2026-10-23 · Cluster: E-commerce Operations

## Cross-border e-commerce stock planning is a forecast bounded by customs clocks

**Cross-border e-commerce stock planning in China is the discipline of deciding how many units of each SKU to hold in a bonded warehouse, at which port, and when to replenish, used to keep a 1210 storefront in stock without holding goods past the point the customs rules allow.** It looks like ordinary inventory planning and is not: an ordinary warehouse lets you sit on slow stock until the market turns, while a bonded position has three legal clocks running against it from the day the goods clear into the zone.

The commercial logic is different too. In bond, the import tax is not yet paid, so a unit's carrying cost is warehouse space plus the cost of the goods — not the duty and VAT that a general-trade import would have settled at the border. That is precisely why bonded stock is the default first position for a foreign brand testing China, and why underestimating the clocks is the most expensive mistake in the model.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">9.1%</span><span class="l">Effective tax on a 13 percent VAT product released as a cross-border retail import order — zero tariff plus import VAT and consumption tax at 70 percent of the statutory rate, within the quota limits</span><span class="src">Source: MOFCOM et al., Notice 49 of 2018 on cross-border e-commerce retail import tax (in force 1 January 2019)</span></div>

## Bonded stock defers tax rather than removing it

**A bonded retail import position is inventory held inside a customs-supervised zone on which duty and import taxes have not yet been assessed, used to serve consumer orders that are taxed at the moment of release rather than at the moment of entry.** China's cross-border retail import tax policy sets the parameters: RMB 5,000 per order and RMB 26,000 per person per year, zero tariff inside those limits, and import VAT plus consumption tax at 70 percent of the statutory rate ([Notice 49 of 2018, Ministry of Finance](https://gss.mof.gov.cn/gzdt/zhengcefabu/201811/t20181129_3079073.htm)).

Two consequences follow for the replenishment plan. First, the cash-flow argument for bonding is real but bounded — the benefit is a deferral, so the gain scales with how long the stock sits and how much tax it would otherwise have settled. Second, the price ceiling per order is a hard cap, not a guideline: a cart that crosses RMB 5,000 falls out of the retail import channel, so high-ticket SKUs need a different route rather than a bigger bonded position.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 26,000</span><span class="l">Annual per-person quota for cross-border retail imports, against a RMB 5,000 per-order limit — the ceiling that caps how many units one customer can take in a year</span><span class="src">Source: MOFCOM, NDRC, MOF, GACC, STA and SAMR, Notice 49 of 2018</span></div>

## The positive list is the boundary of every purchase order

**The cross-border e-commerce retail import positive list is the schedule of tariff lines eligible for the 1210 and 9610 channels, used to screen a product range before any replenishment order is placed.** The 2022 edition carried 1,476 tariff lines and took effect on 1 March 2022, and a line that is absent cannot be sold through the bonded route however good the demand looks in a forecast.

Inside the list, the regime is unusually fast. Notice 486 of 2018 waives first-import licensing, registration and record-filing for goods bought through cross-border retail channels, provided the seller publishes a risk disclosure on the order page and gives consumers access to a Chinese electronic label ([Notice 486, State Council](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2018-12/31/content_5437823.htm)). For a replenishment planner that means a new SKU can go live in weeks, with no registration file to wait on — so the binding constraint on assortment is the list, not a regulator's queue.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">1,476</span><span class="l">Tariff lines on China's cross-border e-commerce retail import positive list, 2022 edition in force from 1 March 2022 — the assortment boundary for any 1210 bonded position</span><span class="src">Source: Customs Tariff Commission and GACC, positive list 2022 edition</span></div>

## Three customs clocks bound the position

**A bonded stock clock is a customs-set deadline that starts when goods enter or leave the zone, used to decide the maximum time a unit may sit in the position before it must be sold, returned or destroyed.** All three clocks run simultaneously, and the shortest one governs.

<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Clock</th><th>Rule</th><th>What it forces into the plan</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Storage</td><td>One year for bonded warehouse goods, extendable once by up to one year with customs approval (GACC Order 105, as amended)</td><td>No position may be planned on a sell-through horizon longer than 12 months</td></tr>
<tr><td>Destruction</td><td>60 days from the customs-signed application, one extension of up to 30 days, video evidence kept 3 years (GACC Announcement 79 of 2025)</td><td>Dead stock must be adjudicated while it still has resale value, not after</td></tr>
<tr><td>Returns</td><td>Application within 30 days, arrival within 45 days, goods fit for resale (GACC Announcement 45 of 2020)</td><td>Returned units re-enter available stock and must be netted off the next order</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

The storage rule comes from the bonded warehouse regulation, which also obliges the operator to keep a true monthly record of goods received, released and remaining, and to report it to customs, which may inspect at any time ([GACC Order No. 105, consolidated text](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/2018-05/29/content_5723452.htm)). In practice the monthly stock statement is the document your replenishment plan has to agree with — a plan that exists only in a spreadsheet and not in the bonded ledger is not a plan.

## Sizing the first position backwards from the quota

**Position sizing is the calculation of how many units of a given SKU to place in bond at launch, used to cover a target reorder cycle without breaching the storage clock or the per-customer quota.** Work it in four steps.

1. Divide RMB 26,000 by your landed retail price to get the maximum units one customer can buy in a year; a RMB 380 product caps at 68 units, a RMB 1,200 product at 21.
2. Multiply by a realistic repeat rate to get expected annual units per buying customer, then by the number of buying customers the launch media plan can plausibly reach.
3. Divide by 365 and multiply by your cover days — 45 to 60 days for a launch, longer only where a campaign is scheduled.
4. Add the campaign uplift, subtract stock already in bond and units in transit that will land inside the cover window.

The step most brands skip is the first. Because the quota is per person, a bonded position cannot be sold deeply into a small group of enthusiasts; it has to be sold broadly. That pushes the assortment decision towards more buyers per SKU rather than more units per buyer, and it argues for a narrow launch range with a defensible hero product rather than a full catalogue shipped into bond.

## Flat shopper numbers make replenishment a share fight

**Cross-border import demand in China is the volume of consumer goods bought through the 1210 and 9610 channels, used as the ceiling against which any replenishment plan must be tested.** China's cross-border e-commerce imports were worth RMB 570.2 billion in 2025, up 2.7 percent, and the mix was entirely consumer goods: beauty, fragrance and personal care at 27.2 percent, food and fresh produce at 23.9 percent ([GACC, 2025 cross-border e-commerce statistics](http://www.customs.gov.cn/tjs/2026-06/16/article_2026061616113844507.html)).

The demand pool is not expanding fast enough to bail out a bad buy. Online shoppers reached 976 million in June 2025, up 0.1 percent in six months ([CNNIC, 56th Statistical Report](https://www.cnnic.net.cn/NMediaFile/2025/0730/MAIN1753846666507QEK67ZS9DH.pdf)). When the shopper count is flat, every incremental unit sold in bond has been taken from another product on the same shelf — so replenishment should concentrate depth on SKUs with proven conversion and treat breadth as an experiment with a fixed budget, not as a hedge.

## Lead time and campaign peaks set the reorder point

**Replenishment lead time is the elapsed time from purchase order to sellable bonded stock, used to place the reorder point far enough ahead that cover never breaks.** Build the number from production time, ocean transit, port handling, bonded putaway and the platform's listing checks, then add the buffer that the season requires.

Seasonality is where bonded planning differs most from general trade. Stock for a June or November campaign has to be in the zone weeks before the peak, but ordering early burns the storage clock and locks capital into a forecast. The resolution is to split the buy: a core position sized on baseline demand that lands early, and a campaign top-up that lands close to the peak and is priced to clear. Brands that order one large container for the peak usually end up with either a stockout in week one or aged stock in January — see our [China campaign calendar](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/double-11-618-campaign-calendar-foreign-brands.html) for how the peaks fall, and [customs clearance timings](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-long-does-customs-clearance-take-china.html) for the port-side variable.

## Five metrics for the monthly replenishment review

**A bonded replenishment review is the monthly meeting at which stock cover, sell-through and age are compared against the plan, used to issue the next purchase order and to adjudicate dead stock.** Five numbers carry the decision.

- Days of cover by SKU and by port — one number per position, not one national average.
- Sell-through at day 90 on each launch SKU, measured on units released against units landed.
- Aged stock beyond 180 days, valued at cost, because this is the population heading for destruction.
- In-stock rate on the top 20 SKUs, which is the only service metric a customer experiences.
- Write-off at destruction, tracked as a cost line rather than absorbed as shrinkage.

## How GOODSINFINITE runs the bonded position

GOODSINFINITE acts as importer of record and bonded fulfilment partner across five locations — Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou and Qingdao — which puts the replenishment decision where the customs filings are: the monthly stock statement, the release-by-release tax settlement, the return filings and, where it comes to it, the destruction application. Brands keep title to their stock; we run the position with them on a monthly cycle so that the reorder point is set on measured cover rather than on a container's worth of optimism. For the wider sequence, start with our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) and the [cross-border operations glossary](https://www.goods-infinite.com/glossary.html).

## FAQ

**How much stock should a foreign brand hold in a Chinese bonded warehouse?** Size from demand and from the quota ceiling. Because orders cap at RMB 5,000 and each customer at RMB 26,000 a year, one buyer can absorb only a limited number of units, so a launch position should cover 45 to 60 days on the top 20 percent of SKUs and a small sample on the tail, held at the port whose catchment matches the launch region.

**How long can 1210 bonded stock stay in a bonded warehouse?** One year as a rule, with a single extension of up to one year where customs agrees there are justified reasons. Treat twelve months as the planning horizon: a unit that cannot sell through inside it must be exported, transferred to another special supervision area, converted to general trade with duty paid, or destroyed.

**What happens to bonded stock that does not sell?** It is destroyed under customs supervision. Announcement 79 of 2025 requires destruction within 60 days of the customs-signed application form, allows one extension of no more than 30 days, requires video evidence kept at least three years, and files the disposal under code 0200 — or 0844 with tax paid if the destruction generates revenue.

**Does bonded stock reduce the import tax a brand pays?** It defers and discounts it. Inside the RMB 5,000 and RMB 26,000 limits, tariff is zero and import VAT plus consumption tax are levied at 70 percent of the statutory rate, an effective 9.1 percent on a 13 percent VAT product and near 23.1 percent on high-end cosmetics. Nothing is payable until release.

**Can any product be replenished into bonded stock?** Only tariff lines on the positive list — 1,476 lines in the 2022 edition effective 1 March 2022. Inside that boundary, Notice 486 of 2018 waives first-import licensing and registration, so SKUs can be added in weeks, provided the listing carries the risk disclosure and Chinese electronic label.

## How to Vet a China Distributor: The Checks, the Red Flags and the Contract Clauses
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/vet-china-distributor-due-diligence
Published: 2026-10-23 · Cluster: Logistics & Distribution

## Definition: what "vetting a China distributor" actually means

Vetting a China distributor means **verifying, against official Chinese government registers and before you sign anything, that the local company you are about to hand your brand, your stock and your pricing to is (a) the entity it claims to be, (b) legally able to do the import and distribution it is promising, and (c) not in a position to appropriate your trademark, your registration certificates or your customers.**

It is not a credit report and it is not a reference call. Those are useful, but they answer a softer question. The hard question is narrower and more actionable: *what does the Chinese government's own public record say about this company, and does my contract survive the answer?*

That distinction matters because of scale. As of the end of May 2025 there were **185 million private-sector business entities registered in China, 96.76% of all market entities**, including more than 58 million private enterprises and 127 million individual businesses ([State Administration for Market Regulation data reported by People's Daily, 28 June 2025](http://sh.people.cn/n2/2025/0628/c134768-41274655.html)). "We are a large Chinese distributor" is a statement that costs nothing to make and is almost impossible to disprove over email. It takes about an hour to disprove properly.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">185 million / 96.76%</span><span class="l">Private-sector business entities registered in China as at end-May 2025, and their share of all market entities — including 58 million+ private enterprises and 127 million individual businesses. Scale is why a distributor's self-description is not evidence.</span><span class="src">Source: State Administration for Market Regulation, reported by People's Daily, 28 June 2025</span></div>

## Why this is a legal problem, not a commercial one

Most foreign brands approach distributor selection commercially — margin, coverage, enthusiasm. The failures that actually destroy a China launch are legal and procedural:

1. **The trademark was filed by the distributor first.** China is first-to-file: under Art. 31 of the Trademark Law, where two parties apply for identical or similar marks on identical or similar goods, the earlier application is preliminarily approved and published. If your distributor filed your brand in China before you did, you are the one bringing an objection.
2. **The registrations sit in the distributor's name.** For regulated categories — food, cosmetics, medical devices, certain electrical goods — the approvals are held by a Chinese entity. If that entity is the distributor's, termination does not end the relationship; it transfers the leverage.
3. **The "exclusive for China" grant was broader than intended.** A single exclusive clause can lock a brand out of channels, platforms and city tiers it never meant to give away, with no performance obligation attached.
4. **The contract contains terms Chinese law will not enforce the way you expect.** Resale price maintenance is the classic example.
5. **The counterparty on the signature page is not the counterparty you checked.** Shell entities with near-identical names are common. The 18-character Unified Social Credit Code is what disambiguates them.

## Step 1 — Verify the entity on the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System

**Registry:** [国家企业信用信息公示系统 (National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System)](https://www.gsxt.gov.cn/), operated by the State Administration for Market Regulation. Free, public, no payment and no login required for basic queries ([Beijing Municipal Administration for Market Regulation](https://scjgj.beijing.gov.cn/zwxx/scjgdt/202503/t20250324_4041940.html)).

Search by the **exact Chinese company name** or, better, by the **Unified Social Credit Code (统一社会信用代码)** — the 18-character identifier on the business licence. Ask for the licence scan up front; a company that will not send one has told you what you need to know.

What the record gives you:

| Field | What you are checking | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Registration status | 存续 / 吊销 / 注销 | A company that has been revoked or cancelled and is still trading is a serious problem, not a technicality |
| Unified Social Credit Code | 18 characters, matches the contract and the invoice | Prevents signature-page substitution |
| Legal representative (法定代表人) | Name to cross-check against court records | Individual-level enforcement records attach to the person, not just the company |
| Business scope (经营范围) | Does the scope actually cover import, distribution, or the specific regulated category? | A trading company cannot lawfully do what its licence does not cover |
| Registered capital, paid-in capital, shareholders | Who actually owns and controls the entity | Identifies affiliates that may strip value |
| Administrative licences | Food, cosmetics, medical device, CCC-scope licences where applicable | Tells you whether it can hold your product legally |
| Administrative penalties | Prior enforcement history | Repeated penalties in your category are predictive |
| Annual reports (年报) | Filed each year, 1 January – 30 June | Gaps are a live signal, not a filing oversight |
| Abnormal operation list (经营异常名录) | Four statutory grounds under Art. 4 of the Measures for the Administration of the List of Enterprises with Abnormal Operations (formerly SAIC Order No. 68, as amended) — failure to publish an annual report, failure to publish required information after being ordered to, failure to register a name change, and **being unreachable at the registered address** | "Unreachable at the registered address" is the single most useful free red flag in the whole system |
| Serious illegal and untrustworthy list (严重违法失信名单) | Listed or not | Brings joint punishment across government agencies |

Two of these deserve emphasis. **Unreachable at the registered address** means the market regulator itself could not find the company where it says it is. And the **serious illegal and untrustworthy list** has recently been rebuilt: SAMR Order No. 128 replaced the 2021 rules and took effect **15 July 2026**, adding commercial bribery, serious intellectual-property infringement including bad-faith trademark filings that harm the public interest, falsified public information, and **evading enforcement of an administrative penalty or ruling** as independent grounds for listing ([SAMR](https://www.samr.gov.cn/); [summary by Dazhou Municipal Administration for Market Regulation](https://scjgj.dazhou.gov.cn/news-show-9978.html)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">15 July 2026</span><span class="l">Effective date of SAMR Order No. 128 on the Serious Illegal and Untrustworthy List, which replaced the 2021 rules (Order No. 44). New grounds for listing include commercial bribery, intentional IP infringement and bad-faith trademark filings, falsified public information, and evading enforcement of a penalty or ruling — all directly relevant to distributor conduct.</span><span class="src">Source: State Administration for Market Regulation Order No. 128; SAMR / local AMR implementing notices</span></div>

## Step 2 — Verify customs standing, not "import and export rights"

Ask a candidate for its customs record and then check it yourself on the [China Customs Enterprise Import and Export Credit Information Publicity Platform (中国海关企业进出口信用信息公示平台)](http://credit.customs.gov.cn). Customs itself has confirmed this is the channel for checking whether a company is an AEO enterprise ([General Administration of Customs, "Customs Policy Direct" No. 4, 13 January 2026](https://www.customs.gov.cn/customs/2026-01/13/article_2026041015241494434.html)).

The legal basis is the **Measures of the Customs of the PRC for the Credit Administration of Registered and Filed Enterprises (GACC Order No. 251, in force 1 November 2021)**, which requires customs to publish: enterprise registration and filing information; the result of customs credit certification or determination; administrative licensing information; administrative penalties; and joint incentive / joint punishment information (Art. 11). The published credit tier is the payoff:

| Credit status | Published effect under GACC Order No. 251 |
|---|---|
| **Advanced certified enterprise (AEO)** | Average inspection rate on imports and exports **below 20% of the average rate applied to enterprises under ordinary management**; priority clearance; reduced audit frequency; possible guarantee exemption; dedicated customs coordinator (Art. 30) |
| **Ordinary management** | Standard measures |
| **Dishonest enterprise (失信企业)** | **Inspection rate of 80% or above**; full guarantee for processing trade; increased audit and inspection frequency (Art. 31) |

A distributor on the customs dishonest list will have four out of five shipments inspected. If that distributor is holding your inventory, the delay lands on you, not on them.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">< 20% vs ≥ 80%</span><span class="l">Average import/export inspection rate for a GACC advanced-certified (AEO) enterprise — below 20% of the rate applied to ordinary enterprises — versus an inspection rate of 80% or above for an enterprise customs has determined to be dishonest. Same goods, same declaration, two completely different clearance profiles.</span><span class="src">Source: GACC Order No. 251, Arts. 30 and 31</span></div>

Two clarifications that save time:

- **"Import and export rights" is nearly meaningless as a claim now.** On 30 December 2022 the NPC Standing Committee deleted Art. 9 of the Foreign Trade Law; MOFCOM stopped processing foreign-trade operator registrations the same day, and companies engaged in import and export obtain the status automatically ([MOFCOM, Foreign Trade Department](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/syxwfb/art/2023/art_fe303b761df547ae8f35af1a691b7c5d.html); [MOFCOM public Q&A](https://gzlynew.mofcom.gov.cn/gzlynew/servlet/SearchServlet?OP=getCommentAnswer&id=4b84f6e0d9f54e98bf200d6963b7058f&siteid=tradeservice&orderFiled=2)).
- **Customs registration is still required.** Art. 11 of the Customs Law requires consignees of imported goods and customs brokers to be registered with customs before handling customs formalities; this is a separate requirement that survived the 2022 trade-law change. This is the document to ask for.

## Step 3 — Check whether the company and its legal representative are being enforced against

**Registry:** [中国执行信息公开网 (China Enforcement Information Publicity Website)](http://zxgk.court.gov.cn/) of the Supreme People's Court. Search the company name and, separately, the legal representative's name.

Look for: 被执行人 (person subject to enforcement), 失信被执行人 (dishonest person subject to enforcement — the "laolai" list, which carries consumption and travel restrictions), 限制消费令 (consumption restriction orders) and termination-of-case records.

The volume here is not marginal. At a Supreme People's Court press conference on 26 January 2026, the court reported that in 2025 **2.3398 million person-times were newly added to the dishonest list, 2.6696 million person-times exited through credit repair, and 18.6518 million persons subject to enforcement performed their obligations under the pressure of enforcement sanctions** ([People's Daily, 27 January 2026](https://cpc.people.com.cn/n1/2026/0127/c64387-40653576.html)). Checking costs five minutes. Not checking is how brands end up holding unpaid invoices from a counterparty that already has twenty of them.

Also worth searching: [China Judgments Online (wenshu.court.gov.cn)](https://wenshu.court.gov.cn/) for prior contract disputes, and [Credit China (www.creditchina.gov.cn)](https://www.creditchina.gov.cn/) for cross-agency credit records.

## Step 4 — Check your own trademark status before you appoint anyone

This step is about you, not the distributor, and it is the one most often skipped.

Under the Trademark Law (as amended in 2019):

- **Art. 31 — first to file.** Where two or more applicants file identical or similar marks for identical or similar goods, the earlier application is preliminarily approved and published.
- **Art. 4 — bad faith.** "Bad-faith trademark registration applications not intended for use shall be rejected."
- **Art. 32 — prior rights and pre-emptive filing.** No application may damage another party's existing prior rights, nor may a party pre-emptively register by improper means a mark already in use by another party that has acquired a certain degree of influence.
- **Art. 15 — the distributor case, stated explicitly.** Where an **agent or representative** registers the trademark of its principal in its own name without authorisation, the registration must be refused and its use prohibited if the principal objects. Art. 15(2) extends the same outcome to an applicant who, **by virtue of a contract, business dealings or other relationship, knew of the other party's earlier-used unregistered mark** on identical or similar goods.
- **Art. 33 — objection window.** An objection against a preliminarily approved mark must be filed within **three months** of publication.
- **Art. 68(4) — administrative penalty.** Bad-faith filings are punishable by warning and fine according to the circumstances.

The 2019 implementing rules — [Provisions on Regulating Trademark Application and Registration (SAMR Order No. 17)](https://www.cnipa.gov.cn/art/2024/1/30/art_3323_190072.html) — spell out in Art. 3 that an agent or representative registering the principal's mark without authorisation, and a party that registers a mark knowing of another's prior use through contract or business dealings, are both bad-faith filings; Art. 5 requires the registry to reject them, and Art. 12 sets administrative fines of up to three times illegal gain capped at RMB 30,000, or up to RMB 10,000 where there is no illegal gain.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">3 months</span><span class="l">The objection window against a preliminarily approved Chinese trademark application, running from publication (Trademark Law Art. 33). Miss it and the fight moves to invalidation, which is slower and more expensive. Search your own brand on the China Trademark Office site before appointing a distributor — and periodically after.</span><span class="src">Source: Trademark Law of the PRC (2019 amendment), Arts. 15, 31, 32, 33, 68</span></div>

**Action:** search your brand in Latin script, in Chinese characters, and in any plausible transliteration on the [China National Intellectual Property Administration trademark portal](https://sbj.cnipa.gov.cn/sbj/index.html), before you sign. Then monitor. Distributor squatting is not usually a pre-planned heist; it is usually a hedge taken after the relationship sours.

## Step 5 — Three clauses Chinese law will not give you

These come up in almost every negotiation, and in each case the foreign brand's instinct is wrong.

### Resale price maintenance

Art. 18 of the Anti-Monopoly Law (as amended 2022) prohibits agreements between an operator and its counterparty that **fix the price for resale to third parties** or **set a minimum resale price**. The agreement is not prohibited if the operator can prove it has no effect of excluding or restricting competition, and there is a safe harbour where the operator can prove its market share in the relevant market is below the threshold set by the enforcement authority and other conditions are met ([NPC Standing Committee decision amending the Anti-Monopoly Law, 24 June 2022](https://www.gov.cn/xinwen/2022-06/25/content_5697697.htm)).

The thresholds were made operational by the 2025 amendment to the Provisions on Prohibiting Monopoly Agreements (SAMR Order No. 111, in force 1 February 2026): for **price-related vertical agreements** both parties' market shares must be below **5%** in every year of the agreement and the annual turnover of the contract goods below **RMB 100 million**; for **non-price vertical agreements** (territory, customer restrictions) the threshold is **15%** market share with no turnover condition — and **both** parties must qualify, every year ([Putian Municipal Administration for Market Regulation summary of SAMR Order No. 111](https://scjgj.putian.gov.cn/gzcy/rdhy/202610/t20261012_2238764.htm)).

**Practical drafting:** a maximum resale price or a recommended retail price, combined with control over brand presentation, channel listing and promotional mechanics. Do not build a mechanism for detecting and punishing price-cutting.

### Commercial bribery conducted "for" you

Art. 7 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law prohibits an operator from bribing, by money or other means, the counterparty's personnel, a unit or individual entrusted by the counterparty, or a unit or individual able to influence the transaction through authority or influence, in order to obtain a transaction opportunity or competitive advantage. Critically, Art. 7(3) provides that **bribery by an operator's personnel is deemed to be the act of the operator** — unless the operator proves the conduct was unrelated to obtaining business for it. Penalties under Art. 19 run from **RMB 100,000 to RMB 3 million**, confiscation of illegal gain, and revocation of the business licence in serious cases.

A distributor that buys shelf space or buyer favour in your brand's name is creating exposure you may end up sharing. Put an anti-bribery covenant in the agreement, require it to flow down to the distributor's own sales staff, and give yourself an audit and termination right.

### "Exclusive for China" without performance

There is no legal obstacle to exclusivity, but a broad grant with no objective performance test is a one-way option written against you. If you grant exclusivity, tie it to measurable commitments — named channels, minimum purchase volumes, listing obligations, marketing spend — tested at defined intervals with a cure period and automatic conversion to non-exclusive on failure.

## Step 6 — Red flags and what they usually mean

These are patterns, not accusations. Each one alone may have an innocent explanation; two or more together is a decision.

| Signal | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| Company declines to send a business licence scan, or the Unified Social Credit Code on the contract differs from the one on the licence | You may be contracting with a different entity than the one you are negotiating with |
| Registered address is "unreachable" on gsxt.gov.cn | The regulator could not find them where they say they are |
| Registered capital is very large, paid-in is zero or nominal, and the entity was incorporated recently | A vehicle, not a business |
| Business scope does not cover your regulated category, or covers it only by a generic "sales of…" formula | It cannot hold your product lawfully, or will subcontract the licence holding to someone you have not vetted |
| Presses hard for exclusivity and a long term before any market test | It is buying optionality at your cost |
| Wants the product registration certificate in its own name as a condition of proceeding | Building termination leverage |
| Asks you not to register your trademark because "we will handle it" | The single highest-risk sentence in China distribution |
| Payment to a personal account, or to a different company's account than the one on the contract | Either tax structuring or fraud; both are your problem |
| Customs credit status is "dishonest" or AEO status claimed but not appearing on credit.customs.gov.cn | Your inventory will sit |
| Legal representative appears on the enforcement list | The control person is already constrained |
| Claims "foreign trade operator registration" as a credential | No longer issued since 30 December 2022 — a stale claim suggests stale advice generally |

## Step 7 — Insure the receivable

Commercial prevention is structural; insurance is the backstop. [China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation (Sinosure)](https://www.sinosure.com.cn/) is China's policy export credit insurer. Its short-term cover responds to commercial risks including **buyer insolvency, buyer default on payment obligations, buyer rejection of goods, and buyer breach causing early termination**, as well as defined political risks ([Sinosure short-term specific-contract policy, 2025 version](https://www.sinosure.com.cn/images/gywm/gsjj/xxpl/bxcpjbxx/2025/02/25/1343959802792808448.pdf)).

Note the fit question honestly: Sinosure's export policies insure **Chinese-registered exporters**. If you sell to a Chinese distributor from an overseas entity, the practical routes are your own market credit insurer, your export credit agency, or structuring the sale through a Hong Kong or mainland trading arm. What Sinosure usefully proves is that **buyer default, insolvency and rejection are insurable, priced risks** — which means the right response to a distributor that refuses any third-party check is not to relax the check, but to shorten the credit.

## The twelve-point pre-signature checklist

1. **Obtain the business licence** and record the 18-character Unified Social Credit Code.
2. **Search gsxt.gov.cn** using that code. Read status, business scope, legal representative, licences, penalties, annual reports, abnormal-operation and serious-illegal-and-untrustworthy listings.
3. **Search credit.customs.gov.cn** for customs credit status. Treat "dishonest" as disqualifying for anyone holding your inventory.
4. **Search zxgk.court.gov.cn** for the company and the legal representative; read wenshu.court.gov.cn for prior contract disputes.
5. **Search your own brand** on the CNIPA trademark portal in Latin script, Chinese characters and likely transliterations. If anything is filed, get advice before signing.
6. **Confirm the signatory's authority** — the licence's legal representative, or a validly sealed power of attorney.
7. **Map the ownership chain.** Shareholders, affiliates, and other entities under the same controlling person.
8. **Confirm the business scope covers the regulated category** and that any required licence is held by an entity you have also vetted.
9. **Decide who holds the product registrations.** If it must be a Chinese entity, prefer your own, or a custodial arrangement with transfer triggers — not the distributor's by default.
10. **Draft the price clause as a maximum or recommendation**, not a minimum, and check the safe-harbour thresholds.
11. **Insert an anti-bribery covenant** with flow-down to the distributor's staff, plus audit and termination rights.
12. **Stage the credit.** Prepayment or a small first order; escalate limits only against demonstrated payment history; no open account on the strength of a relationship.

## Where GOODSINFINITE fits

The failure mode this article describes is almost always a **structural** one: the brand has no China-side presence of its own, so every function — importer of record, registration holder, channel operator, negotiator — has to sit with a counterparty whose interests diverge from the brand's the moment the category proves out.

Our structure is deliberately different. We do not buy your goods and we do not earn a resale margin; we operate on a service fee, which removes the incentive that drives most distributor conflicts.

- **Hong Kong importer of record** — GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED (Kwun Tong, Kowloon) contracts with you as the overseas principal, holds title and settles FX, keeping the brand-owning layer outside the mainland entity you do not yet need.
- **Mainland clearance and compliance** — customs registration, declaration, bonded or general-trade fulfilment, and the product registration work that in a distributor model becomes someone else's leverage.
- **Five-city bonded fulfilment** — Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou and Qingdao, so a distribution conversation starts from your stock already in China rather than from a promise.
- **China-side commercial representation** — office setup, recruitment support, market research, trade-show participation and B2B channel building including 1688.com, plus representation in offline negotiations with Chinese buyers. You keep the buyer relationship; we do the talking in the room.
- **Verified counterparties** — the checks above are the ones we run on the Chinese side before you commit, in Chinese, against the primary registers.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">6,000㎡ + 8,000㎡</span><span class="l">Bonded warehousing and temperature- and humidity-controlled warehousing operated through our network, alongside 300+ enterprises served and our own AEO advanced certification plus 15 partner AEO facilities. Holding your stock in our own bonded footprint rather than a distributor's warehouse is the structural answer to most of the risks above.</span><span class="src">Source: GOODSINFINITE operations</span></div>

## What we deliberately do not assert

This article stays with what we can point to in official text. Three things are commonly claimed in vendor and law-firm content that we will not repeat:

- **We do not give a cost or timeline for Chinese trademark registration.** No official schedule is published and third-party figures vary widely.
- **We do not describe any named company's distributor dispute.** We have no official source for the specifics of any particular case.
- **We do not state that a distributor "cannot" do any particular act beyond what the cited law says.** Art. 15 of the Trademark Law gives a principal a strong objection, not an automatic result; outcomes turn on evidence of the relationship and prior use.

## FAQ

**How can I check whether a Chinese company is legitimate before signing a distribution agreement?** Start with the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System (gsxt.gov.cn), run by the State Administration for Market Regulation. Searching the exact Chinese company name or the 18-character Unified Social Credit Code returns registration status, business scope, legal representative, registered capital, administrative licences, administrative penalties, annual reports, and any listing on the abnormal-operation list or the serious-illegal-and-untrustworthy list. It is free and open to the public. Then cross-check customs credit at credit.customs.gov.cn and court enforcement records at zxgk.court.gov.cn.

**Can my China distributor register my trademark in China and block me?** It can try, and it sometimes succeeds if you have not filed first. China is a first-to-file system under Art. 31 of the Trademark Law. But Art. 15 gives you a direct defence: an agent or representative that registers the principal's trademark in its own name without authorisation must be refused registration and is prohibited from using it, and Art. 15(2) extends that to parties who knew of your earlier-used mark through a contract, business dealings or other relationship. File your own Chinese trademark before you appoint any distributor.

**Is "we have import and export rights" a meaningful claim from a Chinese distributor?** Much less than it used to be. On 30 December 2022 the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress deleted Art. 9 of the Foreign Trade Law, and MOFCOM stopped issuing foreign-trade operator registrations the same day — companies now obtain foreign-trade status automatically. What still matters is customs registration: under Art. 11 of the Customs Law, a consignee of imported goods must be registered with customs to file declarations. Ask for the customs registration record and check it, not for a trade-operator certificate nobody issues any more.

**Can I fix the resale price my China distributor charges?** Be careful. Art. 18 of the Anti-Monopoly Law (as amended in 2022) prohibits agreements that fix the price for resale to third parties or set a minimum resale price. An agreement is not prohibited if you can show it has no effect of excluding or restricting competition, and a safe harbour applies where both parties' market shares and the contract turnover stay below the thresholds set by the enforcement authority. Practically: set a maximum resale price or a recommended price, control brand and channel, and do not write an enforceable minimum retail price into the contract.

**What should a China distribution agreement say about termination and inventory?** Define the territory and channels precisely rather than granting "China" in the abstract; set objective performance thresholds with a cure period; require the distributor to transfer or cancel any e-commerce storefront and platform accounts it opened in your brand name; deal explicitly with remaining inventory and with who owns the customer data; and provide for the return of product registration certificates, which in many regulated categories are held by a local entity and are the distributor's real leverage over you.

**How do I protect against non-payment by a Chinese distributor?** Check the company and its legal representative against the Supreme People's Court enforcement database before you extend credit, start with prepayment or a small first order, keep title until payment where the contract allows it, escalate credit only against actual payment history, and consider export credit insurance — China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation (Sinosure), the state policy insurer, writes cover against buyer insolvency, protracted default and rejection of goods.

## China Market Entry by Region: Where Demand Sits
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-market-entry-regional-demand
Published: 2026-10-21 · Cluster: Market Research

## Regional demand segmentation is the filter a national market size figure cannot provide

**Regional demand segmentation in China is the practice of splitting the national market into customs catchments and consumer geographies, used to decide where a foreign brand places its first bonded stock and its first marketing budget.** A national total, by contrast, describes a case no operator can execute: every cost and every delivery promise in China is regional.

The national figures are not small. Total retail sales of consumer goods reached RMB 50.12 trillion in 2025, up 3.7 percent, of which online physical-goods sales were RMB 13.09 trillion, or 26.1 percent ([National Bureau of Statistics, December 2025 retail release](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202601/t20260120_1962354.html)). But the demand pool has stopped expanding: China had 976 million online shoppers in June 2025, up 0.1 percent in six months, at 86.9 percent penetration ([CNNIC, 56th Statistical Report](https://www.cnnic.net.cn/NMediaFile/2025/0730/MAIN1753846666507QEK67ZS9DH.pdf)). When the number of shoppers is flat, the only growth available to a new entrant is share taken from someone else in a specific place.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">44.3%</span><span class="l">Share of China's 2025 cross-border e-commerce imports taken by just five destinations: Guangdong 14.8%, Jiangsu 8.6%, Zhejiang 8.5%, Shanghai 6.8%, Shandong 5.6%</span><span class="src">Source: General Administration of Customs of China, 2025 cross-border e-commerce trade statistics (published June 2026)</span></div>

## Cross-border import destinations show where the infrastructure sits

**A cross-border import destination share is the percentage of national cross-border e-commerce import value attributed to the province in which the consignment is declared, used as a proxy for where the bonded operators, importers of record and platform sellers serving that demand are based.** China's cross-border e-commerce imports were worth RMB 570.2 billion in 2025, up 2.7 percent, and the goods were entirely consumer products ([GACC, 2025 statistics](http://www.customs.gov.cn/tjs/2026-06/16/article_2026061616113844507.html)).

The concentration is the story. Five destinations take 44.3 percent of the trade, and three of them form a single contiguous manufacturing-and-consumption belt.

<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Destination</th><th>2025 import share</th><th>What it rewards</th><th>Bonded port that serves it</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Guangdong</td><td>14.8%</td><td>Hong Kong adjacency, Cantonese content, electronics and fashion</td><td>Guangzhou / Shenzhen</td></tr>
<tr><td>Jiangsu</td><td>8.6%</td><td>Industrial consumers, inland distribution reach</td><td>Shanghai / Ningbo catchment</td></tr>
<tr><td>Zhejiang</td><td>8.5%</td><td>E-commerce operations depth, cross-border seller density</td><td>Ningbo / Hangzhou</td></tr>
<tr><td>Shanghai</td><td>6.8%</td><td>Highest-value repeat purchase, beauty and premium food</td><td>Shanghai</td></tr>
<tr><td>Shandong</td><td>5.6%</td><td>Northern catchment, cold-chain and food categories</td><td>Qingdao</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

A declaration point is not a consumption point: one Shanghai bonded warehouse can ship to Harbin, and a Guangdong seller can serve a Chengdu customer. Read the shares as a map of where competent operators already are — which is why they also predict where your fulfilment partner, TP and category rivals cluster.

## The three core geographies reward different launches

**China's three core demand geographies — the Greater Bay Area, the Yangtze Delta and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei cluster — are distinct consumer markets rather than three slices of one, used to choose which single region a brand enters first instead of attempting all three at once.** Each has a different cost of attention, a different category depth and a different language register.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">23.9%</span><span class="l">Combined 2025 cross-border import share of the three Yangtze Delta destinations — Shanghai 6.8%, Jiangsu 8.6%, Zhejiang 8.5% — the deepest concentration of premium-category operations in the country</span><span class="src">Source: GOODSINFINITE calculation from GACC 2025 cross-border e-commerce statistics</span></div>

The Yangtze Delta is where premium categories are decided: the densest cluster of beauty, personal-care and imported-food operators, the largest pool of TP and agency talent, and the highest per-capita incomes outside the two first-tier cities. It is also the most expensive place to buy attention.

The Greater Bay Area, measured nationally as Guangdong, is the volume and speed market: Hong Kong adjacency that simplifies sourcing and payment, a Cantonese-language content ecosystem that runs semi-independently of Mandarin platforms, and deep electronics and fashion supply chains.

Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei is the policy and northern-logistics market. Tianjin is a new tier-1 city in the 2025 Yicai ranking and sits on a bonded port with cold-chain capacity, and the cluster's consumer base is large but more price-stratified than the south. Competition for attention is materially lower than in Shanghai, which makes it a rational first test for food, nutrition and household categories aimed at northern distribution.

## City tiers rank infrastructure; they do not rank your customer

**China's city-tier system is a commercial classification of 337 prefecture-level and above cities by commercial-resource density, used by brands to sequence a city rollout rather than to size demand for a product.** The 2025 edition holds four tier-1 cities, fifteen new tier-1 cities, then 30 tier-2, 70 tier-3, 90 tier-4 and 128 tier-5 ([Yicai, 2025 city ranking](http://yicai.com/news/102638963.html)).

The ranking measures commercial infrastructure: how many brands are already present, how dense the retail and media ecosystem is, how quickly new formats arrive. That is exactly what a launch needs to know about execution feasibility — and it is not the same question as whether shoppers in that city pay a premium in your category. Plenty of tier-2 cities outperform tier-1 cities in a single category, and a brand that treats the tier list as a demand forecast will over-fund the top four cities and under-fund the eight cities that actually buy its product.

## Income quintiles, not provinces, set the price ceiling

**Household income quintiles in China are the five equal-sized groups into which the National Bureau of Statistics sorts households by per-capita disposable income, used to count how many buyers can afford a given retail price.** In 2025 per-capita disposable income was RMB 43,377, up 5.0 percent, with urban income at RMB 56,502 against rural income at RMB 24,456 — a ratio of 2.31 ([NBS, 2025 household income release](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202601/t20260120_1962356.html)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">2.31×</span><span class="l">Urban-to-rural per-capita disposable income ratio in 2025 — RMB 56,502 against RMB 24,456 — the spread that any single national average price point ignores</span><span class="src">Source: National Bureau of Statistics of China, 2025 household income and consumption release</span></div>

The quintile averages ran from RMB 10,150 in the lowest group to RMB 103,778 in the highest, and the top two groups together cover roughly 40 percent of households. That band — not the whole population — is the addressable market for most imported consumer goods, and it is geographically uneven: it clusters in the tier-1 and new tier-1 cities and thins out quickly below them.

Two more filters sit on top. The landed price is set by the cross-border tax regime rather than the shelf price at home: within the RMB 5,000 per-order and RMB 26,000 per-person annual limits, tariff is zero and import VAT and consumption tax are levied at 70 percent of the statutory rate. And checkout price carries platform commission, 2 to 5 percent on Tmall Global plus a cross-border payment fee, so the margin test belongs in the region decision.

## The county market is a second-wave question, not a first-entry one

**County-level and rural markets are China's consumption outside city districts, measured separately because their growth rate and channel mix now diverge from urban China.** In 2025 they accounted for 38.7 percent of all retail sales, and rural retail grew 4.1 percent against 3.6 percent in cities, with rural online retail passing RMB 3 trillion for the first time ([MOFCOM, 2025 wholesale and retail review](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/syxwfb/art/2026/art_f8416017c8e24d1f83160afcf0303e10.html)).

The number is real and it is regularly misused. County consumption is driven by availability and value-for-money formats, not by the premium, provenance-led positioning an imported brand carries, so county coverage is usually a year-two consequence of platform reach rather than a reason to open a channel. Urbanisation reached 67.89 percent at the end of 2025 ([NBS statistical communiqué, 2025](https://www.stats.gov.cn/xxgk/sjfb/zxfb2020/202601/t20260119_1962330.html)) — a third of the population outside the urban retail footprint, and very few buyers at a premium price point.

## The bonded port decides what you can promise

**A bonded warehouse location is the customs-supervised zone where 1210 retail-import stock is held before an order is placed, used to convert a national market into a delivery promise for a defined geography.** Bonded retail import accounts for more than 90 percent of China's cross-border retail imports, on the customs administration's own account of the 2025 destruction rules for unsold stock (GACC Order No. 79).

Placement is therefore a demand decision, not a logistics afterthought. Three constraints interact: the catchment the port can reach inside the delivery window you will advertise; the category supervision the port holds, since fresh and frozen goods are restricted to bonded retail import and must clear inspection at a designated site; and the return route, because a bonded return that cannot be resold is a write-off rather than a refund.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">5</span><span class="l">Bonded locations in the GOODSINFINITE fulfilment network — Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou and Qingdao — covering the four largest cross-border import destinations plus the northern cold-chain gateway</span><span class="src">Source: GOODSINFINITE operations, 2026</span></div>

Note what the port map and the demand map do and do not share. Four of the five largest destinations are covered by a bonded port in the same province or municipality; the fifth is Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, which carries far less cross-border import value than its population implies. That gap is an opportunity for a northern-first launch and a warning for anyone who assumes northern demand equals northern import volume.

## A two-week method for choosing the first region

**Region selection is the sequence of filters that narrows China from 337 cities to one bonded port and one launch city, used before any inventory commitment is made.** It can be run on public data in about two weeks.

1. Pull the customs destination shares and confirm which ports serve your two candidate regions.
2. Check your category's weight in the import mix — beauty, fragrance and personal care took 27.2 percent of cross-border imports in 2025, food and fresh produce 23.9 percent — and ask whether your category is a leader or a rounding error in each region.
3. Apply the income quintile test to your landed price, not to your home-market price.
4. Verify the port's supervision status for your category, including cold-chain and designated-site requirements.
5. Run a bonded test with a narrow SKU set in one port, then compare conversion, return reason codes and repeat purchase against the second region before scaling.

## How GOODSINFINITE sequences regional entry

GOODSINFINITE acts as importer of record and bonded fulfilment partner, which makes the region question concrete: the first decision we take with a brand is which of the five bonded locations holds the launch stock, because that single choice fixes the delivery promise, the return route and the replenishment cycle. From there the sequence runs category check against the positive list, income-band price test, single-port 1210 launch, then expansion on evidence. For the wider sequence, start with our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) and the [cross-border operations glossary](https://www.goods-infinite.com/glossary.html).

## FAQ

**Which Chinese provinces take the largest share of cross-border e-commerce imports?** In 2025 the top five were Guangdong at 14.8 percent, Jiangsu at 8.6 percent, Zhejiang at 8.5 percent, Shanghai at 6.8 percent and Shandong at 5.6 percent — 44.3 percent of the national total. Read them as infrastructure gravity rather than a consumer census: they record where the consignment is declared and where the bonded operator, importer of record and platform seller sit.

**Should a foreign brand enter the Greater Bay Area or the Yangtze Delta first?** It depends on category depth. The Yangtze Delta — Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang — was 23.9 percent of cross-border imports in 2025 and holds the deepest concentration of beauty, personal-care and premium-food operations. Guangdong alone took 14.8 percent with Hong Kong adjacency, Cantonese content and a strong electronics and fashion base. Choose the region where your category is less crowded and your price band is thicker.

**Are Chinese city tiers a reliable guide to where imported products sell?** No. Yicai's 2025 ranking sorts 337 cities into four tier-1, fifteen new tier-1, thirty tier-2, seventy tier-3, ninety tier-4 and 128 tier-5 cities on commercial-resource density, connectivity and consumer activity. That ranks infrastructure and execution feasibility, not demand for your category at your price.

**How many Chinese households can afford an imported product at a given price?** Use the quintiles. NBS put per-capita disposable income at RMB 43,377 in 2025, with quintile averages from RMB 10,150 to RMB 103,778 and urban income at 2.31 times rural income. The top two quintiles — roughly 40 percent of households — behave like a market for imported goods, and they cluster in the tier-1 and new tier-1 cities.

**Does the bonded warehouse location change what a brand can sell?** Yes. Stock can only promise the delivery window its port catchment supports, and only carry categories that port supervises — fresh and frozen goods are restricted to bonded retail import under 1210 and must clear a designated site. With bonded import above 90 percent of cross-border retail imports, port choice largely sets the service promise and the replenishment cycle.

## China PIPL & Data Compliance for Cross-Border E-Commerce: The 2026 Rules for Foreign Brands
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-pipl-data-compliance-cross-border-ecommerce
Published: 2026-10-21 · Cluster: Compliance & Registration

## Definition: what "China data compliance for cross-border e-commerce" actually means

"China data compliance for cross-border e-commerce" is the set of obligations a foreign brand takes on the moment it **collects, stores, uses or moves out of China the personal information of Chinese buyers** — order data, name, ID number, phone, address, payment and logistics records — in the course of selling into China through bonded (1210) or direct-mail (9610) channels, or through a domestic store once it has a mainland entity.

The critical thing most overseas sellers get wrong: **this is not a "China entity" question.** China's Personal Information Protection Law has explicit extraterritorial reach. If you have no WFOE, no office and no staff in mainland China but you sell to Chinese consumers, PIPL still governs you — and the practical consequence is not just a privacy policy rewrite, but decisions about **where your data sits, what crosses the border, and who in China is answerable for it.**

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 50m / 5%</span><span class="l">The maximum fine for a serious PIPL violation: RMB 50 million or 5% of the previous year's turnover, whichever applies, plus suspension of the relevant business, revocation of the business licence, and RMB 100,000–1,000,000 on the responsible individuals — who can also be barred from serving as a director, supervisor, senior manager or personal information protection officer</span><span class="src">Source: Personal Information Protection Law, Art. 66</span></div>

## Step 1 — Establish whether PIPL reaches you at all

PIPL Article 3 has two limbs:

- **Art. 3(1)** — processing personal information *within* China.
- **Art. 3(2)** — processing the personal information of individuals in China *from outside* China, where the purpose is **(a) providing products or services to individuals in China**, **(b) analysing or assessing their behaviour**, or (c) other circumstances set out in laws and regulations.

A foreign brand selling into China through cross-border e-commerce meets limb (a) by definition. So does running Chinese-language performance marketing, retargeting Chinese audiences, or maintaining a Chinese-language customer database.

> The moment you ship a 1210 order, you are a "personal information processor" under Chinese law. There is no de-minimis threshold, no "we only have 200 customers" carve-out and no "our server is in Frankfurt" defence.

## Step 2 — Work out who holds which role in a cross-border transaction

Chinese law does not treat "the seller" as a single data controller. Under the six-ministry notice that governs cross-border retail imports (商财发〔2018〕486号), a 1210/9610 transaction has four defined participants, each with distinct duties:

| Participant | Who they are | Data / compliance duty |
|---|---|---|
| **Cross-border e-commerce enterprise** | The **overseas-registered** company selling to Chinese consumers; owner of the goods | Bears product-quality and consumer-rights responsibility; **must entrust one mainland-registered enterprise** to register with customs, file truthfully and bear joint and several civil liability |
| **Platform operator** | Mainland-registered marketplace (Tmall Global, JD Worldwide, Douyin cross-border) | Must verify **transaction authenticity and consumer identity authenticity**; transmits order data to customs; bears advance-compensation liability to consumers |
| **Domestic service provider** | Mainland-registered entity providing declaration, payment, logistics or warehousing | Transmits payment/logistics/warehousing data to customs and accepts follow-up supervision |
| **Consumer (ordering person)** | The mainland buyer | Taxpayer for the cross-border order; annual personal allowance is tied to their identity |

Two consequences follow that matter for data governance:

1. **The overseas brand is not "outside the system."** It is a named, responsible participant — it just discharges part of that responsibility through a mainland-registered entrustee.
2. **Identity authenticity is a legal duty on the platform**, not merely a commercial fraud check. 486号文 expressly requires platforms to monitor abnormal trading such as repeated bulk orders by the same purchaser, payment account, delivery address or phone number, and **ordering under a misappropriated identity**.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">100k / 1m / 10k</span><span class="l">China's three-tier personal information export thresholds for a processor that is not a critical information infrastructure operator, counted cumulatively from 1 January of the current year: under 100,000 individuals (non-sensitive) = exempt; 100,000 to under 1,000,000 (or under 10,000 sensitive) = standard contract or certification required; 1,000,000 or more, or 10,000 or more sensitive = mandatory CAC security assessment</span><span class="src">Source: Provisions on Promoting and Regulating Cross-Border Data Flows (CAC Order No. 16), Arts. 5, 7, 8</span></div>

## Step 3 — Map the four data flows in a cross-border order

Most brands only think about flow 4. All four are in scope.

### Flow 1 — Order, payment and logistics data to customs (mandatory, statutory)

Before a cross-border retail import can be declared, the platform or the overseas seller's mainland agent, the payment company and the logistics company must **each** transmit order, payment and logistics electronic data to customs through the International Trade Single Window or a cross-border e-commerce clearance service platform, and each bears responsibility for **data authenticity** (GACC Announcement No. 194 of 2018, s. III(6)). Overseas cross-border e-commerce enterprises must entrust a mainland agent to register with customs in the agent's locality.

This flow contains the buyer's real name, ID number, phone and delivery address. It is not optional and it is not a "marketing" transfer — it is a statutory filing obligation.

### Flow 2 — Buyer identity verification

Customs separately verifies the ordering person's identity. The consumer confirms the transaction in the "掌上海关" (Customs on Hand) or "掌上单一窗口" (Single Window on Hand) mini-program or app by entering name and ID number and passing **face recognition**. The stated legal basis is the Customs Law, GACC Announcement No. 194 of 2018 and the 486号文 notice, and the stated purpose is to prevent identity and annual allowance misappropriation and smuggling through the cross-border channel.

> Practical rule for brands: **do not build your own copy of this.** Face recognition data is biometric information and falls within the sensitive personal information category in PIPL Art. 28, which triggers separate consent and a stricter necessity test. Leave the biometric step to the customs channel.

### Flow 3 — Order fulfilment data back to the overseas brand

This is the flow that crosses the border: the brand's HQ or ERP receives the order, the buyer's name, phone, address, SKU and payment reference so it can pick, pack, invoice and provide after-sales service.

### Flow 4 — CRM, analytics, retargeting and KOL attribution

The highest-risk flow, and the one least likely to qualify for any exemption. Exporting a Chinese buyer profile for global CRM, lookalike audiences, influencer attribution or AI model training has no contract-necessity justification and is counted against the thresholds in Step 4.

## Step 4 — Choose your export gateway (or establish you qualify for the exemption)

PIPL Article 38 requires a processor providing personal information outside China to satisfy one of four conditions: pass a CAC-organised security assessment, obtain personal information protection certification from a professional body, conclude the CAC standard contract with the overseas recipient, or meet other conditions set by law or the regulator.

Since 22 March 2024, CAC Order No. 16 has reorganised which gateway applies — and Order No. 16 Article 13 states that where the earlier measures are inconsistent, **Order No. 16 governs**.

| Cumulative exports since 1 Jan (non-CIIO processor) | Gateway required |
|---|---|
| Contract-necessity transfers (incl. cross-border shopping), **necessary** for a contract with the individual | **Exempt** from all three (Art. 5(1)) |
| Under 100,000 individuals, non-sensitive | **Exempt** (Art. 5(4)) |
| Data collected abroad, processed in China, re-exported **without adding** any China-sourced personal information or important data | **Exempt** (Art. 4) |
| International trade / transport / marketing data containing **no** personal information and no important data | **Exempt** (Art. 3) |
| Within a free trade zone, data **outside** the zone's published negative list | **Exempt** (Art. 6) |
| 100,000 – under 1,000,000 individuals, or under 10,000 sensitive | **Standard contract** *or* **certification** (Art. 8) |
| 1,000,000+ individuals, or 10,000+ sensitive | **CAC security assessment** (Art. 7) |
| Any important data, or any volume if you are a CIIO | **CAC security assessment** (Art. 7) |

### The exemption most cross-border sellers can actually use

Order No. 16 Article 5(1) exempts transfers that are necessary to conclude or perform a contract to which the individual is a party, and the text names **跨境购物 (cross-border shopping)** expressly, alongside cross-border remittance, cross-border payment, ticketing and visa services.

CAC clarified the scope in its October 2025 policy Q&A: the list is **open-ended** ("等" is not exhaustive), but the exemption only holds if **both** conditions are met — (1) the transfer is for concluding or performing a contract to which the individual is a party, and (2) the transfer is genuinely **necessary**, judged against applicable laws, regulations, national standards and the actual export scenario for the minimum necessary scope. The Q&A gave a useful counter-example: a hotel exporting the personal information of a Chinese resident booking a hotel **inside** China does not qualify.

> What this means in practice: the order fulfilment flow (Flow 3) is generally exempt. The CRM and retargeting flow (Flow 4) is not. Run them through separate legal bases and separate systems.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">10 working days / 3 years</span><span class="l">If you use the standard contract route, you must file the contract and the personal information protection impact assessment report with the provincial cyberspace administration within 10 working days of the contract taking effect — and both the assessment report and the processing records must be retained for at least 3 years. An assessment result, once granted, is valid for 3 years and can be extended by a further 3 years on application made at least 60 working days before expiry</span><span class="src">Source: Measures for the Standard Contract for Outbound Personal Information (CAC Order No. 13), Art. 7; PIPL Art. 56; CAC Order No. 16, Art. 9</span></div>

## Step 5 — The obligations that survive every exemption

This is where most compliance programmes fail. Exemption from the *gateway* is not exemption from the *duties*:

- **Article 10 of Order No. 16** — a processor providing personal information overseas must still perform **notification**, obtain the individual's **separate consent**, and conduct a **personal information protection impact assessment (PIPIA)** under PIPL.
- **PIPL Art. 39** — before exporting, you must tell the individual the overseas recipient's name and contact details, the purpose and method of processing, the categories of personal information, and how the individual can exercise their rights against the overseas recipient — and obtain **separate consent**.
- **PIPL Art. 55(4)** — exporting personal information is a listed trigger for a **pre-transfer** PIPIA. Art. 56 requires the assessment to cover legality/lawfulness, the impact on individual rights and security risk, and whether the protective measures are lawful, effective and proportionate.
- **PIPL Art. 38, final paragraph** — you must take necessary measures to ensure the overseas recipient's processing meets PIPL standards.
- **Network Data Security Management Regulation (State Council Order No. 790, in force 1 January 2025), Art. 21** — your personal information processing rules must be **concentrated, publicly displayed, easily accessible and placed in a prominent position**, and must cover the processor's identity and contact details, purposes/methods/categories, retention period and how the individual exercises rights. Where you collect and onward-provide information, the recipients must be **listed in a manifest**.
- **Same Regulation, Art. 22** — sensitive personal information (biometric, religious belief, specific identity, medical health, financial account, location tracking, and information of children under 14) requires **separate consent**; children under 14 require parental or guardian consent and a dedicated processing rule.

## Step 6 — Appoint a China-side representative and file it

If PIPL Article 3(2) catches you, **Article 53** requires you to either establish a dedicated body in China or **designate a representative** responsible for personal information protection, and to file that body's name or the representative's name and contact details with the competent authority.

The Network Data Security Management Regulation Article 26 pins down the filing channel: the report goes to the **cyberspace administration at the level of the city divided into districts** where the body or representative is located, and that department notifies the relevant competent authorities at the same level.

For a foreign brand running a 1210 test with no mainland entity, the practical solution is to make the designated representative function part of the mainland entrustee relationship you already need under 486号文 — the same mainland-registered enterprise that registers with customs and accepts supervision. Do not leave this as an unassigned legal duty sitting with an overseas entity nobody in China can reach.

## Step 7 — Free trade zone negative lists (a real, under-used lever)

Order No. 16 Article 6 lets a free trade zone publish its own **negative list** of data that stays inside the assessment / standard contract / certification regime. **Data outside the list flows freely** — no assessment, no contract, no certification.

**Tianjin was first.** On 9 May 2024 the Tianjin FTZ Administrative Committee and the Tianjin Commerce Bureau published the *China (Tianjin) Pilot Free Trade Zone Data Export Management List (Negative List) (2024 Edition)* — the first such list approved by a provincial cyberspace committee and filed with the national cyberspace and data authorities after Order No. 16 took effect. It covers **13 broad categories and 46 sub-categories** across eight priority sectors including biomedicine, service outsourcing, finance, internet platforms, automotive, integrated circuits, meteorology and international trade, describing each data category's characteristics with concrete examples. Data outside the list may be exported freely; state secrets, core data and government data are excluded from the list regime and follow their own rules.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">13 / 46</span><span class="l">The Tianjin Pilot Free Trade Zone data-export negative list classifies outbound data into 13 broad categories and 46 sub-categories across eight priority sectors. For an enterprise inside the zone, anything not on the list may be exported without a security assessment, standard contract or certification — the list is a clearance tool, not just a restriction</span><span class="src">Source: China (Tianjin) Pilot FTZ Data Export Management List (Negative List) (2024 Edition), published 9 May 2024</span></div>

> Why this matters commercially: routing your China data operations through a Tianjin FTZ entity can convert an uncertain "do we need to file?" question into a documented checklist exercise. It is one of the few places where China's data regime gives a foreign-invested business a *published* answer rather than a judgement call.

## Step 8 — What changed in 2024–2026 (and what changed on 1 January 2026)

China's data regime moved fast. Five changes matter for a cross-border seller:

| Instrument | Effective | What changed for you |
|---|---|---|
| **Provisions on Promoting and Regulating Cross-Border Data Flows** (CAC Order No. 16) | 22 Mar 2024 | Raised thresholds, created the exemptions (incl. cross-border shopping), extended assessment validity to 3 years, created FTZ negative lists; overrides earlier measures where inconsistent |
| **Network Data Security Management Regulation** (State Council Order No. 790) | 1 Jan 2025 | Consolidated network data duties; Arts. 21–22 on transparency and consent; Art. 26 filing channel for the Art. 53 representative; Art. 35 restates the eight export gateways |
| **Measures for Personal Information Protection Compliance Audit** (CAC Order No. 18) | 1 May 2025 | A processor handling **more than 10 million individuals'** personal information must conduct a compliance audit **at least once every two years**; regulators may compel an audit after a breach affecting 1 million+ individuals or 100,000+ sensitive records |
| **Measures for Personal Information Export Certification** (CAC + SAMR Order No. 20) | 1 Jan 2026 | Gives the certification route a dedicated procedure: available to non-CIIO processors exporting 100,000–1,000,000 individuals (non-sensitive) or under 10,000 sensitive; a PIPIA with separate consent still required first; splitting volumes to dodge assessment is prohibited |
| **Cybersecurity Law (as amended)** | 1 Jan 2026 | Adds Art. 42(2): network operators processing personal information must comply with the Cybersecurity Law, the Civil Code and PIPL. Raises penalty ceilings for failing security protection duties — RMB 500,000–2 million where the breach causes mass data loss or partial loss of CII function, RMB 2–10 million for particularly serious consequences |

Note the direction of travel: the **gateways** have been loosened repeatedly since 2024, while the **accountability, transparency and audit** obligations have been tightened. Planning on the assumption that "China relaxed data export" is a mistake — what was relaxed is the filing burden, not the liability.

## The eight-step runbook

1. **Confirm PIPL scope.** If you sell to individuals in China, Art. 3(2) applies. Record the conclusion.
2. **Draw a data map** of all four flows, with field-level detail, recipient, purpose and destination. Most brands discover flows they did not know existed.
3. **Sort each flow into a legal basis.** Order fulfilment → Art. 5(1) contract necessity. CRM/marketing → count it, or stop exporting it.
4. **Count the volume** cumulatively from 1 January of the current year, sensitive and non-sensitive separately. Establish which tier you are in — and re-check at 80% of the threshold.
5. **Fix the front end.** Publish a compliant processing rule (Art. 21 of Order 790), add recipient manifests, and build a **separate consent** flow for exports with the Art. 39 disclosures.
6. **Run the PIPIA before** any export starts, and retain the report and records for at least 3 years.
7. **Appoint and file the representative** under PIPL Art. 53 / Order 790 Art. 26. If you use the standard contract, file within 10 working days of it taking effect.
8. **Decide where the data physically sits.** If you operate in a free trade zone, check the negative list before assuming you need to file.
