## What we deliberately do not assert

We have kept this article to rules we can point to in official text. Three things are commonly claimed in vendor content that we will not repeat without a source:

- **We do not give a fee or timeline for a CAC security assessment.** No official schedule is published and third-party figures vary widely.
- **We do not state that a Chinese ID number is "sensitive personal information."** PIPL Article 28 lists categories; whether a specific field falls in one is an assessment to be made against Art. 28, not an assumption. Biometric data used in the customs face-recognition step *is* within the listed categories.
- **We do not describe any specific enforcement case or fine against a named company** that we cannot source to an official publication.

## FAQ

**Does PIPL apply to me if I have no Chinese entity?** Yes. PIPL Art. 3(2) captures processing of Chinese residents' personal information from outside China where the purpose is providing products or services to them. Cross-border e-commerce selling is squarely within that.

**Do I need a data export security assessment?** Usually not. The cross-border-shopping contract-necessity exemption (CAC Order No. 16, Art. 5(1)) and the under-100,000-individuals exemption cover most brands. Assessment is mandatory above 1 million individuals or 10,000 sensitive records, or for any important data.

**What data goes to Chinese customs?** Order, payment and logistics electronic data, transmitted separately by the platform/agent, the payment company and the logistics company through the Single Window, each responsible for authenticity. Buyer name and ID number are part of that flow, with a separate buyer identity verification done by the consumer in the customs app.

**Do I need a China-based representative?** If PIPL Art. 3(2) applies to you, yes — Art. 53 requires a dedicated body or designated representative in China, filed with the competent authority (Order 790 Art. 26 specifies the municipal-level cyberspace administration).

**If my export is exempt, is there anything left to do?** Yes. Notification, separate consent and a pre-transfer PIPIA still apply under Order No. 16 Art. 10 and PIPL Arts. 39, 55 and 56.

**What are the penalties?** Up to RMB 1 million for an uncorrected violation; for serious cases RMB 50 million or 5% of the previous year's turnover, business suspension and licence revocation, with RMB 100,000–1,000,000 on responsible individuals and a possible management bar.

## China Cross-Border E-Commerce Listings That Convert
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-cross-border-ecommerce-listings
Published: 2026-10-19 · Cluster: E-commerce Operations

## A cross-border product page in China is a regulated document before it is a shop window

**A cross-border product page in China is the web page on which a marketplace sells an imported product to a mainland consumer, used simultaneously as the storefront, the Chinese-language label and the risk disclosure the buyer must accept before the order is placed.** For most foreign brands it is also the only physical presence the brand has in the country — no shelf, no counter, no sales assistant. Everything the shopper can learn, they learn there.

That dual role is what makes listing work in China different from listing work anywhere else. In a cross-border store the page carries legal duties that a paper label would otherwise carry, and it is judged by a shopper who has never heard of the brand and is comparing it against twenty alternatives on the same search results screen.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">27.2%</span><span class="l">Share of China's cross-border e-commerce imports in 2025 taken by beauty, fragrance and personal-care products, the single largest category; food and fresh produce followed at 23.9%</span><span class="src">Source: General Administration of Customs of China, 2025 cross-border e-commerce trade statistics (published June 2026)</span></div>

## What the page must carry, and what it no longer has to

**China's cross-border retail import regime is the set of rules that lets an overseas seller ship directly to a mainland consumer under customs supervision codes 1210 or 9610, and it is defined by Notice 486 of 2018 issued jointly by the Ministry of Commerce, the NDRC, the Ministry of Finance, Customs, the tax administration and the market regulator.** That notice is the reason a foreign brand can sell into China without a local entity, without a first-import licence and without registering the product.

The trade is explicit. Cross-border retail imports are supervised as goods carried in for personal use, and **first-import approval documents, registration and filing requirements do not apply** ([Notice 486, Section 3](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2018-12/31/content_5437823.htm)). What replaces them is a disclosure duty that lands on the seller and the platform: a risk notice must be shown on the order page or another prominent position, and the consumer must confirm it before ordering. The notice must tell the buyer, in substance, that the goods meet the standards of their country of origin but may differ from Chinese standards, and that the goods come directly from overseas, **may carry no Chinese label, and that a Chinese electronic label is available on the website**.

Read that second clause again, because it defines your job. The Chinese label has not been waived; it has been relocated onto the page. Everything a general-trade importer would print on the pack — product name, ingredients, net content, origin, shelf life, usage warnings, manufacturer — has to exist as readable Chinese on the listing.

A 2025 complaint case shows how the boundary is policed in practice. A consumer bought a Japanese toothpaste from a Taobao store fulfilled out of a comprehensive bonded zone and complained that the product had no Chinese label and no filing. The Qingdao consumer council found no violation: the goods were cross-border retail imports, the seller had given the required risk notice and the Chinese electronic label was available online, so the absent paper label was lawful — and the seller still refunded the buyer ([Qingdao Consumer Council, March 2026](https://www.cqn.com.cn/ms/content/2026-03/16/content_9148482.htm)). The lesson is not that the rules are lenient. It is that the file — notice given, label published, evidence kept — is the defence.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">1,476</span><span class="l">Tariff lines on the catalogue of goods permitted for cross-border retail import, the 2022 edition in force since 1 March 2022 — a product outside this list cannot be listed at all</span><span class="src">Source: Catalogue of Cross-Border E-Commerce Retail Import Goods (2022 edition), MOF et al. Announcement No. 7 of 2022</span></div>

## Why a translated listing loses the search before it loses the sale

**A Chinese marketplace listing is a product record built to be matched against Chinese search queries, used to place the item on the results page where the buying decision is actually made.** Translation preserves meaning and destroys matching. The English title describes the product in the order the source market thinks about it; the Chinese shopper types a category word, an attribute and sometimes a scenario, in that order, often without the brand.

Three mechanics matter. Chinese is written without spaces, so the search engine segments the query itself and rewards titles that contain the exact category term as a contiguous string. Compound category nouns are standard — a product is a "facial essence" or a "sunscreen stick" before it is a product name. And the demand pool is no longer growing: China had 976 million online shoppers in June 2025, up 0.1 percent in six months at 86.9 percent penetration ([CNNIC, 56th Statistical Report](https://www.cnnic.net.cn/NMediaFile/2025/0730/MAIN1753846666507QEK67ZS9DH.pdf)). A new brand does not get new shoppers; it takes a share of an existing results page.

That is why the first listing decision is not the translation but the category. Pick the leaf category a Chinese shopper would search, not the one that best describes the product in your home market, then build the title from the terms that category actually receives. Brands that skip this step get listings that read well and rank nowhere.

## The listing architecture that converts

**A converting cross-border listing is an ordered set of answer blocks, used to move a shopper from a search result to a confirmed order without leaving the page.** The order matters: shoppers scan the title, then the main image, then price and reviews, then the detail page — and abandon at the first block that fails to answer the question in their head.

<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Block</th><th>The question it must answer</th><th>Legal hook</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Title</td><td>Is this the thing I searched for?</td><td>Category term must be accurate; no superlatives</td></tr>
<tr><td>Main image set</td><td>What do I actually receive?</td><td>Image must match the goods; no implied extras</td></tr>
<tr><td>Price and tax line</td><td>What do I pay at checkout?</td><td>Cross-border import tax must be shown, not hidden</td></tr>
<tr><td>Electronic Chinese label</td><td>What is in it and how do I use it?</td><td>Notice 486 electronic label duty</td></tr>
<tr><td>Risk notice and confirmation</td><td>Do I accept cross-border terms?</td><td>Notice 486 disclosure, accepted before order</td></tr>
<tr><td>Detail page</td><td>Why this one rather than the alternative?</td><td>Article 17 disclosure; Article 28 no false claims</td></tr>
<tr><td>After-sales terms</td><td>What if it goes wrong?</td><td>Return window and bonded-return route</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

The title follows a simple ladder: category term first, then the one or two attributes that separate your product from the cheapest alternative, then the scenario, and the brand name last unless it is already known in China. The detail page should be built as objection handling rather than brand storytelling — origin and authenticity, texture or taste, size against a familiar reference, who it is for, what it will not do, and how to use it. The block most often missing is the sixth: stating plainly what the product is not for. It reduces returns and is what Article 17 disclosure looks like done well.

## Five words that get a listing taken down

**China's advertising rules for e-commerce listings are the statutory limits on what a product page may claim, used by the market regulator to police both exaggeration and concealment.** Two statutes apply at once, and a page can breach either.

Article 9 of the Advertising Law prohibits wording such as national-level, highest-grade, best, top or number one, which rules out most of the vocabulary a Western brand's copywriter would reach for ([Advertising Law, mofcom](https://policy.mofcom.gov.cn/claw/clawContent.shtml?id=90361)). Article 11 requires any cited figure, survey or ranking to name its source and validity period. Article 28 defines a false advertisement to include omitting material information — so "大字宣传、小字提醒", promoting a headline benefit in large type while qualifying it in fine print, is a disclosure failure rather than a styling choice.

Alongside this sits Article 17 of the E-commerce Law, which requires product information to be disclosed **comprehensively, truthfully, accurately and in a timely way**, and prohibits fabricated transactions and invented reviews ([E-commerce Law, NPC](http://www.npc.gov.cn/zgrdw/npc/xinwen/lfgz/2018-09/18/content_2061389.htm)). The practical translation for a foreign brand's listing is unglamorous: name the source of every percentage, delete the words that cannot be proved, print the qualification next to the claim rather than under it, and treat the page as an evidentiary record.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">3 years</span><span class="l">Minimum retention period for advertising records under China's Internet Advertising Measures, counted from the end of the publication — the page copy, the evidence behind each claim and the review trail</span><span class="src">Source: SAMR Order No. 72, Internet Advertising Measures, in force 1 May 2023</span></div>

## Reviews, seeding and the disclosure line

**Seeding is the Chinese practice of paying creators and ordinary users to publish product experiences before a brand runs any advertising, used to make a product look already adopted when a shopper first encounters it.** It works, and it is the part of listing operations most likely to be done illegally.

The Internet Advertising Measures require internet advertising to be identifiable, and specifically require content in the form of knowledge introduction, experience sharing or consumption review that carries a purchase link to be **marked prominently as advertising** ([SAMR Order No. 72](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2023/issue_10506/202306/content_6885261.html)). Buying upvotes or manipulating rankings is separately prohibited under the internet content governance rules. For a cross-border brand the operating rule is that paid seeding with a link is advertising from the first post and must be labelled as such, while unpaid organic posts by real customers are not — and a listing whose review base was manufactured fails the E-commerce Law test the moment a competitor or a regulator looks.

## What to measure once the page is live

**Listing measurement is the practice of tracking whether a product page is findable and persuasive separately, used to decide whether to change the title, the images or the price.** Most brands collapse the two into a single conversion rate and then guess.

Track three numbers. Search impression share on your two or three target category terms tells you whether the listing exists as far as shoppers are concerned. Product-page conversion rate tells you whether the page answers the objection once found. Return and complaint reason codes tell you where the page over-promised. Agency-quoted benchmarks put marketplace search conversion at roughly 3 to 6 percent, but those figures are directional and unpublished, so the only meaningful comparison is your own page before and after a single change.

## How GOODSINFINITE builds and holds the page

At GOODSINFINITE the listing is treated as an operational deliverable rather than a translation job. As importer of record and bonded fulfilment partner we hold the customs registration, the positive-list check, the electronic Chinese label build and the risk-notice record; the brand keeps ownership of the store, the creative and the customer data. The workflow starts from the category a Chinese shopper would actually search, then produces the title ladder, the label page and the evidence file behind every claim, because the same document that converts a shopper also answers a regulator. For the wider sequence this page sits inside, start with our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) and the [cross-border operations glossary](https://www.goods-infinite.com/glossary.html).

## FAQ

**Does an imported product sold through a cross-border store need a paper Chinese label?** Not on the physical pack, but the information cannot be missing. Notice 486 of 2018 regulates cross-border retail imports as goods carried in for personal use, so a paper Chinese label is not compulsory and first-import licences, registration or filing are not required. In exchange the seller must give the consumer a risk disclosure on the order page — including that the goods may carry no Chinese label but that a Chinese electronic label can be viewed on the website — and the consumer must accept it before ordering. That electronic label lives on your product page.

**Is a cross-border product page treated as advertising under Chinese law?** Yes, and more than that. Article 17 of the E-commerce Law requires operators to disclose product information comprehensively, truthfully, accurately and in a timely way, and bars fabricated transactions or invented reviews. Page copy that promotes a product is also commercial advertising, so the Advertising Law applies: Article 9 bans superlatives, Article 11 requires cited data to state its source and validity period, and Article 28 defines false advertising. A page can fail on two independent tests — incomplete disclosure and unlawful claims.

**Why do translated listings underperform on Tmall Global and Douyin?** Because Chinese shoppers search by category and attribute, not by a brand name they have never seen. A literal translation keeps the source-market word order and product naming, which rarely match what is typed into a platform search box. Chinese also does not rely on spaces, so the engine infers word boundaries itself; attribute order and the presence of the category term matter more than in English. Rebuild the title from Chinese search demand data instead.

**How many keywords should a cross-border listing title carry?** One primary category term, one or two attribute terms and one scenario — no more. Platform titles are short, and padding them with synonyms crowds out the terms that carry real search volume. Stuffing also creates advertising-law risk, because a title claiming several incompatible benefits can read as misleading under Article 28. Judge the title by whether the right product appears for the two or three searches that matter.

**What should a foreign brand measure after a listing goes live?** Search impression share on the category terms you targeted, product-page conversion rate, and return or complaint rate by reason code. Impression share says whether the listing is findable, conversion says whether the page answers the objection, and reason codes say whether the page over-promised. Agency benchmarks put marketplace search conversion at roughly 3 to 6 percent, but those are directional, so compare your own page before and after a change.

## Product Recall and SAMR Enforcement in China: What Happens If Your Product Is Non-Compliant
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-product-recall-samr-enforcement
Published: 2026-10-19 · Cluster: Compliance & Registration

## In China a recall is a statutory duty that attaches to whoever the law calls the producer — and for an imported product that is usually a party inside China

**If you take one thing from this page, take this: a Chinese recall is not a customer-service decision that your headquarters makes and your distributor executes.** It is a set of hard, dated legal obligations created by four parallel regulatory regimes plus the Civil Code, and each one of them identifies a responsible party by legal status rather than by brand ownership. In roughly every import scenario, that party is a Chinese entity — an importer, a designated agent, a China-based service provider or a marketing authorisation holder's agent — not the foreign manufacturer.

That single structural fact explains why foreign brands get caught out. The brand assumes a recall is something it decides. Chinese law treats it as something a domestic party must perform on a deadline, with a regulator watching, and with a penalty attaching if that party does not move.

> The defect is rarely what costs you. The cost is what happens after you know about the defect and fail to act inside the statutory window.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">89.7% / 86.7%</span><span class="l">In 2025, 970 of the 1,081 consumer product recalls carried out in China — 89.7% — were influenced by a market regulator's defect investigation rather than initiated by the brand; and 86.7% of the units recalled (7.140 million) were recalled for standard-conformity problems, not for dramatic safety failures</span><span class="src">Source: SAMR Notice on National Motor Vehicle and Consumer Product Recalls in 2025 (2026 No. 2), 19 March 2026</span></div>

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">2 working days</span><span class="l">How long you have to report to the provincial market regulator after discovering that a product has caused or may cause death, serious injury or major property loss — or that a recall is being carried out outside China. An overseas recall is itself a mandatory China reporting trigger</span><span class="src">Source: Interim Provisions on the Administration of Consumer Product Recalls (SAMR Order No. 19), Art. 8</span></div>

## The five regimes — and which one governs your product

China has no single recall law. It has five parallel tracks, split by product, and each has its own regulator, its own definition of "producer" and its own clock.

| Product | Governing instrument | Who is deemed responsible |
|---|---|---|
| **Consumer products** (anything bought for household consumption) | [Interim Provisions on the Administration of Consumer Product Recalls](https://www.samr.gov.cn:8020/zw/zfxxgk/fdzdgknr/fgs/art/2023/art_39e525ea64cf4b90b8d0c7acd790946d.html) — SAMR Order No. 19, published 21 November 2019, **in force 1 January 2020** | The producer. **Art. 29:** for imported consumer products, the institution designated by the overseas producer to carry out recalls in China is deemed the producer; **if none is designated, the importer is deemed the producer** |
| **Motor vehicles and trailers** | [Regulations on the Administration of the Recall of Defective Motor Vehicle Products](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2019/content_5468948.htm) — State Council Order No. 626, published 22 October 2012, in force 1 January 2013, revised 2 March 2019 | **Art. 8:** an enterprise established in China that issues the certificate of conformity in its own name — and **an enterprise importing motor vehicles into China for sale is deemed the producer** |
| **Food and food additives** | [Food Recall Administrative Measures](https://www.samrdprc.org.cn/fgbz/gnfg/fg/art/2015/art_0c0c67c331c34431be9fbd65a78b3aa.html) — SAMR Order No. 122, adopted 26 January 2026, published 27 January 2026, **in force 1 December 2026** (replacing the 2015 measures, former CFDA Order No. 12) | The food production or trading operator. **Art. 8:** for contract manufacture, the **principal** carries out the recall and the contractor cooperates |
| **Drugs** | [Drug Recall Administrative Measures](https://www.nmpa.gov.cn/yaowen/ypjgyw/ypyw/20221026172437143.html) — NMPA, published 26 October 2022, **in force 1 November 2022** | The **marketing authorisation holder**. For overseas-produced drugs recalled in China, the **China-designated agent of the overseas MAH organises** the recall |
| **Medical devices** | [Medical Device Recall Administrative Measures](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2017/content_5216439.htm) — former CFDA Order No. 29, published 25 January 2017, **in force 1 May 2017** | **Art. 3:** the domestic registrant or filer, **or the China-designated agent of the overseas manufacturer of an imported device** |

Two things follow from that table. First, if you sell more than one product type you are running more than one recall policy. Second, in four of the five rows, the entity the regulator will call is the one you appointed or relied on inside China — which is precisely why the appointment needs to be made deliberately, in writing, before anything goes wrong.

## The base layer: the Civil Code and the Consumer Rights Protection Law

Everything above sits on two general obligations that apply regardless of product category.

**Article 1206 of the Civil Code** (in force 1 January 2021) states that where a defect is discovered after a product has entered circulation, the **producer and the seller must promptly take remedial measures such as halting sales, issuing warnings and carrying out a recall**; where they fail to act promptly or their measures are inadequate and the damage expands, they bear tort liability for the expanded damage as well. Where a recall is carried out, the producer and the seller must bear the necessary expenses incurred by the injured party. **Article 1207** then adds punitive damages where a party knowingly produced or sold a defective product, or failed to take effective remedial measures, causing death or serious harm to health.

**Article 19 of the Consumer Rights Protection Law** is the mirror-image duty for operators: on discovering that a product supplied is defective and poses a danger to personal or property safety, the operator must **immediately report to the competent administrative department and inform consumers**, and take measures including halting sales, warnings, recall, harmless disposal, destruction and halting production — and where a recall is carried out, the operator must bear the consumers' necessary expenses.

Note what neither article says: nothing here lets a brand decide whether to recall. The duty attaches on discovery.

## The consumer goods track — the one most foreign brands are actually on

Most overseas consumer brands selling physical goods in China fall under SAMR Order No. 19. The mechanics matter more than the principles.

**What counts as a defect.** Article 3 defines a consumer product as a product purchased or used by a consumer for household consumption, and a **defect (缺陷)** as an unreasonable danger to personal or property safety that exists **across a whole batch, model or category** — arising from design, manufacture or warnings. This is the critical difference from Anglo-American practice: a one-off faulty unit is a warranty issue; a systematic problem is a defect, and only defects trigger this regime.

**What counts as a recall.** Also Article 3: supplementary or corrected warning labels, repair, replacement, return — any measure that eliminates the defect or reduces the safety risk. Recalls in China are frequently label-and-warning fixes, not product returns.

**The mandatory reporting triggers (Article 8).** Producers and other operators must report to the provincial market regulator in their locality **within 2 working days** of discovering either that the product has caused or may cause death, serious personal injury or major property loss, **or that a recall is being carried out outside China**. That second limb catches brands that run a global recall and assume China is covered by the press release. It is not.

**The investigation.** Article 9 requires the producer to organise an investigation and analysis immediately on discovering a possible defect. If the provincial regulator spots the possible defect first, it must notify the producer within 3 working days of discovery, and the producer must report the results back.

**Defect investigation by the regulator (Articles 10–12).** If the producer fails to investigate as notified, or the regulator considers the results insufficient to show there is no defect, the regulator organises a defect investigation. It can enter premises, copy documents and records, interview parties, commission technical analysis and risk assessment, and — if necessary — summon the producer for a meeting.

**Objection (Article 13).** A producer who disagrees has **10 working days** from receipt of the recall notice to raise an objection with supporting materials. The regulator then examines them and, if necessary, commissions testing, inspection, appraisal or expert论证, and notifies the outcome.

**Ordered recall (Article 14).** Where a producer neither recalls as notified nor objects within the deadline, or where a defect is confirmed after appraisal and it still does not recall, **SAMR itself orders the recall**, and the producer must carry it out immediately.

**The recall itself (Articles 15–21).** The producer must immediately stop production, sale and import of the defective consumer product and notify other operators to stop trading — and must bear consumers' necessary expenses arising from the recall (Article 15). Other operators must stop trading and assist (Article 16). The recall plan goes to the provincial regulator **within 10 working days** of concluding a defect exists in a voluntary recall, within 10 working days of receiving the regulator's notice in a notified recall, and to **SAMR** within 10 working days of being ordered to recall (Article 17). The regulator publishes the plan via the consumer product recall information system, and the producer must **publish the recall information publicly within 3 working days** of filing the plan and accept public enquiries; other operators must display it in stores and on websites (Article 19). Progress summaries go in **every 3 months**, a final summary within **15 working days** of completion, and **recall records must be kept for at least 5 years** (Article 21).

**Penalties.** Article 25: breaches of Articles 8(1), 11(2), 15–17, 19(2), 20 or 21 draw an order to rectify from the provincial regulator and, if unrectified, a fine of **RMB 10,000 to 30,000**. Article 24 is the serious one: **a producer that still refuses or delays after being ordered to recall is dealt with under Article 56 of the Consumer Rights Protection Law** — which permits confiscation of unlawful gains, a fine of **one to ten times** those gains (or up to **RMB 500,000** where there are none), and in serious cases an order to suspend business for rectification or revocation of the business licence. Article 27 then requires the ordered recall and the administrative penalty to be **entered into the credit file and published by law**, and Article 28 makes clear a recall does not discharge any other liability.

## The motor vehicle track — where "importer" literally means "producer"

If you bring vehicles into China for sale, Article 8 of State Council Order No. 626 does the work: the producer is the enterprise established in China that issues the certificate of conformity in its own name, and **an enterprise importing motor vehicle products into China for onward sale is deemed that producer**. There is no separate importer liability question; the importer *is* the producer.

The regime is the strictest of the five. Records of design, manufacture, marking, inspection and first-owner information must be kept **at least 10 years** (Article 9), and information filed with the regulator includes **recalls carried out outside China** (Article 10(4)). On confirming a defect, the producer must immediately stop production, sale and import and carry out the recall (Article 12). Objections run **15 working days** (Article 15).

Under the [Implementing Measures](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/2020-11/03/content_5723712.htm), the recall plan must be filed **within 5 working days** of confirming the defect or of being ordered to recall (Article 24); the information must be published **within 5 working days** of filing and owners notified by registered post **within 30 working days** (Article 26); recall records must be kept **at least 10 years** (Article 29); progress reports go in **every 3 months** with a final report within **15 working days** (Article 30); and a vehicle whose defect has not been eliminated **may not be sold or delivered for use** (Article 33).

The penalties are calibrated in three tiers: **RMB 50,000–200,000** for record-keeping, filing and reporting failures (Article 22); **RMB 500,000 to 1,000,000** plus confiscation of unlawful gains and possible licence revocation for refusing to cooperate with a defect investigation, failing to implement a filed plan, or failing to notify sellers (Article 23); and — the one to note — **a fine of 1% to 10% of the value of the defective motor vehicles**, plus confiscation and possible licence revocation, for failing to stop production, sale or import of defective vehicles, **concealing a defect**, or **refusing to recall after being ordered to** (Article 24). A percentage-of-value penalty on a vehicle fleet is a different order of exposure from a fixed administrative fine.

## The food track — and the 1 December 2026 change

Food recall is governed by the Food Safety Law and, from **1 December 2026**, by a fully rewritten set of measures.

**Article 63 of the Food Safety Law** (2025 revision) establishes the recall system: a food producer discovering that its food does not meet food safety standards, or that there is evidence it may harm human health, must immediately stop production, recall food already on the market, notify relevant operators and consumers, and record the recall and notification. Operators must immediately stop trading. Recalled food must be rendered harmless or destroyed so it cannot re-enter the market — with a narrow carve-out letting a producer whose food was recalled for a **label, mark or instruction manual** failure sell it on after remedial measures, provided food safety is assured and the remedy is disclosed to consumers. Recall and disposal must be reported to the county-level market regulator, which may supervise on site, and where an operator fails to recall or stop trading, the regulator at county level or above **may order it to do so**.

**SAMR Order No. 122** (adopted 26 January 2026, published 27 January 2026, in force 1 December 2026, replacing former CFDA Order No. 12 of 2015) rebuilds the procedure around three grades:

| Grade | Trigger (Art. 9) | Start-up deadline from discovering the risk (Art. 11) | Completion from filing the plan (Art. 15) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Grade one** | May cause acute poisoning, sub-acute poisoning, serious harm to health, or death | **24 hours** | Within **10 days** |
| **Grade two** | May cause chronic poisoning or general harm to health | **36 hours** | Within **20 days** |
| **Grade three** | Other cases of non-conformity with food safety standards | **48 hours** | Within **30 days** |

The start-up deadlines are the headline change: the current 2015 measures run at 24 / 48 / 72 hours, and the 2026 rewrite compresses grades two and three to **36 and 48 hours**. Article 24 adds process reporting — a **daily** report for grade one, every **5 days** for grade two and every **10 days** for grade three, with a final report within **5 days** of completion. Article 23 sets record retention at no less than **6 months after the end of shelf life and no less than 2 years**. Article 19 obliges third-party online food platforms that become aware that a listed product is within recall scope to take the necessary measures to stop it continuing to sell on the platform and to press the seller to publish the recall notice prominently.

Penalties split three ways: **Article 33** — a producer or operator that still refuses to recall after being ordered to is punished under **Article 124(9) of the Food Safety Law**, which carries confiscation of unlawful gains and the food, plus RMB 50,000–100,000 where the value is under RMB 10,000 and **ten to twenty times the value** where it exceeds that, with licence revocation in serious cases. **Article 34** — failing to start within the deadline, or to prepare the plan, issue notices or announcements, keep records or report, draws an order to rectify and, if unrectified, **RMB 5,000 to 50,000**. **Article 36** is the commercial lever: a party that recalls and disposes of food **voluntarily may by law be given a lighter or reduced penalty, or no penalty at all**, while recall never discharges other liability. Article 29 puts ordered recalls and recall penalties into the credit file and publishes them through the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System.

## Drugs and medical devices — where the China agent is the addressee

Both regimes place the obligation on a designated China party, and both define the overseas recall as a reporting event.

**Drugs.** Under the [Drug Recall Administrative Measures](https://www.nmpa.gov.cn/yaowen/ypjgyw/ypyw/20221026172437143.html) (NMPA, in force 1 November 2022), the **marketing authorisation holder** is the party responsible for controlling risk and eliminating hazards; manufacturers, distributors and users must assist. Recalls are graded: **grade one** where use has caused or may cause serious harm to health; **grade two** where the harm is temporary or reversible; **grade three** where use would generally not cause harm but the product must be recovered for other reasons. On deciding to recall, the MAH must immediately publish recall information via its own website or industry media, and for **grade one and grade two** must also apply to have it published on the provincial drug regulator's website, which links to the NMPA site (Article 15). Notification must reach manufacturers, distributors and users **within 1, 3 or 7 days** by grade (Article 16), and progress is reported **daily, every 3 days or every 7 days** by grade (Article 17). Records must be kept **5 years and not less than 1 year after the expiry of the drug's shelf life**. Recalled drugs in principle may not return to market. For **overseas-produced drugs**, recalls to be carried out in China are organised by the **China-designated agent of the overseas MAH**.

**Medical devices.** Under [former CFDA Order No. 29](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2017/content_5216439.htm) (in force 1 May 2017), Article 3 defines the production enterprise as the domestic registrant or filer — **or, for an imported device, the China-designated agent of the overseas manufacturer**. Article 6 is the key operational rule: that agent must **promptly report** recalls carried out **only** outside China, and must **organise and implement** any recall that involves action inside China. Recalls are graded the same three ways as drugs, with notification to operators, users or consumers within **1, 3 or 7 days**. A production enterprise that refuses to recall is punished under Article 66 of the Medical Device Supervision and Administration Regulation — confiscation of the devices, a fine of RMB 20,000–50,000 where the value is under RMB 10,000 and **five to ten times the value** where it exceeds that, and in serious cases an order to suspend production or business and ultimately revocation of the registration certificate. Distributors and users that refuse to cooperate face a warning, an order to rectify and, if they still refuse, a fine of up to RMB 30,000.

## The cross-border e-commerce overlay — the 2026 rules that matter most to importers

This is the layer that foreign brands most often miss, because bonded cross-border imports (1210) feel like a different world from general trade. They are not, for recall purposes.

**The 2018 base rule.** The six-ministry [Notice on Improving the Supervision of Cross-Border E-Commerce Retail Imports](https://swj.guilin.gov.cn/zwgk/fdzdgknr/tzgg/t26886179.shtml) (商财发〔2018〕486号) allocates responsibility by role. The **cross-border e-commerce enterprise** bears primary responsibility for product quality and safety, must entrust a domestically registered enterprise to register with customs and bear truthful declaration responsibility, and **bears joint and several civil liability**. Its consumer-protection responsibilities expressly include **establishing a recall system for substandard or defective goods**, and on discovering a quality or safety risk it must **immediately stop selling, recall goods already sold, dispose of them properly so they cannot re-enter the market, and promptly report the recall and disposal to customs and other regulators**. Platforms must press sellers to recall and may **suspend a seller's cross-border e-commerce business** for failing to recall voluntarily.

**The 2025 consumer goods rule.** SAMR [Announcement No. 21 of 2025](https://www.samrdprc.org.cn/fgbz/gnfg/fg/art/2025/art_4877fde1545c49b18eef1806f521e069.html) (12 June 2025) on strengthening recall supervision of consumer products sold online adds the provision that matters commercially. **Article 6: a domestic service provider registered in China and engaged in cross-border e-commerce retail-import consumer product business under entrustment from a cross-border e-commerce enterprise is deemed the importer of the consumer product, or the institution designated by the overseas producer to carry out recalls in China, and bears the recall obligation.** Read together with Article 29 of SAMR Order No. 19, this closes the gap: if no one has been designated, the importer carries the duty — and for cross-border retail imports, the mainland service provider is now deemed to be that importer. Anyone acting as that service provider is accepting a statutory recall duty by operation of law, whether or not the contract says so.

**The 2026 food rule.** SAMR and MOFCOM [Announcement No. 1 of 2026](https://www.samr.gov.cn/zw/zfxxgk/fdzdgknr/spcjs/art/2026/art_b0bcafe73bf747279b27cef39d04e6b1.html) (signed 7 January 2026, published 13 February 2026) tightens food further. The cross-border e-commerce enterprise bears primary responsibility for the safety of retail-imported food and **must entrust a domestic food production or trading enterprise (the entrusted enterprise) to handle recalls**, define the recall process, and **file that enterprise's details with the platform**. On discovering a risk it must immediately stop selling and instruct the entrusted enterprise to recall. The platform must supervise and **suspend platform services to any seller that does not voluntarily recall**. Parties that fail to perform these obligations are dealt with strictly by law and **referred for inclusion in credit management**.

Practically: if you sell food into China through the bonded cross-border channel, you now need a named mainland food enterprise with a defined recall process on file with your platform — before the first order ships, not after a problem surfaces.

## What actually triggers a recall in China — the 2025 evidence

The official statistics are the most useful risk-calibration tool available, and they point somewhere most brands do not expect.

SAMR's [Notice on National Motor Vehicle and Consumer Product Recalls in 2025](https://www.samrdprc.org.cn/xwdt/gzdt/202603/t20260320_115273.html) (2026 No. 2, 19 March 2026) records **1,081 consumer product recalls covering 8.236 million units** in 2025 — down 1.7% in number but **up 81.3% in units** on 2024, with cumulative totals of 7,066 recalls and 113 million units since the regime began. Two lines inside that data should reset how a foreign brand plans:

- **970 of 1,081 recalls (89.7%)** — covering 5.609 million units, 68.1% of the total — were **recalls influenced by a market regulator's defect investigation**. Voluntary, brand-initiated recalls are the minority. The regulator is the usual initiator.
- **86.7% of recalled units (7.140 million, across 1,061 recalls) were recalled for 标准符合性问题 — failure to conform to Chinese mandatory standards.** By defect cause, manufacturing accounted for 87.2% of units, marking and labelling for 11.1%, and design for only 1.7%.

The picture for motor vehicles is similar in shape: **190 recalls covering 6.846 million vehicles**, with 55 recalls covering 2.934 million vehicles (42.9%) influenced by SAMR supervision, and cumulative totals of 3,265 recalls and 121 million vehicles.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">7,066 / 1.13亿件</span><span class="l">Cumulative Chinese consumer product recalls by the end of 2025: 7,066 recall actions covering 113 million units — recall is a mature, routinely applied regulatory instrument, not an exceptional event. Regulators received 37,000 consumer defect reports in 2025 alone</span><span class="src">Source: SAMR Notice on National Motor Vehicle and Consumer Product Recalls in 2025 (2026 No. 2)</span></div>

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">6,000㎡ + 8,000㎡</span><span class="l">Bonded warehousing and temperature- and humidity-controlled warehousing operated through our network, alongside 300+ enterprises served and our own AEO advanced certification plus 15 partner AEO facilities — the physical infrastructure that determines whether recalled stock can actually be segregated, quarantined and accounted for</span><span class="src">Source: GOODSINFINITE operations</span></div>

The operational reading is straightforward. Most China recalls are **conformity failures found by a regulator**, not heroic safety interventions by brands. That means the highest-return investment is not a crisis plan — it is pre-shipment conformity checking against Chinese GB standards, and a documented defect-information collection and analysis system, which Article 7 of SAMR Order No. 19 already requires you to have.

## The penalty ladder at a glance

| Conduct | Consumer products | Motor vehicles | Food | Medical devices |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Procedural failures (records, filing, plan, publication, reports) | Order to rectify; **RMB 10,000–30,000** if unrectified (Art. 25) | Rectify; **RMB 50,000–200,000** if refused (Art. 22) | Rectify; **RMB 5,000–50,000** if unrectified (Art. 34) | — |
| Failing to stop sale / production / import, or not eliminating the defect | Same as above | — | — | — |
| Refusing to cooperate with a defect investigation | Rectify; **RMB 50,000–1,000,000** for non-cooperation with investigation (motor vehicles, Art. 23) | | | Warning, rectify, up to **RMB 30,000** (distributors/users) |
| **Refusing or delaying an ordered recall** | Routed to **Consumer Rights Protection Law Art. 56**: confiscation of gains, **1–10× gains** (or up to **RMB 500,000**), suspension for rectification or **licence revocation** in serious cases | **1%–10% of the value of the defective vehicles** (Art. 24) + confiscation + possible revocation | **Food Safety Law Art. 124(9)**: RMB 50,000–100,000 under RMB 10,000 value, **10–20× value** above it; licence revocation in serious cases | **Regulation Art. 66**: confiscation; RMB 20,000–50,000 under RMB 10,000 value, **5–10× value** above it; suspension or revocation in serious cases |
| Collateral consequences | **Credit file entry and public disclosure** (Art. 27) | Published by the regulator (Art. 18) | **Credit file + National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System** (Art. 29) | Published |
| Civil exposure | **Civil Code Art. 1206** — liability for expanded damage; **Art. 1207** punitive damages; **Consumer Rights Protection Law Art. 19** (consumer expenses) and **Art. 55(2)** (up to **2× the loss** where a defect is knowingly supplied causing death or serious harm) | | | |

## A recall runbook that fits the Chinese deadlines

1. **Decide who the addressee is, in writing.** Under Art. 29 of SAMR Order No. 19 (or the relevant regime), name the institution that will perform recalls in China. If you do not, the importer is deemed the producer by default — and you will have no control over who that turns out to be.
2. **Stand up the defect-information system now.** Article 7 requires producers and operators to have a system for collecting, verifying and analysing defect information. Regulators ask for it during an investigation, and its absence is itself a breach.
3. **Check the 2-working-day trigger on every overseas recall.** Any recall you run elsewhere is a China reporting event. Build it into the global recall checklist, not the China-specific one.
4. **Know your grade thresholds before the incident.** For food, the 24 / 36 / 48-hour start-up clocks under SAMR Order No. 122 begin when you discover the risk, not when you finish investigating.
5. **Prefill the recall plan template.** Article 18 (consumer products) and Article 12 (food) both list required contents: scope, defect, emergency measures, specific measures, responsible unit, contact details, timetable. Drafting these under a 10-working-day deadline is where brands lose time.
6. **Line up the physical side.** Recalled stock must be segregated, prevented from re-entering the market, and either remediated or destroyed with records kept — 5 years for consumer goods, 10 years for vehicles. In a bonded 1210 model, plan how recalled inventory moves out of bonded status.
7. **Remember the upside.** Article 36 of the food measures and the general structure of the consumer goods regime both reward a voluntary recall: prompt, self-initiated action is the single most reliable way to keep an incident in the administrative-fine band rather than the ordered-recall band.

## Where this sits in the wider compliance picture

Recall is the back end of a chain that starts with product classification and conformity. If you have not yet established which agency regulates your product, start there — [Which Chinese Agency Regulates My Product?](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/which-chinese-agency-regulates-my-product.html) maps GACC, SAMR, NMPA and CNCA. If your concern is who carries import liability before anything goes wrong, [Importing Into China Without a Local Company](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/importing-into-china-without-a-local-company.html) and [Hong Kong Entity for China Import](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/hong-kong-entity-china-import.html) set out the importer-of-record structures that also determine who the regulator will call in a recall. For the bonded channel specifically, [What Is 1210 Bonded Import?](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/what-is-1210-bonded-import.html) explains the customs model that the 2026 cross-border recall rules now sit on top of, and [China Import Product Labelling Requirements](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-import-product-labelling-requirements.html) covers the marking failures that account for 11.1% of recalled units by defect cause.

## Cold-Chain Storage in China Bonded Warehouses
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-cold-chain-warehousing
Published: 2026-10-16 · Cluster: Logistics & Distribution

## A cold-chain warehouse in China is a compliance asset first and a logistics asset second

**A cold-chain warehouse in China is a temperature-controlled storage facility licensed and equipped to hold food inside a legally defined temperature band, used to keep imported food safe between the port and the buyer.** That band is not a commercial promise negotiated with a 3PL. It is set by a mandatory national standard, enforced by two regulators on opposite sides of the border.

> Cold-chain storage is the one part of a China import plan where the cheapest option is the most likely to destroy the consignment.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">-18°C / 0–10°C</span><span class="l">The temperature limits China's mandatory food cold-chain standard sets for frozen and chilled food respectively, applying to both transport and storage; transit temperatures must be logged at intervals of no more than 10 minutes</span><span class="src">Source: GB 31605-2020, Food Safety National Standard — Hygiene Specification for Food Cold Chain Logistics, issued 11 September 2020, in force 11 March 2021</span></div>

## The two numbers that govern every frozen and chilled consignment

**GB 31605-2020 is a mandatory food-safety national standard, issued jointly by the National Health Commission and the State Administration for Market Regulation on 11 September 2020 and in force since 11 March 2021, that fixes the temperature, monitoring, handover and documentation requirements for food cold-chain logistics.**

- **Frozen food: no higher than -18°C. Chilled food: 0°C to 10°C** — in transport and in storage, unless the label or category standard sets a tighter band.
- Transport temperature must be monitored continuously, ideally at intervals no longer than 10 minutes; cold-store records at intervals no longer than 30 minutes.
- On handover the outer carton's surface temperature is measured; if it is out of range, the **core** temperature is measured too.
- Goods sit at least **10 cm** clear of walls and floor, batches stacked separately.

The duty sits in the Food Safety Law. Article 33(6) requires equipment used to store, transport and load food to meet the food-safety temperature and humidity requirements, and the next paragraph extends that duty to **non-food businesses storing or transporting food for others** — which is what a third-party cold store is. Article 132 attaches the penalty: an order to correct and a warning, then suspension of business plus a fine of RMB 10,000–50,000, with licence revocation in serious cases.

## Three storage regimes, and which one your product fits

**A bonded warehouse in China is a customs-supervised storage facility inside a special customs supervision area or a type-B bonded logistics centre, used to hold goods that have not yet completed import declaration and duty payment.** The regime decides when duty is paid, who may legally buy, and how much temperature evidence you owe.

<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Regime</th><th>Legal status of the goods</th><th>When duty is paid</th><th>Who can buy</th><th>Cold-chain implication</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><strong>1210 cross-border bonded import</strong> (网购保税进口)</td><td>Under customs supervision, not yet imported</td><td>Order by order, as each consumer buys</td><td>Individual consumers, via a registered cross-border platform</td><td>Needs a bonded facility with cold-chain capability and per-order picking inside the band; product must be on the positive list</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Bonded logistics storage</strong> (保税仓储, general-trade goods)</td><td>Under customs supervision, duty deferred</td><td>On declaration out of the bonded area</td><td>Any domestic buyer, once declared and labelled</td><td>Bulk cold-chain storage, blast-freeze capability, and re-export without the goods ever entering the domestic market</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Duty-paid domestic storage</strong> (完税仓储)</td><td>Imported; a domestic food business</td><td>Already paid at import</td><td>Any buyer</td><td>Full domestic food-storage obligations, food business licence, and a GB 31605-2020 evidence chain from the port onward</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

Bonded storage defers duty, so unsold stock can be re-exported or destroyed without a refund claim ([bonded warehouse costs and process](bonded-warehouse-cost-process.html)). Duty-paid storage is where you move once the product must carry a Chinese label and Chinese VAT invoicing.

## What the 1210 bonded route changes about your cost of entry

**Cross-border e-commerce retail import is a customs regime in which a consumer buys directly from an overseas seller and the goods clear at order level under supervision code 1210 or 9610, used to avoid the ordinary import tariff and licensing path for products on the published positive list.** It is why a foreign brand can sell imported food in China without a domestic entity.

- **Single order limit RMB 5,000; annual limit per consumer RMB 26,000.**
- Inside the limits the **tariff is provisionally 0%** and import VAT and consumption tax are levied at **70% of the statutory amount** — a good carrying 13% VAT effectively pays about **9.1%**.
- Premium cosmetics (above RMB 10 per millilitre or gram, or RMB 15 per sheet) add a 15% consumption tax, roughly 23.1% effective.
- The positive list covers **1,476 tariff lines** after the January 2022 adjustment.

Two cold-chain specifics matter more than the rates. Frozen aquatic products only became eligible with the 2019 edition of the list. And **several temperature-sensitive categories may only enter through bonded import** — fresh aquatic products and fresh or dried fruit are restricted to the 1210 route, so for them bonded cold-chain storage is not a cost optimisation but the only legal door.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 5,000 / RMB 26,000</span><span class="l">The per-order and per-consumer annual limits for cross-border retail import in China, inside which the tariff is provisionally 0% and import VAT and consumption tax are levied at 70% of the statutory amount</span><span class="src">Source: Cai Guan Shui [2018] No. 49, Ministry of Finance, GACC and State Taxation Administration, effective 1 January 2019; limits restated by the Tianjin Municipal Commerce Bureau</span></div>

## What customs actually inspects on a cold-chain consignment

**GACC Order No. 249 is China's Administrative Measures for the Safety of Imported and Exported Food, promulgated on 12 April 2021 and in force from 1 January 2022, used to govern how imported food is registered, declared, inspected, recorded and recalled.** Article 28 puts cold-chain performance inside the inspection scope. Item (7) requires customs to check **freshness, whether core temperature meets requirements, whether the cold-chain ambient temperature meets the relevant standards, whether temperature-control equipment is operating normally, and whether temperature records meet requirements** — and customs may order a boiling test. A warehouse without a continuous record fails this clause even if the product is perfect.

- **Article 24** lets customs require import through **designated ports and designated supervision sites**, so the entry facility must hold your band at the point of arrival.
- **Article 27** requires the entry quarantine approval, where needed, **before the trade contract is signed** — a rule that has ended shipments contracted first and approved second.
- **Article 30** requires imported fresh and frozen meat to carry durable Chinese-and-English markings stating origin, product name, manufacturer registration number and batch.
- **Article 21** requires import and sales records kept for **at least six months beyond shelf-life expiry**, or two years after sale where no shelf life is stated.

## The pandemic-era cold-chain controls are gone — the paperwork is not

**GACC Announcement No. 131 of 2022 is the customs notice that unwound border COVID controls for cargo, issued on 28 December 2022 and effective 8 January 2023, used by importers as the reference point for what no longer applies.** Overseas suppliers still quote the 2020–2022 regime.

From 8 January 2023, customs **cancelled all port-level nucleic-acid monitoring and testing for imported cold-chain goods**. The State Administration for Market Regulation confirmed in parallel that no nucleic-acid test certificate or disinfection certificate is required when purchasing or storing imported cold-chain food, and that such food **no longer enters a centralised supervision warehouse**.

The food-safety duty did not go with them: importers must still retain the **customs declaration and the entry inspection and quarantine certificate**. The 2026 position is no COVID certificates, but a complete temperature record.

## Why a returned frozen unit is a write-off, not a resale

**Article 25 of the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests is the provision that grants Chinese online shoppers a seven-day no-reason return right, and it expressly excludes fresh and perishable goods from that right.** For temperature-sensitive imports that is the difference between a returns policy and a write-off.

The excluded categories include **fresh and perishable goods**; the Implementing Regulations bar sellers from widening the list and require excluded goods to be marked prominently and confirmed by the buyer at purchase. Cross-border returns are separately governed — application within 30 days, arrival within 45 days, original condition and **fit for secondary sale**. A frozen unit delivered to a consumer's door cannot meet that test, so perishable lines should be modelled as non-returnable ([cross-border e-commerce returns](china-cross-border-ecommerce-returns.html)).

## Which of the five gateway cities can actually hold your temperature band

**A national backbone cold-chain logistics base is a designated logistics hub built under China's 14th Five-Year Plan for cold-chain development, used to anchor cold-chain flows on a national trunk-and-branch network.** There were **105 such bases by June 2025, covering all 31 provincial-level regions** — the plan's target, and a better filter than asking whether a city has cold storage.

Cold storage reached **267 million cubic metres in 2025, up 5.53% year on year**, cold-chain demand was **381.4 million tonnes, up 4.50%**, and revenue **RMB 556.71 billion, up 3.84%**, with growth now driven by online grocery and instant retail. Having shifted from capacity expansion toward value service, the newer facilities are the ones with automated temperature management and audit-grade records.

For imports the filter is narrower: a facility **inside a customs-supervised area, able to hold your specific band, and able to generate records customs will accept**. Build the warehouse and port shortlists together — see [China bonded-to-consumer delivery](china-bonded-to-consumer-delivery.html).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">267 million m³ / 105 bases</span><span class="l">China's total cold storage capacity in 2025 and the number of national backbone cold-chain logistics bases covering all 31 provincial-level regions, against cold-chain demand of 381.4 million tonnes in the same year</span><span class="src">Source: China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing, Cold Chain Committee, 2025 cold-chain operating data released 28 January 2026</span></div>

## A five-step sequence for temperature-sensitive goods

**A cold-chain import plan is a sequence decision rather than a supplier decision, used to fix the regime, the facility and the evidence chain before freight is booked.** Reversing the order produces consignments that clear customs and then fail at the warehouse gate.

1. **Confirm market access and category first** — the GACC market-access list, overseas manufacturer registration, and entry quarantine approval, which must exist before the contract is signed ([GACC food registration](gacc-food-registration.html)).
2. **Choose the regime — 1210 bonded or general trade — before booking freight.** It decides whether goods sit under customs supervision, whether they need a Chinese label at entry, and whether you need a domestic entity.
3. **Close compliance gaps before the first shipment.** Registrations, quarantine approvals and Chinese labelling artwork carry lead times longer than freight ([China import product labelling requirements](china-import-product-labelling-requirements.html)).
4. **Select a facility that can prove the band, not one that claims it** — 90 days of continuous temperature records, calibration certificates, the layout with wall and floor clearance, and the handover logs. A brochure instead of a data file is a no.
5. **Write the returns and write-off rule before launch** — which units are non-returnable, and what happens to stock that fails a mid-life excursion.

## How GOODSINFINITE handles temperature-sensitive imports

**GOODSINFINITE is an import and distribution operator with customs-supervised storage in China, used by overseas brands to import and hold goods without setting up a local company.** Temperature-sensitive categories run through its five-city gateway footprint — **Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou and Qingdao** — with bonded storage for supervised goods and temperature-and-humidity-controlled storage where a product's own standard is tighter than the national floor. The operator holds AEO advanced certified status in its own right, which affects inspection rates on what it declares.

The evidence chain has to satisfy two regulators: customs under Article 28(7), the market regulator under Article 33(6). One party holding the goods, the declaration and the temperature record makes those two audits one conversation. If the bonded-versus-general-trade decision is still open, start with the [China market entry guide](guide-china-market-entry.html) and the [import glossary](glossary.html).

## FAQ

**Do I need a Chinese entity to store imported food in a bonded warehouse in China?** You do not need a Chinese subsidiary, but you cannot leave the goods unsupervised. GACC Order No. 249, Article 19 requires the food importer to file with the customs house at its place of domicile, and the party filing the declaration must be registered in mainland China and hold a customs registration code. In the 1210 cross-border model the selling enterprise may sit offshore while import, storage and declaration run through a mainland-registered service provider or importer of record. Brands avoiding a China entity entirely contract an importer of record under a Hong Kong or offshore trading entity; brands that also want to hold domestic stock and issue Chinese VAT invoices need the mainland entity.

**What temperature must imported frozen and chilled food be stored at in China?** GB 31605-2020 sets -18°C or lower for food requiring freezing, and 0°C to 10°C for food requiring refrigeration, during both transport and storage. Where a product's label or category standard specifies a narrower band, that narrower band applies. Transport temperatures must be monitored continuously with recording intervals ideally no longer than 10 minutes, and cold-store temperature records must be taken at least every 30 minutes.

**Are the COVID-era cold-chain disinfection and testing requirements still in force?** No. GACC Announcement No. 131 of 2022, issued 28 December 2022 and effective 8 January 2023, cancelled all port-level nucleic-acid monitoring for imported cold-chain goods. SAMR's follow-up notice confirmed that from the same date no nucleic-acid or disinfection certificate is required when purchasing or storing imported cold-chain food, and that such food no longer enters a centralised supervision warehouse. The food-safety duties remain: retain the customs declaration, the entry inspection and quarantine certificate, and the purchase and sales records.

**Can I store imported food in a bonded warehouse in China and sell it later?** Yes — that is the main commercial reason to use one. Goods in a customs-supervised bonded facility have not completed import declaration, so duty and import-stage taxes are deferred until declaration. On the 1210 route the goods stay under supervision and are taxed order by order as consumers buy, which suits imported food sold in retail packs. Two limits apply: the product must be on the cross-border retail import positive list, and anything sold domestically must satisfy Chinese labelling and market-placement rules at declaration.

**Why can imported frozen food not use an ordinary warehouse?** Because temperature control is a legal requirement rather than a service level. Article 33(6) of the Food Safety Law requires storage, transport and loading equipment to meet the temperature and humidity requirements needed for food safety, and the following paragraph extends that duty to non-food businesses storing or transporting food for others. Article 132 attaches penalties of an order to correct plus warning, then suspension of business and a fine of RMB 10,000–50,000 for non-compliance, with licence revocation in serious cases. Customs reinforces it under Article 28(7) of GACC Order No. 249, which makes core temperature and the condition of cold-chain control equipment part of the on-site inspection.
