## Importing Pet Food to China: GACC Quarantine Access, MOA Registration and the 2026 Rule Change
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/importing-pet-food-to-china
Published: 2026-10-16 · Cluster: Compliance & Registration

## Pet food is feed in China, not food — and that single classification decides which government approvals you need

**If you take one thing from this page, take this: Chinese law does not treat pet food as food.** It is classified as feed (饲料), which means the entire food-import apparatus that most overseas brands know — GACC Decree 248 overseas food manufacturer registration, food importer filing, the food track under the Food Safety Law — is the wrong door. Pet food runs on two separate tracks that sit in two different ministries, and both must be cleared before a single bag can legally be sold in China.

The clarification is not a technicality. The General Administration of Customs applies a **quarantine access regime** to overseas pet food and a **registration regime** to overseas pet food manufacturing plants, while the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs applies a **product import registration regime** to the product itself. Countries get access. Plants get registered. Products get certificates. Three separate gates, and a foreign brand that clears two of them still cannot ship.

> The two-track structure is the reason pet food launches in China fail. Brands register the product, discover the plant is not on the GACC list, and lose a shipping season.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">15% / 10% / 6.5%</span><span class="l">The most-favoured-nation duty rate on retail-packed dog and cat food (HS 23091010 canned, HS 23091090 other), the 2026 provisional duty rate applied to both, and the MFN rate on other prepared animal feed (HS 23099090) under the 2026 Tariff Adjustment Plan</span><span class="src">Source: 2026 Tariff Adjustment Plan, provisional import duty schedule (State Council Tariff Commission)</span></div>

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">5 years + 5 years</span><span class="l">How long a GACC overseas pet food manufacturer registration lasts, and how long an MOA feed import registration certificate lasts — two certificates on two clocks, both renewable but neither usable to cover the other</span><span class="src">Source: Administrative Measures for Inspection and Quarantine Supervision of Import and Export Feed and Feed Additives, Art. 13; Administrative Measures for Registration of Imported Feed and Feed Additives, Art. 14</span></div>

## The three product categories — and why only two of them need MOA registration

Article 2 of the **Pet Feed Administrative Measures** (issued as Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs Announcement No. 20 of 27 April 2018, in force 1 June 2018) defines pet feed as industrially processed products for direct consumption by pets, also called pet food, and splits it into three categories with three different compliance burdens:

| Category | Statutory definition | MOA import registration certificate required? |
|---|---|---|
| **Pet compound feed** (宠物配合饲料) | Multiple feed raw materials and additives blended to a ratio to meet nutritional needs at a life stage or physiological/pathological state; alone it satisfies the pet's full nutritional needs — this is everyday complete kibble and wet food | **Yes.** Required for import under Art. 14 |
| **Pet additive premix feed** (宠物添加剂预混合饲料) | Nutritional additives — amino acids, vitamins, trace minerals, enzymes — blended with a carrier or diluent; this covers supplements and nutritional powders | **Yes.** Required for import under Art. 14 |
| **Other pet feed** (其他宠物饲料) | Products formulated for rewarding a pet, interacting with it, or stimulating chewing and tearing — treats, jerky, dental chews, snack sticks | **No MOA product registration.** Still needs GACC quarantine access, a registered plant, a compliant Chinese label and hygiene compliance |

That third row is the most valuable line in this article, because it is the one that gets misread in both directions. Treats-only brands assume they are exempt from everything and discover the quarantine permit problem at the port. Complete-food brands assume treats follow the same rule and over-budget the registration.

What does **not** change across categories: Article 15 requires pet feed exported to China to be packaged with a Chinese label meeting the Pet Feed Labelling Provisions, hygiene indicators meeting the Pet Feed Hygiene Provisions, and raw materials and additives drawn from the **Feed Raw Materials Catalogue** and **Feed Additives Catalogue**. Article 4 is blunt about the consequence: it is prohibited to use any substance outside those two catalogues to produce pet feed. If a formulation contains an ingredient that is not on the Chinese catalogue — including ingredients perfectly legal in the EU or US — the product is not registrable as formulated.

## Track one — GACC: country access, plant registration, importer filing, quarantine permit

The customs track is governed by the **Administrative Measures for the Inspection and Quarantine Supervision of Import and Export Feed and Feed Additives** — originally AQSIQ Order No. 118 of 20 July 2009, amended five times and most recently by **GACC Order No. 283**, published 27 April 2026, with the feed amendments **in force from 1 November 2026**.

**Step 1 — Is your country on the access list?** Article 7 requires GACC to set inspection and quarantine requirements by feed product category, conduct a risk analysis for any country exporting to China for the first time, and publish the resulting list of permitted countries and product categories. Pet food sits inside the published access list for animal and plant quarantine. If your country has no access, the process is a government-to-government exercise: the exporting country's competent authority applies to GACC, GACC issues a risk assessment questionnaire, and if the assessment passes the two sides negotiate a protocol and GACC publishes the access. A brand cannot self-nominate; the route runs through the exporting country's ministry.

**Step 2 — Is your plant on the GACC register?** Overseas manufacturers must be examined and found satisfactory by the competent authority of the exporting country, then **recommended by that authority to GACC**. GACC reviews the recommendation, decides whether to conduct an on-site抽查 based on risk, and publishes the plants it registers on its official website. Article 13 sets the registration at **5 years**; renewal must be requested by the exporting country's competent authority **6 months before expiry**, with GACC able to conduct a retrospective review of the exporting country's regulatory system and spot-check applicants. Plants that fail the spot check are refused, and the reason is notified back to the exporting authority.

This is a country-driven, not brand-driven, process. Your government has to recommend you. That is why the plant registration timeline is the single least controllable variable in a pet food launch.

**Step 3 — Importer filing.** Article 26 puts feed importers under a filing regime: the importing enterprise must file with the local customs house **before or at the time of its first inspection declaration**. This is a mainland-entity obligation.

**Step 4 — The quarantine permit.** Article 15 states that where an imported feed requires an entry animal and plant quarantine permit, it must be obtained. Under the **Administrative Measures for Quarantine Approval of Entry Animals and Plants** (AQSIQ Order No. 25, as amended), Article 4 requires the applicant to be **a unit with independent legal-person status that signs the foreign trade contract directly**, and Article 5 requires the application to be made and the permit obtained **before the trade contract is signed**. GACC maintains the list of products requiring approval and adjusts it dynamically — Announcement No. 77 of 2024, for example, removed quarantine approval for plant-origin feed and several other categories. Whether your specific consignment needs a permit is therefore a live check against the current list, not a fixed rule.

Customs' own service guidance shows how granular this gets: for **risk level I** feed, the applicant must provide evidence of the production, processing and storage unit; where pet food raw materials originate from approved establishments in a third disease-free country, a statement of raw material origin is required; and for non-single-ingredient feed, a composition statement or a label showing the detailed composition plus a declaration on whether restricted ingredients are present. Approval decisions are due within 20 working days of acceptance.

**Step 5 — Declaration and inspection.** Article 16 requires the owner or agent to declare to customs before or at the time of entry, providing certificate of origin, trade contract, bill of lading, invoice and, depending on the product, the exporting country's inspection and quarantine certificate.

## Track two — MOA: the product import registration certificate

The agriculture track is governed by the **Administrative Measures for the Registration of Imported Feed and Feed Additives**, made under the Feed and Feed Additives Regulation. Article 3 is the operative prohibition: an overseas enterprise exporting feed or feed additives to China for the first time must obtain an import registration certificate, and **without it the product may not be sold or used in China**.

Article 4 decides who can file, and it is the clause that blocks brands without a mainland presence: registration is filed **by the overseas enterprise's office resident in China, or by a Chinese domestic agency entrusted to act**. For pet compound feed and pet additive premix feed, Article 14 of the Pet Feed Administrative Measures says the same thing in pet-specific terms.

The procedural clock is fixed:

1. **Examination — 10 working days** from acceptance (Art. 9). If the dossier passes, the applicant is told to send samples to the designated testing institution.
2. **Re-testing — 3 months** (Art. 10). The designated institution completes re-testing of the quality standard and the samples. Where a national or industry standard method exists it takes priority. The overseas enterprise has 15 working days from receipt of the report to request a re-check if it disputes the result (Art. 11).
3. **Certificate — 10 working days** after a passing re-test (Art. 12), followed by publication.
4. **Validity — 5 years** (Art. 14).
5. **Post-certification filing — 6 months** (Art. 22). The overseas enterprise must establish a sales organisation or appoint a sales agent in China and file it with the ministry within 6 months of obtaining the certificate; any change must be re-filed within 1 month.

The application dossier under Article 7 is substantial and must be submitted in Chinese and English in duplicate, together with samples: the application form; the power of attorney and the agent's qualification documents; proof that the product is approved for production and use in the country of production plus registration data from other countries and marketing history; product name, composition, physicochemical properties, scope of use and method of use; production process, quality standard, test method and test report; the label, trademark and Chinese label artwork used in the country of production; and, for microbial or fermentation products, details of strain deposition.

Two penalty provisions are worth reading before you appoint an agent. Article 29 provides that false dossiers or samples lead to rejection and a **one-year freeze** on applications from that overseas enterprise and its registration agent; where a certificate was obtained by deception, it is revoked, **the registration agent is fined between RMB 50,000 and 100,000**, and both are barred for **three years**.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">10 days / 3 months / 10 days</span><span class="l">The statutory MOA registration clock: 10 working days for dossier examination, 3 months for laboratory re-testing, 10 working days to issue the certificate — before the formulation is fixed, before the Chinese label is printed and before any sales channel can be signed</span><span class="src">Source: Administrative Measures for the Registration of Imported Feed and Feed Additives, Arts. 9, 10, 12</span></div>

## What changes on 1 November 2026

GACC Order No. 283 re-issues the feed inspection and quarantine measures with amendments that take effect **1 November 2026**. For pet food importers, four changes matter commercially:

- **Business records: 2 years becomes 3 years.** Article 27 now requires importers to keep records for **no less than 3 years**, covering the declaration number, product name, quantity/weight, packaging, exporting country or region, overseas exporter, the overseas manufacturer's name **and its registration number**, the entry goods inspection and quarantine certificate, and the downstream flow of the goods. Article 28 adds that customs reviews those records and **tightens inspection and quarantine on the importer's feed where the review fails**. Record-keeping is now a clearance-speed issue, not an admin issue.
- **Labelling is tied to the national standard.** Article 25 now expressly requires import feed packaging to meet Chinese safety and hygiene requirements and to carry a label conforming to **China's national feed labelling standard**. Feed raw materials that are imported in bulk for processing rather than direct feeding may be imported unpacked, but must still carry a compliant label and use compliant containers and transport, with no cross-mixing in transit. Where China restricts the feeding scope of an animal-origin feed, the retail package must state that scope.
- **Risk grading drives the clearance path.** The measures apply product risk grading and enterprise classification, with customs adopting different inspection and quarantine supervision models and adjusting them dynamically. The practical consequence is that two pet food SKUs from the same brand can face materially different inspection intensity.
- **Registration validity is explicit at 5 years**, with renewal through the exporting authority six months before expiry.

If you are mid-launch, the cheapest action is to extend your record-retention policy to three years now and re-check your Chinese label against the national feed labelling standard before 1 November, rather than discovering the gap at inspection.

## Labels, hygiene and the catalogue problem

Chinese labelling is where otherwise-approvable pet food gets refused at the port. The **Pet Feed Labelling Provisions** (Annex 3 to MOA Announcement No. 20) require the label to state product name, raw material composition, guaranteed analysis values, net content, storage conditions, directions for use, precautions, production date, shelf life, manufacturer name and address, the licence document number and the product standard. The label must carry the statement **"本产品符合宠物饲料卫生规定"** in a prominent position and be accompanied by a product quality inspection certificate.

Generic names are regulated, not optional. Pet compound feed must use a generic name containing "宠物配合饲料", "宠物全价饲料", "全价宠物食品" or "全价", and must state the target animal species and life stage; if species is not stated it defaults to all breeds and sizes, and if life stage is not stated it defaults to all life stages. Products formulated for a specific physiological or pathological state must carry the word "处方". Pet additive premix feed must use "宠物添加剂预混合饲料", "补充性宠物食品" or "宠物营养补充剂". Other pet feed must use **"宠物零食"**. Where a brand name is also shown, it must sit after or below the generic name and in a font no larger than it.

Two formulation-level points deserve their own line. First, the **Feed Raw Materials Catalogue** and **Feed Additives Catalogue** are closed lists — Article 4 of the Pet Feed Administrative Measures prohibits any substance outside them. Second, hygiene indicators must meet the **Pet Feed Hygiene Provisions**; Announcement No. 20 set 1 January 2019 as the date from which domestically produced and imported pet feed must comply.

## Duty, taxes and classification

Retail-packed dog and cat food is classified in **HS heading 2309**. Per the 2026 Tariff Adjustment Plan's provisional duty schedule:

| HS code | Product | MFN rate | 2026 provisional rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23091010 | Retail-packed canned dog or cat food | 15% | 10% |
| 23091090 | Other retail-packed dog or cat food | 15% | 10% |
| 23099090 | Other prepared animal feed | 6.5% | 4% |

Import-stage VAT is charged at the applicable rate under the **VAT Law**, with the actual rate confirmed at declaration. Both 2309 headings carry the inspection and quarantine code for entry animal and plant products and the entry goods clearance requirement, which is the customs-side marker that the GACC track applies. Preferential rates under free trade agreements and RCEP may apply depending on origin — worth checking before you price, because the spread between MFN and agreement rates on this heading is wide.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">6,000㎡ / 8,000㎡ / 300+</span><span class="l">GOODSINFINITE's bonded warehousing footprint, temperature- and humidity-controlled storage, and the number of enterprises served — plus our own AEO advanced certification and 15 partner AEO enterprises, with fulfilment across Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou, Qingdao and Tianjin. Pet food is a shelf-life and temperature product: the bonded model lets you hold stock in China under customs supervision and release it into channels as orders land</span><span class="src">Source: GOODSINFINITE operational data</span></div>

## Where foreign brands actually get stuck

The legal structure produces four predictable failure points.

**1. No mainland party, no permit and no certificate.** The quarantine permit requires an applicant with independent legal-person status that signs the contract directly. The MOA registration must be filed by a China office or a Chinese domestic agency. Both are hard requirements, and both sit upstream of the first shipment. A **Hong Kong entity as importer of record** is the standard structure that solves the first, and a contracted Chinese agency solves the second — but they must be in place before filing, because the registration certificate is issued in the name of the product and the certificate holder must then file a China sales organisation or agent within six months.

**2. The ingredient list is not a Chinese ingredient list.** A formulation built for EU or US compliance routinely contains something outside the Feed Raw Materials Catalogue or Feed Additives Catalogue. Reformulating after the dossier is submitted costs a full re-test cycle — three months under Article 10.

**3. Country access is assumed, not verified.** "We already export to China" is not the same as "our plant is on the GACC register for pet food". The register is plant-specific and product-specific, and it is maintained by recommendation from the exporting authority.

**4. The 1 November 2026 transition.** Importers whose records run on a two-year retention policy, or whose labels meet the Pet Feed Labelling Provisions but not the national feed labelling standard now referenced in Article 25, will meet friction at inspection rather than at registration.

For most brands the sequencing that works is: confirm country access and plant registration → lock a mainland or Hong Kong importer structure and agency → fix the formulation against the catalogues → file MOA registration for compound and premix products → prepare the Chinese label → then book production. Running channel conversations in parallel is fine; running registration after production is not.

The alternative for brands that want to test demand before committing to a registration cycle is the bonded cross-border model, which moves product for consumer orders under a different customs regime — see [What Is 1210 Bonded Import?](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/what-is-1210-bonded-import.html) and [1210 Bonded vs Direct Mail](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/1210-bonded-vs-direct-mail.html) for how that route compares. It is a demand-testing tool, not a substitute for the feed registrations once you intend to trade through domestic channels.

## China Trade Shows for Foreign Brands: Canton Fair, CIIE and How to Exhibit
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-trade-shows
Published: 2026-10-14 · Cluster: Market Research

## Exhibiting in China means one thing above all: two separate legal events — your people and your goods — plus a third decision about what happens when the show ends

**A China trade show is not a marketing booking; it is a temporary import operation, a visa exercise and a distribution decision stacked on top of each other.** Most foreign brands plan the booth and discover the customs question in week two. The correct order is the opposite: the goods rule decides what you can physically bring, the visa rule decides who can stand behind the booth, and the post-show rule decides whether a conversation on the stand can turn into a delivered order.

That framing answers the question behind "which are the best trade shows in China for foreign brands?" The answer is not one show. It is four national-level fairs with four different buyers, plus a decision about which one matches the channel you intend to build.

> The stand is the cheapest part. The expensive part is what you do with the goods when the lights go out.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">155万㎡ / 3.2万 / 31.4万</span><span class="l">The Canton Fair's exhibition area, the number of exhibiting companies at the 140th session, and the overseas buyers who attended the 139th session from 220 countries and regions — the largest buyer pool any foreign brand can reach in a single week in China</span><span class="src">Source: Canton Fair official site (cantonfair.org.cn); State Council Information Office press conference on the 140th session, 18 September 2026</span></div>

## The four national shows worth a foreign brand's budget

| Show | Hosts | Timing & place | What it is good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **China Import and Export Fair (Canton Fair / 广交会)** | Ministry of Commerce and the Guangdong Provincial People's Government; organised by the China Foreign Trade Centre | Two sessions a year in Guangzhou — spring and autumn; the 140th session runs 15 October – 4 November 2026 across three phases | The broadest buyer pool in China. Foreign brands exhibit in the **International Pavilion (进口展)**, held in phases 2 and 3 |
| **China International Import Expo (CIIE / 进博会)** | Ministry of Commerce and the Shanghai Municipal People's Government; organised by the CIIE Bureau and the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai) | 5–10 November 2026 (9th session) at the National Exhibition and Convention Center, Shanghai | The only national-level expo themed on **imports** — six business exhibition zones plus an innovation incubation zone (创新孵化专区). The best fit for brands that want to sell into China rather than source from it |
| **China International Consumer Products Expo (CICPE / 消博会)** | Ministry of Commerce and the Hainan Provincial People's Government | April, in Hainan (Haikou main venue with sub-venues) | China's first national-level exhibition themed on consumer goods; strongest for beauty, food, lifestyle and premium consumer brands, and tied to Hainan Free Trade Port policy |
| **China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS / 服贸会)** | Ministry of Commerce and the Beijing Municipal People's Government | September, in Beijing | Services, digital, licensing and B2B service models rather than physical product |

Two practical notes. First, all four are **government-hosted national exhibitions**, which is why they come with on-site customs, IP and trade-dispute services that commercial shows do not have. Second, the fair that is right for you is decided by the buyer you need: sourcing and distribution partners across the whole country points to the Canton Fair; Chinese importers and platform buyers for a finished consumer product points to CIIE or CICPE.

## Can a foreign company actually exhibit — and what does the application require?

Yes, and no Chinese entity is required to stand on the floor. The Canton Fair's International Pavilion admission rules are explicit: the exhibitor must be a company **legally registered outside mainland China**, and must provide a copy of its certificate of incorporation bearing the company seal, or other valid proof. Group companies, subsidiaries, joint-venture partners and representative offices with a substantive legal relationship to the applicant may co-exhibit, provided supporting documents and authorisation are filed. Exhibits must fall within the published International Pavilion product scope.

The application pack is where first-timers lose weeks. Expect to produce:

1. A company registration certificate (business licence equivalent) plus corporate and product introductions.
2. Evidence connecting you to the brand — **proof of origin, overseas brand registration, proof of the relationship with the overseas brand owner, or an exhibition authorisation**.
3. The completed application form, exhibition terms and online-exhibition responsibility letter, each company-sealed.
4. Payment of the participation fee after the organiser issues the payment notice — payment in full is what confirms the booth.
5. Registration on the exhibitor system (参展易捷通) for first-time exhibitors.

Applications can be filed directly with the China Foreign Trade Centre or through contracted overseas recruiters, and the organiser warns that the official exhibitor system is the only legitimate channel. Note the contrast with selling online: a foreign brand can exhibit without a mainland entity, but holding a domestic **storefront** on a Chinese B2B marketplace requires a mainland-registered business — the distinction is set out in [selling on 1688 as a foreign brand](selling-on-1688-china-b2b.html).

## Getting the goods in: temporary import, ATA carnets and the six-month clock

Exhibition goods are a defined customs category, not an awkward edge case. Article 3 of **GACC Order No. 233** (Administrative Measures for the Temporary Import and Export of Goods, published 7 December 2017, in force 1 February 2018, as amended by GACC Order No. 273 of 28 October 2024) lists, as its first category, goods displayed or used at exhibitions, trade fairs, conferences and similar activities.

Three consequences follow, and they are the ones that matter operationally:

- **Duty is deferred, not waived.** Article 37 of the **Customs Tariff Law** (in force 1 December 2024) provides that goods temporarily imported for display or use at exhibitions, fairs and conferences may lawfully defer customs duty, provided they are re-exported within **six months** of importation, with extensions handled under GACC rules. Goods not re-exported within the period must pay duty.
- **Licences are generally not required.** Article 5 of Order No. 233 exempts temporary import/export goods from licence presentation, except where a treaty, law, administrative regulation or GACC rule provides otherwise. This is why a product that would normally need a registration certificate can still be shown — but note that *showing* is not *selling*; the registration chain resumes the moment you place the product on the market, as mapped in [which Chinese agency regulates my product](which-chinese-agency-regulates-my-product.html).
- **The clock is real.** Article 10 of Order No. 233 gives six months for re-export, with extensions up to three times of no more than six months each. Article 13 requires the formal import or export declaration to be completed **before** that deadline if the goods are not leaving.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">6 + 3 × 6 months</span><span class="l">The statutory window for exhibition goods: six months to re-export from the date of importation, extendable up to three times for no more than six months each — after which the goods must be re-exported, re-imported, or converted to a normal declaration and taxed</span><span class="src">Source: GACC Order No. 233 (as amended 2024), Arts. 10 and 13; Customs Tariff Law Art. 37</span></div>

### ATA carnet or ordinary temporary import?

An **ATA carnet** is the "passport for goods" for temporary admission, and in China the issuing and guaranteeing authority is the **China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT / China Chamber of International Commerce)**, authorised by the State Council and GACC. Article 9 of Order No. 233 confirms that for carnet-covered goods, CCPIT provides a **general guarantee** to GACC — which is the practical reason a carnet holder does not post a bond at the border, while a non-carnet temporary import does.

The carnet's limits are exactly where exhibitors get caught: it covers commercial samples, exhibition goods and professional equipment; it **does not cover** perishables or consumables, **goods imported for the purpose of sale**, goods intended as gifts, or goods imported for processing. It is valid for one year and can be used across multiple countries and multiple entries. Applications run through CCPIT's ATA system (eatachina.com), and the applicant must be the goods owner or a person free to dispose of them.

Where a carnet is not appropriate — because you intend to leave stock behind, or the goods are consumable — customs offers alternative supervision codes: customs records exhibition filing, and goods can clear as **2600** (temporary import/export goods), **2700** (exhibition goods), an ATA carnet, or ordinary trade **0110** if they are being imported properly. Small samples and consumables distributed free to visitors during the fair can be relieved of import duty and import-stage taxes within a **reasonable quantity and total value** that customs assesses against the nature of the exhibition, the exhibitor's scale and visitor numbers.

## Getting your people in: the M visa and the invitation letter

Attending a fair is commercial activity, so the correct category is the **M visa**. Under Article 7(8) of the Regulations on the Administration of the Entry and Exit of Foreigners (as amended in 2025), an applicant for an M visa must submit an invitation letter issued by the Chinese commercial or trade partner.

The Chinese Visa Application Service Centre's M-visa material list specifies what that letter must contain:

- **Invitee details** — name, gender, date of birth, passport number, etc.
- **Visit details** — purpose of the visit, arrival and departure dates, places to be visited, the relationship with the inviting entity, and the source of funds for the stay.
- **Inviting entity details** — name, address and telephone, the entity's official seal, and the signature of its legal representative (or of the inviting person, with their position stated), plus the date of invitation.
- **Inviting entity's business licence**, and a note in the letter if a multiple-entry visa is requested.

In practice the invitation can come from the Chinese counterparty you are meeting, the fair organiser's overseas recruiter, or the mainland service provider running your China-side programme. For genuinely urgent business travel — a last-minute stand problem, a signing — **port visas** in the trade (M) category are available under the National Immigration Administration's facilitation measures, on an invitation letter from an authorised or registered inviting entity.

## Selling from the stand: the step that surprises first-time exhibitors

This is where the temporary-import logic and the commercial logic collide, and it is worth stating plainly: **if the goods will be sold, they are not temporary-import goods.**

- Under the ATA carnet system, **goods imported for the purpose of sale are excluded**. If you sell carnet goods in China and they never leave, the guaranteeing chamber is exposed to the import taxes, and the holder is on the hook.
- Under Order No. 233, goods that will not be re-exported must complete a **normal import declaration before the deadline** (Art. 13). That means a Chinese importer of record, classification, duty and import VAT — the same chain any commercial shipment follows, set out in [importing into China without a local company](importing-into-china-without-a-local-company.html).
- Once goods move from the stand into commerce, **labelling and product-compliance obligations attach** — Chinese-language labelling is a market-placement requirement, not a display requirement, and the details are in [China import product labelling requirements](china-import-product-labelling-requirements.html).

The one structural exception is CIIE. A joint notice of the Ministry of Finance, GACC and the State Taxation Administration (Cai Guan Shui [2020] No. 38) grants **exemption from import duty, import-stage VAT and consumption tax** on a reasonable quantity of imported exhibits **sold during the CIIE exhibition period**, excluding prohibited imports, endangered species products, tobacco, alcohol, automobiles and products on the catalogue of major technical equipment not eligible for duty exemption. Per-exhibitor relief is capped: listed categories 1–5 by quantity, and **US$20,000** for other exhibits. Exhibits sold above the limit, and exhibits unsold during the fair that are not re-exported afterwards, are taxed under the ordinary rules. Confirm the current session's policy with the organiser before you plan a sell-through.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">US$20,000</span><span class="l">The per-exhibitor ceiling on duty- and tax-relieved sales of imported exhibits during the China International Import Expo for categories outside the scheduled list — above it, or for unsold goods not re-exported, ordinary taxation applies</span><span class="src">Source: Ministry of Finance, GACC and STA, Cai Guan Shui [2020] No. 38</span></div>

## Intellectual property: the fair has its own enforcement system

China's national fairs run on-site IP machinery, and it is fast. At the Canton Fair, intellectual property and trade dispute reception stations are staffed during the exhibition; on receipt of a complaint the exhibitor is notified and has **24 hours** to choose one of two paths — voluntarily remove the complained-of exhibit, in which case no infringement determination is made and the dispute ends, or file a defence with evidence through the system, in which case the station investigates and determines whether infringement is indicated. Determinations and sanctions follow the fair's own measures on complaints of suspected IP infringement, and repeat display of an item already found to be complained of, or display of items already adjudged infringing by a court or administrative decision, is treated as an aggravating factor. The expert teams are drawn from national, provincial and municipal IP administrations.

The defensive work happens before you ship: China is a first-to-file jurisdiction, and exhibiting an unregistered brand is exactly the scenario where that bites — see [trademark registration for foreign brands in China](china-trademark-registration-foreign-brand.html).

## After the show: converting a stand into a channel

A fair produces conversations, not sales. Turning them into revenue means picking the import route that matches what you promised on the stand:

1. **Cross-border e-commerce (1210 bonded)** — fast, low-commitment, keeps inventory in a bonded zone until an order arrives, ideal for validating demand with real orders. The mechanics are in [what is 1210 bonded import](what-is-1210-bonded-import.html).
2. **General trade import** — the route for shelf distribution, retail and B2B invoicing in RMB; requires the full compliance set and a mainland importer.
3. **A distributor or agent** — reach without your own entity, with the control trade-offs set out in [finding a China distributor](china-distributor-for-foreign-brands.html).
4. **Your own China presence** — an office, staff and a mandate, which is what [appointing a China commercial representative](china-commercial-representative.html) is for.

Before you commit to any of them, pressure-test what you heard on the stand with structured research rather than booth enthusiasm — the method is in [China market research for foreign brands](china-market-research-foreign-brands.html).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">6,000㎡ + 8,000㎡</span><span class="l">Bonded warehouse (6,000㎡) plus temperature-controlled storage (8,000㎡), a self-operated AEO Advanced Certification with 15 partner AEOs, five-city fulfilment across Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou and Qingdao, and service to 300+ enterprises</span><span class="src">Source: GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED operations</span></div>

## How GOODSINFINITE works a China trade show

We are not a stand builder. We are the part that happens before and after — and the part that is legally yours to get wrong.

- **Before the fair.** Product-scope and compliance pre-check so what you ship is actually admissible; ATA carnet or temporary-import planning; M-visa invitation letters and itinerary paperwork; buyer pre-qualification so the diary is full before you land.
- **At the fair.** Chinese-speaking staff on the stand, real-time qualification of distributors, wholesalers and platform buyers, and on-the-spot handling of IP or dispute notices within the fair's 24-hour windows.
- **After the fair.** Follow-up negotiation in Chinese under a written mandate, conversion of interest into 1210 bonded or general-trade orders, bonded warehousing and fulfilment, and the option of standing up an office and hiring local staff if the pipeline justifies it.

You keep the brand, the pricing decision and the customer relationship. We run the China-side mechanics that make the conversations real.

## FAQ

**Can a foreign brand exhibit at the Canton Fair without a Chinese entity?** Yes — the International Pavilion exists precisely for that. The exhibitor must be a company legally registered outside mainland China, must provide a sealed copy of its certificate of incorporation, and must produce evidence connecting it to the brand: proof of origin, overseas brand registration, proof of the relationship with the brand owner, or an exhibition authorisation. Applications go to the China Foreign Trade Centre or a contracted recruiter, and exhibits must be within the published product scope. Selling domestically at scale, issuing Chinese VAT invoices and acting as importer of record still require a mainland entity.

**Do I pay customs duty on goods I bring into China for a trade show?** Not if they leave again. Article 37 of the Customs Tariff Law (in force 1 December 2024) allows goods temporarily imported for display or use at exhibitions, fairs and conferences to defer duty, provided they are re-exported within six months. Temporary import/export goods are also exempt from licence presentation under Article 5 of GACC Order No. 233 unless an exception applies. Small samples distributed free to visitors during the fair can be relieved of import duty and import-stage taxes within a reasonable quantity and value assessed by customs.

**How long can exhibition goods stay in China?** Six months from importation or exportation under Article 10 of GACC Order No. 233, extendable up to three times for no more than six months each. When the extension expires, the goods must be re-exported, re-imported, or converted to a normal declaration. Goods for exhibitions running 24 months or longer may be granted further extension by the competent directly-affiliated customs house.

**Can I sell my samples or products from the booth?** Not under an ATA carnet — goods imported for the purpose of sale are excluded from the carnet system. To sell, the goods must be moved onto a normal import declaration with a Chinese importer of record, paying duty and import VAT before the temporary-import deadline (Order No. 233, Art. 13), and market-placement requirements such as Chinese labelling then apply. The exception is the CIIE, where Cai Guan Shui [2020] No. 38 relieves import duty, import VAT and consumption tax on a reasonable quantity of imported exhibits sold during the fair, subject to per-exhibitor limits including a US$20,000 ceiling for unlisted categories.

**What visa does my team need to attend a trade fair in China?** An M visa. Article 7(8) of the Regulations on the Administration of the Entry and Exit of Foreigners requires an invitation letter from the Chinese commercial or trade partner. Per the Chinese Visa Application Service Centre checklist, the letter must state the invitee's personal details, the visit details (purpose, arrival and departure dates, places visited, relationship with the inviting entity, source of funds) and the inviting entity's details (name, address, telephone, official seal, signature of the legal representative), and the inviting entity's business licence is required. Urgent business travel can use an M-category port visa under the National Immigration Administration's facilitation measures.

## Zhihu Marketing for Foreign Brands in China
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/zhihu-marketing-foreign-brands-china
Published: 2026-10-14 · Cluster: Marketing & New Media

## Zhihu is China's decision-support library, not a social network

Zhihu marketing is the practice of placing brand answers, articles and promoted content inside China's largest question-and-answer community, so that a brand is present at the moment a buyer researches a category rather than at the moment a feed is scrolled. The "China's Quora" label undersells what it has become: as of 30 June 2026 Zhihu carried roughly **993 million** pieces of content from **81.5 million** creators ([Zhihu Q2 2026 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1835724/000110465926101523/tm2624122d1_ex99-1.htm)) — a library large enough that Chinese search engines and AI assistants treat it as a reference for how things work in China.

The mechanics matter more than the size. Zhihu users arrive through a question or a search, not a feed, and a strong answer keeps ranking for years, not 48 hours. Effort compounds here; the platform rewards explanation over reach.

The audience is also narrower than the "social platform" framing implies: as of 30 June 2026, about 51.5% of active users were under 30 and about 46.8% were women ([H1 2026 interim report](https://www.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0826/2026082600417_c.pdf)), and Zhihu reported that daily active users spend more than 41 minutes a day in the app ([Q4 2025 results, March 2026](https://www1.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0325/2026032500618_c.pdf)). People read on Zhihu; they do not flick past it.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">993 million</span><span class="l">Cumulative pieces of content on Zhihu as of 30 June 2026, up about 9% year on year, written by 81.5 million creators — the corpus Chinese search and AI products index</span><span class="src">Source: Zhihu Q2 2026 unaudited results and H1 2026 interim report, June 2026</span></div>

## Why Zhihu matters more in the AI era, not less

An AI citation source is a corpus that large language models and AI search products retrieve answers from, and Zhihu has spent two years positioning itself as one. Its own AI search product, Zhihu ZhiDa (知乎直答), launched in June 2024 and grew from million-scale to ten-million-scale monthly users within a year, adding a professional search mode over licensed literature databases covering more than 50 million Chinese and English documents ([reported March 2026](https://finance.sina.com.cn/roll/2026-03-25/doc-inhseyvw3592569.shtml)). The stated priority for 2026 is to accelerate AI-related commercialisation and raise Zhihu's position in the wider AI ecosystem.

The content mix is moving the same direction: AI-related professional content grew about **37%** year on year in Q2 2026, and Zhihu's expert data solutions — licensing content to model developers — completed a first commercial validation across several model capability areas. Read that as a signal about whose voice becomes the default: when a Chinese buyer asks an AI assistant about your category, the answer is often assembled from Zhihu answers written by someone else. Absence is not neutral.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">37%</span><span class="l">Year-on-year growth in AI-related professional content on Zhihu in Q2 2026, as the platform began licensing its expert content to model developers</span><span class="src">Source: Zhihu Q2 2026 results, quarter ended 30 June 2026</span></div>

## What a foreign brand can actually buy on Zhihu

Zhihu marketing formats fall into two families — organic presence through a verified organisation account (机构号), and paid distribution through 知+ (Zhi+), the platform's native content-promotion product. Every paid format attaches to an answer, an article or a question, never to a display banner.

Zhihu publishes no rate card, so every figure quoted is a broker number. Published agency quotes for 2026 put the minimum prepayment at RMB 5,000–10,000, listed click prices from RMB 0.35 with realised prices nearer RMB 2–2.5, a recommended daily budget from RMB 500, and an agency service fee typically 5–8% of the amount loaded. Treat all of it as directional.

The platform's own revenue is more telling. Marketing services revenue was RMB 199.0 million in Q2 2026, down from RMB 222.8 million a year earlier — a decline Zhihu attributes to its own "proactive and ongoing refinement of service offerings" rather than to falling advertiser demand. The platform is curating its feed inventory and steering demand towards content it considers worth ranking.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 199.0 million</span><span class="l">Zhihu marketing services revenue in Q2 2026, down from RMB 222.8 million a year earlier — a reduction Zhihu attributes to its own restructuring of ad supply, not to weaker advertiser demand</span><span class="src">Source: Zhihu Q2 2026 unaudited results, quarter ended 30 June 2026</span></div>

## Why most overseas brands cannot open a Zhihu account themselves

A Zhihu organisation account is the verified brand identity that unlocks publishing, analytics and paid distribution, and the eligibility rules published by authorised agencies are built on mainland credentials: a mainland enterprise business licence or individual-business licence, the legal representative's identity document, a corporate bank account, and an ICP filing for any campaign landing page ([agency eligibility checklist](https://m.zhihu-ad.com/z/1102.html)). Individual accounts are not accepted, and Zhihu does not sell advertising directly — accounts are opened and serviced through certified agencies.

One wrinkle matters for anyone using a Hong Kong holding structure: at least one authorised agency's eligibility table also lists Hong Kong companies, admitted on a Business Registration Certificate issued by the Hong Kong Inland Revenue Department. That is agency documentation, not a platform rule, so confirm it in writing — but for a brand already importing through a Hong Kong entity it is the cheapest test of whether a mainland company is really needed.

A foreign brand without a mainland entity has one practical route: an agency that contracts as advertiser under its own licence. It is faster than incorporating, but the account, the followers and the data belong to the agency, and the brand still carries the labelling and liability for what the content says.

## The labelling and disclosure rules that govern Zhihu content

Zhihu content compliance is the set of labelling, sourcing and disclosure rules that apply to anything a brand publishes or pays for. Four carry most of the risk.

Under SAMR Order No. 72, in force since 1 May 2023, content that shares knowledge, experience or product testing and carries a shopping link must be conspicuously marked 广告 — advertising ([SAMR, 2023](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2023/issue_10506/202306/content_6885261.html)). That is the shape of a 知+ answer with a product card, and the penalty runs through Article 59 of the Advertising Law to a fine of up to RMB 100,000.

Second, the Advertising Law requires any figure cited in advertising to state its source and validity period ([Advertising Law, 2021 amendment](https://policy.mofcom.gov.cn/claw/clawContent.shtml?id=90361)) — a rule that bites on a platform built on statistics.

Third, AI-generated content must be labelled. The Measures for the Labelling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content, issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China with the MIIT, the Ministry of Public Security and the NRTA, took effect on 1 September 2025: AI-generated text, images, audio and video need both a visible label and metadata-level marking, and removing or altering them is banned ([CAC, 2025](https://www.cac.gov.cn/2025-03/14/c_1743654685899683.htm)). Zhihu has moved the same way: its H1 2026 interim report says it strengthened AI-generated content disclosure and identification and reinforced creators' responsibility for accuracy, while governing low-quality AI content that lacks factual basis. An agency producing thirty answers a month from a model, with no disclosure, is manufacturing a liability.

Fourth, engagement cannot be bought. CAC Order No. 5 bans traffic fraud, fake registration and account manipulation ([CAC Order No. 5, 2020](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2020/content_5492511.htm)), which covers purchased upvotes. Paid promotion through 知+ is legitimate because the platform labels it; purchased organic support is a different product.

## When Zhihu should be your lead China channel

A lead China channel is the platform a brand commits its first 6 to 12 months of content to, and Zhihu earns that role in high-consideration categories where buyers research before they spend: B2B and industrial supply, enterprise software, education, financial products, medical aesthetics and premium durables. There, Zhihu answers rank in Baidu, feed AI answers, and keep working for years.

It is the wrong lead channel where demand is impulse-led or visual. Beauty, fashion, food and household goods are decided on Xiaohongshu and transaction trends on Douyin; there, Zhihu's job is defensive — owning the answer to "is it worth it" and "is it safe" before a competitor or an anonymous account does.

## A 90-day Zhihu sequence for a brand with no China team

A Zhihu sequence is a staged entry plan: map the questions in month one, build the answering machinery in month two, and amplify only what has already earned organic traction in month three.

Month one is research. Export the questions Chinese buyers actually ask — category basics, comparisons, price expectations, safety and after-sales complaints — and record who owns each one today. In most categories the top answers belong to competitors, distributors, or a personal account that has quietly become the category authority.

Month two is structure. Open an organisation account through an agency if you hold no mainland licence, publish 10 to 15 useful answers under the brand's name, and settle the disclosure question: whether content is AI-assisted, who approves claims, and how data is sourced. Answers that sell lose; answers that explain win the ranking.

Month three is amplification, and only of content that already performs. Put 知+ behind the two or three answers earning organic upvotes, target by interest and city rather than broad reach, and keep the landing page ICP-filed.

## How to measure Zhihu honestly

Zhihu measurement is the practice of judging the channel on demand-side evidence — brand-term search volume, answer ranking persistence, share of AI answers and lead quality — rather than on views. Track how your answers rank month over month, whether your brand appears in the top three answers for your five most important category questions, cost per qualified lead, and whether conversations open with "I read your answer on Zhihu".

Two traps are worth naming: views are driven by question traffic, so one popular question can deliver six figures of impressions with no commercial intent; and because rankings take weeks to move, a 30-day evaluation always reports failure. Judge it over two quarters, on leads rather than reach.

## FAQ

**Should a foreign brand be on Zhihu?** Yes, if your category is researched rather than impulse-bought. Zhihu answers rank in Baidu, feed Chinese AI assistants, and stay useful for years, so the platform compounds where feed advertising decays. B2B, industrial, education, financial, medical-aesthetic and premium durable brands should treat it as a core channel; beauty, fashion and food brands usually lead on Xiaohongshu and use Zhihu defensively, to own the sceptical questions about their category.

**Can a foreign company open a Zhihu advertising account without a Chinese entity?** Not directly. Zhihu does not sell advertising itself — accounts are opened through certified agencies — and the eligibility list is built on mainland credentials: a mainland enterprise or individual-business licence, a legal representative's ID, a corporate bank account, and an ICP filing for the landing page. Brands without a mainland entity work through an agency that contracts as advertiser, which is faster but leaves the account, the followers and the data with the agency.

**How much does Zhihu advertising cost?** Zhihu publishes no rate card, so every figure is an agency quote. Published agency quotes for 2026 put the minimum prepayment at RMB 5,000–10,000, listed click prices from RMB 0.35 with realised prices nearer RMB 2–2.5, a recommended daily budget from RMB 500, and an agency service fee typically 5–8% of the amount loaded. The cheapest entry is not media — it is the answers you publish for free.

**How is Zhihu different from Quora for a brand?** Zhihu is a larger relative to its market, it is indexed by Baidu, and it is one of the corpora Chinese AI products retrieve from, so a ranking answer keeps working outside the platform. Its audience is also younger and more female than the Quora stereotype suggests: 51.5% of active users were under 30 and about 46.8% were women as of June 2026, with daily active users spending more than 41 minutes a day in the app.

**Does AI-generated content need a label on Zhihu?** Yes. China's labelling measures for AI-generated synthetic content took effect on 1 September 2025 and require both a visible label and metadata-level marking on AI-generated text, images, audio and video, with a ban on removing them. Zhihu has tightened its own mechanisms too: its H1 2026 interim report says it strengthened AI-generated content disclosure and identification and reinforced creators' responsibility for accuracy, while governing low-quality AI content that lacks factual basis.

## Appointing a China Commercial Representative: What a Local Representative Can Legally Do
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-commercial-representative
Published: 2026-10-13 · Cluster: Market Entry & Entity

## Appointing a China commercial representative means one thing above all: a mandate plus a power of attorney — not an entity

**A China commercial representative is a mainland company or individual you appoint to act for you in China under a written mandate, while legal liability for what they do in your name stays with you.** Appointing one is a contract question, not a company-registration question. Under China's Civil Code you have three distinct tools — an **agency mandate** (委托代理), a **commission agency** (行纪) and an **intermediary engagement** (中介) — and they give the person on the ground very different powers.

That single distinction answers most of the question "how do I appoint a local representative or commercial agent in China?" The confusion is usually terminological. "Representative", "agent", "distributor" and "representative office" are used interchangeably in market-entry decks; in Chinese law they are four different instruments with four different liability profiles, and only one of them gives you an office with your name on the door.

> A representative is not a substitute for an entity. It is a substitute for *you being there* — and it can only carry the powers the law and your mandate actually give it.

## Three different legal animals hide behind the word "representative"

The Civil Code separates them cleanly, and the separation matters the moment a Chinese buyer asks who is liable.

| | Intermediary (居间/中介) | Agent (委托代理) | Commission agent (行纪) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legal basis | Civil Code Art. 961–966 | Civil Code Arts. 161–175, 919–936 | Civil Code Arts. 951–960 |
| What they do | Report opportunities, broker introductions | Act **in your name**, within your mandate | Trade **in their own name**, on your account |
| Who is bound to the Chinese buyer | You, directly | You, directly (Art. 162) | The commission agent (Art. 958) |
| Who is paid if no deal closes | No remuneration, unless agreed for expenses (Art. 964) | According to the mandate contract | According to the mandate contract |
| Typical use | Sourcing, distributor introductions, events | Negotiations, tenders, liaison, procurement | Import/trading intermediary that contracts onward |

Two consequences follow, and both are commercially significant.

First, an **intermediary has no authority to bind you**, which is exactly what many brands want in the exploratory phase — but Article 964 means a pure intermediary who produces nothing is owed nothing, unless you agreed to reimburse defined costs. Second, **bypassing the intermediary does not save the fee**: Article 965 provides that a principal who, after using an intermediary's services, circumvents the intermediary and contracts directly must still pay. If your concern is being cut out of your own supply chain, the relevant protection is a non-circumvention clause — and Chinese law already points that way.

## What a representative can do — and the five things only an entity can do

With a correctly drafted written mandate, a China-side representative can negotiate, take quotes, attend tenders, visit factories, run market research, handle inspections, manage logistics providers and represent you in Chinese-language discussions with buyers and platforms.

Five functions remain outside a representative's reach no matter how broad the mandate:

1. **Be the importer of record.** The declaration must be filed by a mainland enterprise registered with customs. A representative office's permitted activities are liaison only, which is why importing for resale is not one of them; the entity question is set out in [importing into China without a local company](importing-into-china-without-a-local-company.html).
2. **Issue a Chinese VAT invoice.** Domestic B2B buyers expect one, and an offshore principal cannot issue it — see [selling on 1688 as a foreign brand](selling-on-1688-china-b2b.html).
3. **Employ your China staff.** Only an employer established inside China falls within the Labor Contract Law, and a representative office must engage staff through the local foreign-affairs service unit.
4. **Hold product-specific approvals** that require a Chinese licence or filing holder — the registration chain is mapped in [which Chinese agency regulates my product](which-chinese-agency-regulates-my-product.html).
5. **Hold a domestic storefront or licence** in your brand's own name on platforms such as 1688.

Everything else — the actual work of being present, talking, qualifying and following up in China — a representative can do.

## The four ways to put someone on the ground in China

<div class="table-wrap">
<table>
<tr><th>Route</th><th>What it is</th><th>What it can do</th><th>Main constraint</th></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Commercial representation agreement</strong></td><td>A mainland company or individual appointed under a Civil Code mandate, with a written power of attorney</td><td>Negotiate, introduce, research, represent you in talks, handle local liaison</td><td>Cannot employ your staff, issue invoices, hold licences or be importer of record; a mandate that habitually binds you creates tax exposure</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Representative office (代表处)</strong></td><td>A registered non-profit liaison office of the foreign enterprise, with a chief representative and up to three representatives</td><td>Market research, display and promotion; liaison for sales, service, domestic procurement and domestic investment</td><td>May not engage in for-profit activity — penalties of RMB 50,000 to 500,000; staff must be engaged via the foreign-affairs service unit; annual report due by 30 June</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>WFOE</strong></td><td>A wholly foreign-owned mainland company</td><td>Everything: import, invoice, employ, hold licences, hold storefronts</td><td>Full incorporation, capital, tax registration, ongoing compliance — the heaviest option</td></tr>
<tr><td><strong>Dispatched or outsourced staff</strong></td><td>Personnel provided through a licensed dispatch or services provider</td><td>Feet on the ground quickly, without an entity</td><td>Dispatch is limited to temporary, auxiliary or substitute positions and capped at 10% of the user entity's workforce; "outsourcing" that is really dispatch is a known enforcement target</td></tr>
</table>
</div>

The route that is right for you is decided by a single question: **does the person need to bind you, or merely represent you?** If they need to sign, you need either a properly scoped power of attorney or an entity. If they only need to open doors and qualify buyers, the lightest route — a representation agreement — is usually enough, and it is reversible.

### The representative office, specifically

China's rules on the foreign representative office are settled and, from 2024, current: the **Administrative Regulations on Registration of Resident Representative Offices of Foreign Enterprises** (State Council Order No. 584, published 19 November 2010, in force 1 March 2011, third amendment 10 March 2024). The regulation defines the office as a **non-profit** establishment with no legal personality (Art. 2), prohibits for-profit activity (Art. 13), and lists what is permitted (Art. 14): market research, display and promotion connected with the foreign enterprise's products or services, and liaison activity connected with product sales, service provision, domestic procurement and domestic investment. Where a law or State Council rule requires approval for such activity, approval must be obtained.

Registration sits with the market regulation authority of the province, autonomous region or municipality (Art. 5), and the office must file an annual report between 1 March and 30 June that includes its activity and audited income and expenditure (Art. 6). One chief representative may be appointed, with one to three representatives (Art. 11), and the office's term may not exceed the foreign enterprise's own existence (Art. 16). The penalty structure is what practitioners actually cite: unregistered operation carries RMB 50,000–200,000 (Art. 35); **for-profit activity carries RMB 50,000–500,000, confiscation of the proceeds and of the tools, equipment, materials or products used, and revocation of the registration certificate in serious cases.** Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan enterprises register their mainland offices by reference to the same rules (Art. 44).

Two practical points follow. A representative office is a **liaison vehicle, not a sales vehicle** — it can support domestic procurement and sales liaison, but it cannot invoice Chinese customers or book the foreign enterprise's revenue. And it is **not an employer**: Article 11 of the State Council's 1980 Provisional Regulations on Administration of Resident Representative Offices — still in force — requires the office to entrust the local foreign-affairs service unit, or another designated unit, when it engages staff. The staff are contracted by that unit and dispatched to the office, which is why a representative office cannot simply sign employment contracts of its own. China's Supreme People's Court confirmed in Judicial Interpretation (II) on labour disputes (Fa Shi [2025] No. 12, in force 1 September 2025, Art. 5) that a lawfully established representative office may be a party to a labour dispute case, and that the foreign enterprise can be joined — a procedural clarification that makes disputes easier to litigate, not a grant of employer status.

### The tax consequence of a mandate that goes too far

This is the clause most representation agreements get wrong. Article 5 of the **Implementation Regulations for the Enterprise Income Tax Law** (State Council Order No. 512) defines an establishment or place in China to include management, business and office establishments — and then adds: where a non-resident enterprise **entrusts a business agent in China** to conduct production or business operations, *including entrusting a unit or an individual to habitually conclude contracts on its behalf, or to store and deliver goods*, **that business agent is deemed to be an establishment or place of the non-resident enterprise in China.**

In plain terms: a representative who introduces, researches and reports does not, of itself, give you a taxable presence. A representative who **routinely signs contracts in your name**, or warehouses and delivers your goods, may. The drafting consequence is direct — if you want the light route, the mandate should say that the representative has **no authority to conclude contracts binding on you**, that orders are subject to your written confirmation, and that the representative does not hold or deliver your inventory. If you want a representative who can close deals without you, that is a legitimate choice, but it is a choice with an income-tax price, and it should be modelled before signature rather than discovered at assessment. Note also that a representative office is itself taxed under a deemed-assessment method: under the SAT's Provisional Measures for Tax Administration of Resident Representative Offices of Foreign Enterprises (Guo Shui Fa [2010] No. 18), where books are inadequate the tax authority may assess income, and **the deemed profit rate may not be lower than 15%**; the conversion formula was amended by SAT Announcement No. 28 of 2016, effective 1 May 2016, to *taxable income = current-period expenses ÷ (1 − deemed profit rate) × deemed profit rate*.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">15%</span><span class="l">The floor on the deemed profit rate applied to a representative office's converted expenditure, where the tax authority assesses income rather than accepting a filed return — so a representative office is taxed on its cost base, not on its results</span><span class="src">Source: SAT, Provisional Measures for Tax Administration of Resident Representative Offices (Guo Shui Fa [2010] No. 18), Art. 8; SAT Announcement No. 28 of 2016</span></div>

## The appointment document: what the power of attorney has to say

The Civil Code is unusually specific about the instrument itself. **Article 165: where the authorization for agency is in writing, the power of attorney shall state the agent's name, the matters entrusted, the scope of authority and the duration, and shall be signed or sealed by the principal.** Article 162 supplies the consequence — an act performed by the agent within the scope of authority and in the principal's name **binds the principal**.

That has three drafting implications for a foreign brand. First, an open-ended "full authority" mandate is a poor instrument: the four elements are the ones Chinese counterparties and courts look for, and broad authority invites the argument that an act fell inside it. Second, the mandate must be **time-limited** — and Article 173 lists how it ends: expiry of the term or completion of the matter, revocation by the principal, resignation by the agent, loss of capacity, death, or termination of the legal person or unincorporated organisation. A representation agreement should mirror those termination triggers so the contract and the power of attorney end together. Third, **the signature block matters**: a foreign enterprise's power of attorney needs an authorised signatory, and — where it is used before Chinese authorities, banks or courts — authentication.

Authentication got significantly easier in 2023. The **Hague Apostille Convention entered into force in China on 7 November 2023**: public documents issued in another contracting state, including corporate powers of attorney, now need only that state's **apostille** and no longer a Chinese consular legalization, and the same applies in reverse. China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that the change cuts the time to put a document in usable form from roughly 20 working days to a few days — an average reduction of about 90% across contracting parties — and removes consular legalization fees. Where your home state is not a contracting state, the older legalization route still applies, and it should be built into the timeline rather than discovered at the bank counter.

## How to appoint a China representative in five steps

**1. Write the mandate from the liability backwards.** Decide first whether the representative may conclude contracts binding on you (tax consequence, above) and whether the relationship is agency, commission agency or intermediary. That decision fixes everything else.

**2. Match the vehicle to the function.** Liaison and research only → representation agreement, or a representative office if you want a registered presence under your own name. Sales, invoicing, licences, storefronts, employment → an entity. Hiring quickly without an entity → dispatch or outsourced services, within the 10% cap and the three-position rule.

**3. Issue a power of attorney that satisfies Article 165** — named agent, enumerated matters, defined authority, fixed term, signed and sealed — and that is authenticated (apostille where available) before it is needed.

**4. Verify the counterparty before appointing it.** A mandate is only as good as the entity that holds it; confirm the registration, scope of business, legal representative and any abnormal-operations listing through the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System ([gsxt.gov.cn](https://www.gsxt.gov.cn/)) rather than relying on a deck.

**5. Put reporting and controls in the contract.** What the representative may spend, what pricing floors bind it, how quotes and buyer data are reported, who owns the relationship, and what happens on termination. Commission structures, expense-only mandates and retainer-plus-success-fee mandates produce very different incentives; choose deliberately.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">10%</span><span class="l">The ceiling on dispatched workers as a share of a user entity's total workforce, on temporary, auxiliary or substitute positions only — the reason "just hire two people in Shanghai" is not a standalone structure</span><span class="src">Source: MOHRSS, Provisional Regulations on Labor Dispatch (Order No. 22, in force 1 March 2014), Arts. 3–4</span></div>

## FAQ

**Can a foreign company appoint a China commercial representative without setting up a Chinese company?** Yes. Appointing a representative is a contract plus a power of attorney, not an entity. Under the Civil Code you can appoint a mainland company or individual as your agent — Article 165 requires a written power of attorney stating the agent's name, the matters, the scope of authority and the duration — as a commission agent trading in its own name for your account (Art. 951), or as an intermediary who only introduces counterparties (Art. 961). What you cannot do without an entity is employ staff, issue Chinese VAT invoices, hold a domestic storefront or act as importer of record; those functions require a mainland-registered enterprise.

**Does appointing a China representative create a permanent establishment?** It can. Article 5 of the Implementation Regulations for the Enterprise Income Tax Law provides that where a non-resident enterprise entrusts a business agent in China to conduct production or business operations — including entrusting a unit or an individual to habitually conclude contracts on its behalf, or to store and deliver goods — that agent is deemed to be an establishment or place of the non-resident enterprise in China. A representative limited to research, introductions and reporting sits outside that formulation; one who routinely binds you does not.

**Can a representative office in China sign contracts and invoice customers?** No. Under State Council Order No. 584, as amended in 2024, a representative office is a non-profit office with no legal personality and may not engage in for-profit activity. Its permitted activities are market research, display and promotion for the foreign enterprise's products or services, and liaison for sales, service provision, domestic procurement and domestic investment. Invoicing Chinese customers for the foreign enterprise's goods, or booking its revenue, falls outside that scope; the penalty for for-profit activity is RMB 50,000 to RMB 500,000, with revocation of the registration certificate in serious cases.

**Can a foreign company hire employees directly in China?** Not as the employer. The Labor Contract Law applies to employers established within China, and an offshore company is not one. A representative office must, under Article 11 of the 1980 State Council rules still in force, entrust the local foreign-affairs service unit to engage staff, who are contracted by that unit and dispatched to the office. Separately, dispatched workers may not exceed 10% of a user entity's total workforce and may only be used on temporary, auxiliary or substitute positions under the MOHRSS Provisional Regulations on Labor Dispatch (Order No. 22).

**Does a power of attorney for a China representative need consular legalization?** Usually not any more. The Hague Apostille Convention entered into force in China on 7 November 2023: public documents issued in another contracting state, including a corporate power of attorney, need only that state's apostille, with no Chinese consular legalization. China's MOFA confirmed the change cuts average cross-border document time from about 20 working days to a few days. For non-contracting states, the traditional legalization route still applies.
