## Weibo Marketing for Foreign Brands in China
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/weibo-marketing-foreign-brands-china
Published: 2026-10-12 · Cluster: Marketing & New Media

## Weibo is not "China's Twitter" — it is the country's public-opinion layer

Weibo marketing is the practice of using China's dominant public microblogging platform — the arena where breaking news, celebrity events and public argument break — to build brand visibility, reputation and search presence rather than direct-response sales. The Twitter analogy misleads: X has no hot search list that sets the national agenda for six hours, and Weibo sells no verification badge as a marketing product. What it sells is a position inside a conversation millions of people are already having.

The platform's own numbers frame the opportunity honestly. In June 2026 Weibo reported 561 million monthly active users and 254 million daily active users ([Weibo Q2 2026, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1595761/000110465926098504/tm2623262d1_ex99-1.htm)); a year earlier those were 588 million and 261 million ([Weibo Q2 2025, HKEX](https://www.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2025/0814/2025081400642_c.pdf)). Roughly 27 million monthly actives disappeared while daily actives barely moved — a stable habit-driven core on a thinning casual audience. You do not build a Weibo presence for reach; you build it to be present when your category is discussed.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">561 million</span><span class="l">Weibo monthly active users in June 2026, down from 588 million a year earlier — while daily actives stayed almost flat at 254 million, down from 261 million.</span><span class="src">Source: Weibo Q2 2026 results (SEC) and Q2 2025 results (HKEX), June 2026 vs June 2025</span></div>

## The three jobs Weibo does better than any other Chinese platform

A China hot search (热搜) is a live ranking of the topics generating the fastest-rising discussion volume on Weibo, used by brands, media and the public as the default index of what the country is paying attention to. It behaves like a national timer: a topic enters the list, holds attention for a few hours, and is gone.

A Weibo Super Topic (超话) is a topic-scoped community with its own feed and moderators, used by brands and fan communities to concentrate ongoing discussion instead of scattering it across the public timeline. It is the part of Weibo that is quietly growing: Q2 2026 results show Super Topic daily active users and discussing users both up double digits year on year, with video watch time also up double digits against flat overall monthly actives.

The third job is search. Weibo's stated 2026 priorities are hot events, social and search, with its AI search product handling multi-turn questions and being embedded into post, video and hot-topic browsing. Weibo is therefore no longer only a feed you buy into — it is a corpus that Chinese search engines and AI assistants read from, including the criticism.

## What a foreign brand can actually buy on Weibo

Weibo advertising is sold as a menu of placements — two premium formats, hot search and splash, plus four working formats: feed advertising, internal search, content heating and creator contracts — used by brands for launch reach, awareness and brand-term defence. The split matters because only the premium two reach people who do not already follow you.

<div class="table-wrap">
<table>
<tr><th>Format</th><th>What it is</th><th>Typical job</th><th>How it is bought</th></tr>
<tr><td>Hot search and topic-page placement (热搜、话题页)</td><td>Reserved advertising positions inside the ranked hot search list or on a topic page, labelled as advertising</td><td>Launch-day reach and media pickup — the only placement that scales beyond your existing followers</td><td>Reserved in advance through Weibo's sales team or an authorised agency; inventory is limited and books out around major events</td></tr>
<tr><td>Super FansTong feed ads (超级粉丝通)</td><td>Native promoted posts in the home, follow, discovery and video feeds, targeted by region, age, interest and behaviour</td><td>Awareness, interaction, follower growth, traffic to a Tmall Global or brand store</td><td>Self-serve or agency, but the account requires mainland business credentials</td></tr>
<tr><td>Weibo search ads</td><td>Keyword auction inside Weibo's own search results</td><td>Defending your brand term and capturing people already searching for you</td><td>Same advertising account as feed ads</td></tr>
<tr><td>Content heating (粉丝头条)</td><td>Paying to lift a specific post you have already published</td><td>Cold-starting a post, or amplifying one that is performing</td><td>In-app, per post, no separate account needed</td></tr>
<tr><td>Creator posts via 微任务</td><td>Weibo's official creator marketplace, where briefs, contracts and payment run through the platform</td><td>Seeding, review content and third-party credibility</td><td>Through the marketplace, or an agency holding the advertising account</td></tr>
<tr><td>Splash screen (开屏)</td><td>Full-screen takeover when the app opens</td><td>One moment of maximum exposure on launch day</td><td>Reserved in advance, sold by day part and city</td></tr>
</table></div>

Weibo publishes no rate card, so every price you are quoted is a broker number. Composite agency quotes for 2026 put feed advertising and Weibo internal search at roughly RMB 0.5–3 per click, enterprise verification at RMB 600 plus an annual review fee, and reserved hot-search placements in the RMB 100,000-plus per day range — several times higher in a launch week. Treat all of it as directional, not published.

What the platform's money says about demand is more useful than the price list. Advertising and marketing revenue was US$381.0 million in Q2 2026, down 1% year on year after growing 2% a year earlier; handset and online-game demand fell while internet services and automobile grew, and Alibaba's Weibo ad spend rose 10% to US$39.2 million. Content marketing and celebrity marketing are where Weibo says its difference lies.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">US$381.0 million</span><span class="l">Weibo advertising and marketing revenue in Q2 2026, down 1% year on year, as handset and online-game demand fell and internet services and automobile grew. Alibaba's Weibo ad spend rose 10%.</span><span class="src">Source: Weibo Q2 2026 unaudited results, June quarter 2026</span></div>

## Why most overseas brands cannot open a Weibo ad account themselves

A Weibo blue-V enterprise account (企业蓝V) is the verified business identity that unlocks advertising, analytics and the creator marketplace, and it is issued only against a mainland Chinese business licence. The barrier is not the RMB 600 fee or the five-day review but the document set behind it: a business licence with matching scope, the legal representative's identity, a corporate bank account, a landing page with an ICP filing, and any sector licence the product requires.

A foreign brand therefore has two routes, and they are not equivalent. It can establish a mainland entity and operate its own account, buying control of the data and the audience relationship at the cost of setup time; or it can work through an authorised agency or Tmall partner that contracts as advertiser under its own licence. The second is faster, but the account, the data and the followers belong to the agency — while the content still carries your name for labelling and liability.

## The rules that decide what you can say, and what you can never buy

Weibo advertising compliance is the set of labelling, endorsement and ranking rules that govern what a brand may publish or buy on the platform, enforced by SAMR, the CAC and the platform itself. Three rules matter more than the rest.

Under SAMR Order No. 72, the Measures for the Administration of Internet Advertising in force since 1 May 2023, content that shares knowledge, experience or product testing and carries a shopping link must be conspicuously marked 广告 — advertising ([SAMR, 2023](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2023/issue_10506/202306/content_6885261.html)). That covers creator posts your agency arranged, not only paid placements; the penalty runs through Article 25 to Article 59 of the Advertising Law — correction plus a fine of up to RMB 100,000 on the publisher.

Endorsement is the second rule. The Advertising Law requires that an endorser has actually used the product and bars endorsers under ten years old. Weibo is where celebrity-led campaigns work best, so an ambassador campaign needs a documented usage basis, not just a signed contract.

The third rule is ranking. The CAC's Provisions on the Ecological Governance of Network Information Content, in force since 1 March 2020, ban traffic fraud, hijacking and account manipulation ([CAC Order No. 5, 2020](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2020/content_5492511.htm)), and name microblog hot lists as a key area where platforms must not present scandal-mongering or mismatched headlines. In November 2024 four departments ordered platforms to publish the algorithms behind their hot search rankings and crack down on paid comment armies ([CAC, 2024](https://www.cac.gov.cn/2024-11/24/c_1734143936205514.htm)); in July 2025 the CAC's Qinglang campaign named paid list-pushing — 刷榜打榜买榜 — as a target ([CAC, 2025](https://www.cac.gov.cn/2025-07/29/c_1755503642582366.htm)). Reserved, labelled positions are legitimate; a guaranteed organic hot search is a different product.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 100,000</span><span class="l">Maximum administrative fine on the ad publisher for failing to identify advertising, including creator content with a shopping link that is not marked 广告</span><span class="src">Source: SAMR Order No. 72 (2023), Article 25, referring to Article 59 of the Advertising Law</span></div>

## When Weibo should be your lead China channel, and when it should not

A lead China channel is the one platform a brand commits its first 6 to 12 months of content and budget to, and Weibo is the right lead only when Chinese demand for the category is event-driven rather than search-driven. That fits sports and outdoor, automobiles, consumer electronics, entertainment-adjacent food and drink, and any brand whose entry story rests on an ambassador, a sponsorship or a public launch.

Search-led categories fit elsewhere. Beauty and skincare, home, and mother-and-baby brands are usually better served leading on Xiaohongshu, where decisions are made by comparison and search, with Douyin leading where the transaction itself is the trend. Whichever route you take, one part of Weibo is not optional: Chinese search engines and AI assistants read it, and negative posts there have a long half-life in results for your brand name.

## A 90-day Weibo sequence for a brand with no China team

A 90-day Weibo sequence is a staged entry plan: audit in month one, choose the operating route in month two, and run one concentrated campaign in month three rather than a drip. Start by auditing mention volume under your brand name, the negative-to-positive ratio, and whether resellers or grey-market accounts already occupy your brand term. Most Western brands find their Chinese name is in someone else's hands.

Month two is structural — choose between a mainland entity operating its own account and an agency contracting as advertiser, and confirm whether you need a verified brand account before planning spend. Month three is one well-built moment: publish the launch narrative, seed eight to fifteen mid-tier creators through the creator marketplace so the content is contracted and labelled correctly, then pair one reserved placement with search ads defending your brand term.

## How to measure Weibo without fooling yourself

Weibo measurement is the practice of judging a campaign on demand-side evidence — brand-term search volume, share of voice and sentiment ratio — rather than follower counts or impressions. Track brand-term search volume on Weibo and Baidu, exposure and dwell time on your topic page, share of voice against named competitors, the negative-to-positive ratio, and whether your store sees an organic-session lift in the 72 hours after a hot moment.

Follower counts are a poor proxy in China, where purchased audiences are cheap and a single event can move numbers by six figures without moving a single purchase. Because Chinese platforms expose less attribution than Western ad networks, pair platform metrics with a demand check you control: brand-term search lift, branded traffic, and the volume of unprompted mentions.

## FAQ

**Should a foreign brand be on Weibo?** Yes, but rarely as a lead channel. Weibo is where Chinese public opinion about your category forms, and posts there are indexed by Baidu and quoted by Chinese AI search products, so monitoring is mandatory whether or not you advertise. Buy media there when your Chinese demand is event-driven — launches, ambassadors, sponsorships, trade shows — and lead with Xiaohongshu or Douyin when demand is search-led or transaction-led.

**Can a foreign company open a Weibo advertising account without a Chinese entity?** Not directly. Advertising, analytics and the creator marketplace all sit behind an enterprise blue-V account, which is issued against a mainland business licence with a legal representative, a corporate bank account and a landing page with an ICP filing. Brands without a Chinese entity work through an authorised agency or Tmall partner that contracts under its own licence, while the brand remains responsible for what the content says.

**How much does Weibo advertising cost?** Weibo publishes no rate card, so all figures are broker quotes. Composite agency quotes for 2026 put feed advertising at roughly RMB 0.5–3 per click, Weibo internal search at RMB 0.5–3 per click, enterprise verification at RMB 600 with an annual review fee, and reserved hot-search placements in the RMB 100,000-plus per day range, quoted far higher during major launches. Treat them as directional: the same placement is quoted at very different levels in a launch week.

**Can you buy a place on the Weibo hot search list?** Reserved advertising positions inside the hot search list can be bought in advance, and they are labelled as advertising. Manipulating the ranking itself is not marketing — the CAC's content governance rules ban traffic fraud, fake accounts and account manipulation, the 2024 four-department algorithm action ordered platforms to publish their ranking logic and crack down on paid comment armies, and the 2025 Qinglang campaign names paid list-pushing (刷榜打榜买榜) as a target. Any agency promising a guaranteed organic hot search result is selling you a regulated act.

**Is Weibo still worth it in 2026, given falling active users?** The decline is real — monthly actives fell from 588 million in June 2025 to 561 million in June 2026, while daily actives barely moved, from 261 million to 254 million. What that describes is a stable habit-driven core and a thinner casual audience. For a brand, Weibo has shifted from a reach channel to a reputation and heat channel, and its value should be judged on share of voice and search lift rather than impressions.

## China Joint Venture or WFOE for China Market Entry
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-joint-venture-vs-wfoe
Published: 2026-10-09 · Cluster: Market Entry & Entity

## Why the joint venture question is now commercial, not legal

For most of China's reform era the joint venture was not an option, it was the only door. The Equity Joint Venture Law of 1979 made a Chinese partner a legal precondition for foreign manufacturing, and an entire generation of entry strategy was built around finding the right one. That door was removed on 1 January 2020, when the Foreign Investment Law took effect and repealed all three of the old foreign-investment statutes ([Law of the PRC on Foreign Investment, NPC](http://www.npc.gov.cn/englishnpc/c2759/c23934/202012/t20201222_384049.html)).

What replaced it is a system nobody designed for joint ventures: pre-establishment national treatment plus a negative list. Outside a short list of restricted activities, a foreign company is treated exactly as a Chinese one at the point of establishment. The commercial result is visible in the data. In 2025 China registered 70,392 new foreign-invested enterprises, up 19.1%, while actual foreign direct investment fell 9.5% to RMB 747.69 billion — more entrants, each committing less capital. In the first half of 2026 the pattern held: 31,617 new foreign-invested enterprises, up 5.3%, on RMB 402.14 billion of investment, down 5% ([MOFCOM, July 2026](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/xwfb/rcxwfb/art/2026/art_ea6d68fe5ee74367a2be1ca271765033.html)).

"Should I take a Chinese partner?" has therefore become a question about capability and control, not about permission. The answer is different for a beauty brand testing Tmall Global and for a company building a Chinese manufacturing base, and it is worth answering deliberately rather than by inherited reflex.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">31,617</span><span class="l">New foreign-invested enterprises registered in China in the first half of 2026, up 5.3% — while actual FDI fell 5% to RMB 402.14 billion. More entrants, smaller cheques.</span><span class="src">Source: MOFCOM monthly FDI release, July 2026</span></div>

## A China joint venture is a limited liability company incorporated in China and owned jointly by a foreign investor and Chinese shareholders, governed since 1 January 2020 by the Company Law rather than by the repealed Equity Joint Venture Law

A China joint venture (中外合资企业) is now a shareholding arrangement, not a separate legal species. Article 31 of the Foreign Investment Law states that the organisational form, governance and rules of activity of a foreign-invested enterprise follow the Company Law and the Partnership Enterprise Law — the same statutes that govern a purely domestic company. The old vocabulary survives in conversation, but in registration documents what you are setting up is an ordinary limited liability company with two categories of shareholder.

Two consequences follow. The protections once specific to joint ventures — prescribed profit-sharing, mandatory board seats, statutory licence terms — are no longer defaults; today they exist only if your articles of association and shareholders' agreement create them. And joint ventures incorporated before 2020 were given five years to keep their original organisational form, a window that closed on 31 December 2024.

## What a Chinese shareholder is still legally required for

The Special Administrative Measures for Foreign Investment Access — the negative list — is the single document that decides whether a foreign investor may own 100% of a Chinese business or must share it. The 2024 edition, issued as NDRC and MOFCOM Order No. 23 and in force since 1 November 2024, cut the national list from 31 entries to 29 and removed the last two manufacturing restrictions: publication printing, previously reserved for Chinese control, and the production of certain traditional Chinese medicine preparations. Manufacturing is now the first major sector with zero foreign-access restrictions ([State Council policy interpretation, September 2024](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/202409/content_6973149.htm)).

The five consecutive revisions between 2017 and 2021 already took the national list from 93 entries to 31 and the separate free-trade-zone list from 122 to 27, with the free-trade zones clearing manufacturing restrictions in 2021 ([NDRC interpretation, November 2024](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/202411/content_6988059.htm)). What remains in the 29 entries sits in agriculture and seed breeding, energy and resources, telecommunications, media and publishing, education and healthcare, and only a subset of those entries still requires a Chinese controlling shareholder or caps foreign equity. For a consumer-goods brand, the negative list does not require a partner.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">0</span><span class="l">Manufacturing restrictions remaining on China's national foreign-investment negative list. The 2024 edition cut the list from 31 entries to 29 and cleared the sector entirely.</span><span class="src">Source: NDRC &amp; MOFCOM Order No. 23 of 2024, in force 1 November 2024</span></div>

## The structures that replaced the old binary choice

Choosing an entry structure means deciding who is legally responsible for importing, registering and selling the product in China, and how much of the brand's margin and control that party takes. Three structures cover the overwhelming majority of consumer-brand entries, and a fourth is only for cases where a partner's licence is genuinely the product.

<div class="table-wrap">
<table>
<tr><th>Structure</th><th>Control and capital</th><th>Typical time to first sale</th><th>When it fits</th></tr>
<tr><td>Overseas or Hong Kong entity + licensed importer of record</td><td>No Chinese entity, no Chinese equity. The importer declares and holds the customs relationship.</td><td>6–10 weeks (GOODSINFINITE case benchmark)</td><td>Cross-border and bonded retail tests; a first read on demand before committing capital</td></tr>
<tr><td>WFOE (wholly foreign-owned company)</td><td>100% foreign ownership. Capital subscribed and paid in within five years.</td><td>3–6 months including licences (GOODSINFINITE case benchmark)</td><td>Domestic e-commerce, general trade, onshore staff, invoicing in renminbi, own import licence</td></tr>
<tr><td>Joint venture with a Chinese shareholder</td><td>Shared ownership and shared board control. Your partner's capital and capability arrive with their rights.</td><td>3–7 months plus negotiation</td><td>Restricted activities, or where a licence, key account or factory cannot be contracted</td></tr>
<tr><td>Distribution agreement only</td><td>No equity, no registration. The distributor owns the customer relationship.</td><td>4–8 weeks</td><td>Fast shelf access in a category where brand control matters less than coverage</td></tr>
</table>
</div>

The commercial distinction is between owning a capability and renting it. A licensed importer of record, a Tmall partner and a distributor all supply the Chinese counterparty that customs and platforms require without any equity changing hands — which is why "do I need a Chinese partner" and "do I need a Chinese company" are different questions.

## Capital and control rules that tightened in 2024

Registered capital rules are where most structure decisions are quietly decided. The revised Company Law took effect on 1 July 2024 and requires shareholders of a limited liability company to pay in their subscribed capital within five years of establishment, ending the era of arbitrarily long subscription periods. The State Council's implementing regulation, Order No. 784, set the transition: companies registered on or before 30 June 2024 whose remaining contribution period would still exceed five years from 1 July 2027 must adjust it to five years or less by 30 June 2027 ([State Council Order No. 784, July 2024](https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/content/202407/content_6960376.htm)).

Most sectors have no statutory minimum registered capital, so the number in the articles is a choice — but it is no longer a free one. A large nominal figure is now a legal obligation with a five-year clock, and a joint venture partner who cannot fund their share of it becomes a liability on your balance sheet. Under the Company Law, voting rights default to the proportion of capital contributed unless the articles provide otherwise, so any protection you want — reserved matters, board composition, transfer restrictions on your partner's stake, a route out — has to be written into the articles and the shareholders' agreement. Governance is a drafting exercise, and it is cheaper than litigation.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">30 June 2027</span><span class="l">Deadline for Chinese companies registered before mid-2024, including foreign-invested ones, to cut any remaining capital contribution period to five years or less</span><span class="src">Source: State Council Order No. 784, implementing the revised Company Law (2024)</span></div>

## Policy incentives now favour structure over partnership

China's incentive framework has also shifted toward rewarding structure rather than partnership. The 2025 Action Plan for Stabilising Foreign Investment, circulated in February 2025, pushes deregulation in telecommunications, healthcare and education and commits to revising the rules on foreign acquisition of domestic enterprises, including lowering the threshold for cross-border share swaps ([State Council General Office, 2025](https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2025/issue_11906/202503/content_7011165.html)). The revised Catalogue of Industries Encouraging Foreign Investment, effective 1 February 2026, expanded to 1,679 entries — a net increase of 205 on the 2022 edition — with 619 national and 1,060 regional entries ([NDRC and MOFCOM, December 2025](https://www.gov.cn/lianbo/202512/content_7052652.htm)). Those benefits attach to what an entity does on the ground, not to who owns it, which again favours choosing the right structure over adding a partner for appearances.

## A decision sequence that holds up

- **Confirm the activity is off the negative list.** If it is not restricted, a Chinese shareholder is a choice, not a requirement — price it accordingly.
- **Decide what you are optimising for.** Speed to first sale, control of the brand, or reach into offline distribution rarely point to the same structure.
- **Check whether the capability can be contracted.** Import declaration, licence holding, platform operation, warehousing and last-mile delivery are all purchasable services.
- **If you incorporate, test the capital plan against the five-year rule.** Size registered capital to what you can fund, and insist your partner does the same.
- **Write governance before you sign equity.** Board seats, reserved matters, dividend policy, non-compete and exit mechanics are negotiated once, when you have leverage — then reviewed in year two, when a contracted partner's performance makes the equity conversation cheaper.

## FAQ

**Do I need a Chinese joint venture partner to sell in China?** Almost never. The national negative list that still requires Chinese ownership covers 29 restricted entries, concentrated in agriculture, energy, telecommunications, media, education and healthcare — manufacturing has required no Chinese partner since 1 November 2024. Cross-border retail, general trade through an importer of record, bonded storage and most consumer categories are all open to a wholly foreign-owned company or an overseas entity.

**Is a China joint venture still a distinct legal form?** No. Since 1 January 2020 the Foreign Investment Law has governed all foreign investment, and it repealed the Equity Joint Venture Law along with the other two old foreign-investment statutes. A joint venture today is simply a limited liability company with both foreign and Chinese shareholders, organised under the Company Law. Chinese-foreign equity joint ventures established before 2020 had five years to keep their original organisational form, a window that closed on 31 December 2024.

**What is the real difference between a joint venture and a WFOE?** Both are Chinese limited liability companies. The difference is shareholding and, therefore, control: a WFOE is wholly owned by the foreign investor, while a joint venture splits equity with a Chinese shareholder. Registration time and the capital rules are broadly the same. The joint venture adds a co-owner to every decision, which is why it should be chosen for the capability a partner brings, not for legal necessity.

**How much registered capital do I need, and when must it be paid in?** Most sectors have no statutory minimum registered capital. Since the revised Company Law took effect on 1 July 2024, shareholders of a limited liability company must pay in their subscribed capital within five years of establishment. Companies registered before 30 June 2024 whose remaining contribution period runs beyond five years from 1 July 2027 must adjust it to five years or less by 30 June 2027, a deadline that applies to foreign-invested companies as well.

**When is a Chinese partner genuinely worth the equity?** When the licence, the key account, the distribution network or the government relationship cannot be rented. Most of what brands want from a partner — import declaration, licence holding, platform operation, retail distribution — can be contracted with an import agent, a Tmall partner or a distributor. Our default recommendation is to contract for 12 to 24 months, prove revenue, and only then consider converting the relationship into equity.

## Selling on 1688 as a Foreign Brand: China's B2B Marketplace Needs a Mainland Entity
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/selling-on-1688-china-b2b
Published: 2026-10-09 · Cluster: E-commerce Operations

## Selling on 1688 as a foreign brand resolves to one legal fact: 1688 is a domestic wholesale marketplace, and its seller door opens only to a mainland-registered market entity

**1688.com is Alibaba's domestic wholesale marketplace — the platform where Chinese factories, wholesalers and retailers trade with each other inside China.** Listings are in Chinese, prices are in renminbi, delivery is to Chinese addresses, and the trading rules are China's domestic e-commerce rules. Its supplier onboarding requires a **mainland China business licence** in the seller's own name.

That single line answers most of the question "how do I sell on 1688 as a foreign brand?" The confusion is usually directional. Teams read "Alibaba" and assume 1688 is a Chinese-language mirror of the same shop — sign up, upload a catalogue, ship. It is not. 1688 is a **China-inward** channel, and a foreign company cannot open a 1688 store in its own name. What it can do is own or partner with a mainland entity that holds the licence and the storefront.

> The entity question is settled before the strategy question. Until a mainland market entity exists — owned or contracted — there is no 1688 store to design, price or staff.

## Gate one: China's e-commerce law requires every online seller to hold a market entity

The **E-Commerce Law of the PRC**, in force since 1 January 2019, is explicit. Article 10: *电子商务经营者应当依法办理市场主体登记* — online business operators must register as market entities. The carve-outs are narrow: individuals selling self-produced farm products or home handicrafts, individuals providing licensed convenience services, and *零星小额* (small and sporadic) trade.

How small is small was left open until the SAMR's **Network Transaction Supervision Measures** (Order No. 37, in force 1 May 2021) fixed the number in Article 8: an individual whose **cumulative annual online turnover does not exceed RMB 100,000 — combining all stores on all platforms — does not need to register.** Above that threshold, registration is mandatory; and where the activity requires an administrative licence at all, registration is mandatory regardless of size.

For scale, SAMR reported to the National People's Congress in 2024 that more than **15 million** natural-person online stores on platforms remained unregistered — 59.1% of all platform operators — precisely because most sit inside that exemption.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">¥100,000</span><span class="l">The only practical line that lets an individual sell online in China without registering a market entity — cumulative annual turnover across every store on every platform</span><span class="src">Source: SAMR Order No. 37 (Network Transaction Supervision Measures), Art. 8; SAMR reply to the NPC, 2024</span></div>

1688's own supplier documentation follows the statute. Its onboarding guide requires a valid **mainland business licence** — enterprise or individual industrial and commercial household — whose business scope covers the goods being sold, the legal representative's identity documents, and, in higher-risk or high-ticket categories such as 3C and building materials, a **corporate bank account** bound for settlement and deposits. The platform validates the licence in real time against the National Enterprise Credit Information Publicity System, so a mismatched or expired licence is rejected before a human ever reviews it. Category qualifications sit on top: food needs a food business licence; cosmetics need filing or registration depending on origin; listed electronics need CCC certification; medical devices need filing or registration. Some categories — cosmetics and fire-safety equipment among them — accept an **enterprise licence only**, not an individual household licence. The platform also charges a category-based deposit and a paid annual membership tier, and the amounts are set by the platform rather than negotiated.

## Gate two: foreign investors cannot use China's cheap entity, so the vehicle has to be a company

China has a lighter vehicle than a company — the **个体工商户 (individual industrial and commercial household)**, a sole-trader licence that is far cheaper and faster to obtain. For a foreign-owned brand that door is closed by law.

The **Special Administrative Measures for Foreign Investment Access (Negative List), 2024 edition** — NDRC and MOFCOM Order No. 23, published 6 September 2024 and in force from 1 November 2024 — states in its explanatory provisions that **foreign investors may not operate as an individual industrial and commercial household, as the investor in a sole-proprietorship enterprise, or as a member of a farmers' professional cooperative.**

The good news is that the sector itself is open. In the 2024 negative list the only entry under *wholesale and retail* is a prohibition on foreign investment in the wholesale and retail of tobacco leaf, cigarettes, redried tobacco leaf and other tobacco products. Everything else in wholesale and retail falls outside the list, which under the list's own terms means it is administered on a **national-treatment basis** — so a wholly foreign-owned enterprise (WFOE) with a wholesale and retail business scope is the standard vehicle, and 100% foreign ownership is available.

The practical sequence for a foreign brand that wants to sell wholesale in China therefore runs: incorporate the mainland company → obtain the business licence with the right scope → complete tax registration and taxpayer status → open the corporate bank account and enterprise payment account → secure category qualifications → then the platform store. That is a project measured in months, not days. [WFOE vs. representative office](wfoe-vs-representative-office.html) compares the entity options; [China joint venture or WFOE](china-joint-venture-vs-wfoe.html) covers what a Chinese shareholder is still legally required for.

## Direction test: 1688 sells into China, Alibaba.com sells out of it

The two platforms share a parent and face opposite ways. Getting this wrong is the most common and most expensive error in a "should we be on 1688?" conversation.

<div class="table-wrap">
<table>
<tr><th>Dimension</th><th>1688.com</th><th>Alibaba.com</th></tr>
<tr><td>Purpose</td><td>China domestic wholesale (内贸)</td><td>Global cross-border trade (外贸)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Language and currency</td><td>Chinese / renminbi</td><td>Multilingual / US dollars</td></tr>
<tr><td>Who sells</td><td>Mainland-licensed enterprises and individual households</td><td>Chinese suppliers geared for export</td></tr>
<tr><td>Who buys</td><td>Chinese retailers, wholesalers, factories, live-commerce and cross-border sellers</td><td>Overseas importers and distributors</td></tr>
<tr><td>A foreign brand as seller</td><td>Not directly — a mainland entity must hold the licence and the store</td><td>Yes — this is the export-facing route</td></tr>
<tr><td>Do the goods need to be in China?</td><td>Yes — domestic settlement and domestic delivery</td><td>No — goods are exported from China</td></tr>
</table>
</div>

1688 does have a cross-border face, but it points the other way. [global.1688.com](https://global.1688.com/), the platform's "跨境专供" channel, is built for **overseas buyers** sourcing from Chinese factories. Xinhua reported that 1688's cross-border order volume grew more than 70% in 2024 and that the platform planned to enter 15 overseas countries and regions in 2025, serving overseas small and mid-sized B2B buyers — including cross-border purchasing agents, overseas marketplace sellers and independent-store operators.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">96 million</span><span class="l">1688's buyer base, up from 65 million two years earlier, with paid buyer members above 10 million — the reason the channel is worth the entity cost</span><span class="src">Source: Xinhua / 1688, February 2025 (news.cn)</span></div>

In September 2025, at an "AI跨境·国货出海" event in Shenzhen, 1688 launched **"超级工厂全球版"** — a certification standard for factories with genuine cross-border capability, gated on cross-border transaction scale, an overseas warehouse or warehousing partnership, storefronts on mainstream cross-border platforms, and at least one further condition (original-equipment manufacturing for a known brand, inclusion in the 专精特新 "小巨人" list, or a high Sesame Credit rating). Approved factories receive a **"超级工厂全球供"** badge and priority in the cross-border buyer recommendation pool.

Every one of those moves serves overseas buyers sourcing from China. None of them creates a route for a foreign brand to sell on 1688 without a mainland market entity.

## What a foreign brand actually needs to sell B2B in China

Five requirements, in order of when they block you.

**1. A mainland market entity with the right scope.** Typically a WFOE. A Hong Kong company is an offshore entity: it can be your trading counterparty, contract holder and IP holder, but it cannot hold a mainland business licence or a 1688 store in its own name. See [using a Hong Kong entity to import into China](hong-kong-entity-china-import.html).

**2. Tax registration and invoice capability.** Chinese B2B buyers expect a Chinese VAT invoice — for corporate purchasers, a 增值税专用发票 (VAT special invoice) so they can deduct input VAT. Under the **VAT Law passed on 25 December 2024 and in force since 1 January 2026** (which replaced the Interim Regulations on VAT), the rate on the sale of goods is **13%**, and a small-scale taxpayer is one with annual taxable sales **not exceeding RMB 5,000,000**, on a 3% simplified levy rate. The structural point for a foreign brand is blunt: **an offshore company cannot issue a Chinese VAT invoice.** Without a mainland entity — or a mainland partner that invoices — you cannot complete a compliant domestic B2B sale, whatever the platform.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">13%</span><span class="l">Standard VAT rate on the sale of goods under the VAT Law in force since 1 January 2026; small-scale taxpayer threshold is RMB 5 million of annual taxable sales</span><span class="src">Source: VAT Law of the PRC, Arts. 9–10 (cpc.people.com.cn)</span></div>

**3. Category qualifications.** Platform-side listing permission is not product permission. Food, cosmetics, medical devices, listed electronics and other regulated categories each carry their own gate, and 1688's onboarding checks them per category. See [which Chinese agency regulates my product](which-chinese-agency-regulates-my-product.html).

**4. The goods physically in China.** 1688 is domestic trade. Your imported products must be landed in China, normally under **general trade**, with customs duty and import VAT paid, and held in domestic stock that a licensed entity can deliver from.

**5. A person on the ground.** Chinese wholesale closes in Chinese, on DingTalk and WeChat, and often in person. Store operation is not a listing exercise — it is buyer qualification, quotation, credit terms, after-sales and relationship maintenance. That is a headcount question as much as a platform question.

## Why the goods question decides the model

Two ways to have sellable stock in China, and they lead to different structures.

If the product is **made in China** — your own contract manufacturing or an OEM factory — stock exists domestically and the 1688 route is a licence-and-operations problem: choose the entity, get the scope, list, staff it.

If the product is **imported**, the goods must clear duty before they can be sold domestically. General trade puts duty and import VAT on at the border, and the goods then sit in domestic stock. Bonded storage is different: goods in a bonded warehouse have not yet paid duty, and bonded cross-border retail — the 1210 model — is a business-to-consumer channel for individual end consumers, with per-order clearance and consumer-facing delivery. It is not a wholesale route, so it cannot substitute for landed, duty-paid inventory when the objective is distribution to Chinese business buyers. [What 1210 bonded import is](what-is-1210-bonded-import.html) sets out the difference; [China import taxes and landed cost](china-import-taxes-landed-cost.html) covers the arithmetic.

This is the practical divide between a cross-border launch and a domestic wholesale build. A cross-border storefront can be run from offshore through a 1210 bonded structure with no Chinese company — that is the lean test. A 1688 distribution channel cannot: it needs the entity, the invoice capability and the duty-paid stock. Choose the channel and you have chosen the structure.

> Cross-border tells you whether the market wants the product. Domestic wholesale tells you how much of it the market will take. They are sequential questions, not alternatives.

## What the channel is worth — and what it costs in control

1688 is not primarily a place to sell single units. It is where you reach the **Chinese resellers, regional wholesalers, retail chains, live-commerce sellers and cross-border merchants** that then distribute your product onward. A single working 1688 relationship can put your brand into hundreds of downstream storefronts: Xinhua reported that 1688's distribution business grew order volume 70% in 2024 across 20 downstream marketplace channels, with one-click listing into multiple platforms.

The trade-off is real. An open wholesale channel means many sellers quoting your product, and price discipline has to be managed deliberately — through tiered pricing, authorised-seller structures and packaging differentiation — or the listing price collapses and gray-market leakage follows. The upside is data: you see end-buyer demand directly, keep the customer list and hold the brand relationship, which is what a pure distributor agreement gives away. For most brands the right answer is a mainland-operated store you control, not a distributor's catalogue you never see.

## FAQ

**Can a foreign company open a store on 1688 in its own name?** No. 1688 is Alibaba's domestic wholesale marketplace, and its supplier onboarding requires a mainland China business licence held by an enterprise or an individual industrial and commercial household, with a business scope covering the goods, plus the legal representative's ID and, in several categories, a corporate bank account. An offshore company — including a Hong Kong company — is not a mainland market entity and cannot open a 1688 seller account directly. In practice the store is held by a mainland entity you own, or by a partner operating it for you.

**Can I sell on 1688 as an individual, without a business licence?** Not at the scale of a distribution channel. Article 10 of the E-Commerce Law requires online operators to register as market entities; the only practical exemption is small and sporadic trade, defined by the SAMR's Network Transaction Supervision Measures (Order No. 37, Art. 8) as cumulative annual online turnover of no more than RMB 100,000, combining all stores across all platforms. Above that line registration is mandatory, and 1688's onboarding checklist assumes a licence in the seller's own name.

**Can a foreign investor register the mainland entity as an individual industrial and commercial household (个体工商户)?** No. The 2024 negative list for foreign investment access (NDRC and MOFCOM Order No. 23, in force 1 November 2024) excludes foreign investors from operating as individual industrial and commercial households, as sole-proprietorship enterprise investors, or as farmers' professional cooperative members. A foreign brand therefore needs a company, typically a WFOE. Wholesale and retail sit outside the negative list except for tobacco products, so a wholesale/retail business scope is available on a national-treatment basis.

**Is 1688 the right platform to reach buyers outside China?** No. For buyers outside China, the export-facing route is Alibaba.com. 1688's cross-border channel, global.1688.com ("跨境专供"), is a buyer-side door for overseas purchasers sourcing from Chinese factories, and its "超级工厂全球版" certification recognises Chinese factories with cross-border capability. 1688 itself settles in renminbi, delivers domestically and follows domestic trading rules — it is a channel into China, not out of it.

**Do I have to import my goods into China before selling them on 1688?** Effectively yes. 1688 is domestic trade: orders settle in renminbi and delivery is to Chinese addresses, so imported products must first be landed in China, normally under general trade, with customs duty and import VAT paid, and held in domestic stock. Cross-border bonded retail (1210) is a business-to-consumer channel for individual consumers and is not a B2B wholesale route, so it cannot replace landed inventory if 1688 distribution is the objective.

## China Consumer Segmentation by City Tier and Income
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-consumer-segmentation-city-tier-income
Published: 2026-10-07 · Cluster: Market Research

## Why "China" is always a segmentation question

Every foreign brand arrives with the same first question — how big is the market — and the honest answer is that the national number is the least useful figure available. China's total retail sales of consumer goods reached RMB 50.12 trillion in 2025, up 3.7% ([National Bureau of Statistics, December 2025 retail release](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202601/t20260120_1962354.html)) — a number large enough to justify almost any decision and precise enough to inform almost none. What actually decides whether an entry case survives is which slice of that 50 trillion behaves like your customer, and where those people live.

## China consumer segmentation is the practice of splitting the national market into groups of buyers who differ in income, geography, age and buying behaviour, so a brand can choose a beachhead instead of scattering budget

China consumer segmentation (消费者细分) is the analytical step that converts "China" into three or four addressable groups, each with its own price ceiling, channel preference and content diet. It exists because the three axes that drive Chinese consumer behaviour — city tier, household income quintile and age cohort — do not move together: a 28-year-old in Chengdu may outspend a 45-year-old in a tier-3 city on cosmetics while spending less on healthcare, and both may outspend the national average. Segmenting first changes product mix, price architecture and channel choice at the same time.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 43,377</span><span class="l">China's per-capita disposable income in 2025, up 5.0% — the national average that hides every segment you actually care about</span><span class="src">Source: National Bureau of Statistics, 2025 household income release (Jan 2026)</span></div>

## The city-tier framework: how 337 Chinese cities are graded

China's city-tier system is a commercial classification rather than an administrative one: the Yicai New Tier-1 Cities Institute scores 337 prefecture-level and above cities each year on commercial-resource density, connectivity, consumer activity, new-economy competitiveness and future potential, then sorts them into tiers. In the 2025 edition the ranking held four tier-1 cities (Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou) and fifteen new tier-1 cities — Chengdu, Hangzhou, Chongqing, Wuhan, Suzhou, Xi'an, Nanjing, Changsha, Zhengzhou, Tianjin, Hefei, Qingdao, Dongguan, Ningbo and Foshan — followed by 30 tier-2, 70 tier-3, 90 tier-4 and 128 tier-5 cities ([Yicai, 2025 city ranking](http://yicai.com/news/102638963.html), republished by the [Luoyang Municipal Government](https://m.ly.gov.cn/2025/05-29/568652.html)).

The practical value is the availability lag. Yicai measures roughly a 1.5-month gap between a brand launching in Shanghai and appearing in Chengdu, with Hangzhou and Nanjing inside six months — which means a brand can run a tier-1 pilot and a new tier-1 follow-on almost as one campaign, rather than a decade apart as the old "first tier-1, then wait" playbook assumed. New consumption categories such as coffee and sports/outdoor have already reversed the direction in Chengdu and Hangzhou.

<div class="table-wrap">
<table>
<tr><th>Tier</th><th>Cities (2025)</th><th>What it means for a foreign brand</th></tr>
<tr><td>Tier 1</td><td>4 — Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen, Guangzhou</td><td>Price ceiling and trend-setting. Highest imported-goods penetration, most competitive shelf.</td></tr>
<tr><td>New tier 1</td><td>15 — incl. Chengdu, Hangzhou, Chongqing, Wuhan, Suzhou, Tianjin</td><td>The volume growth engine. Nearly tier-1 willingness to pay at lower media cost.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Tier 2</td><td>30</td><td>Prove replication. Requires a distributor or a lighter channel model.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Tier 3–5</td><td>288</td><td>Reach through e-commerce and live commerce rather than physical distribution.</td></tr>
</table>
</div>

## What the household income distribution actually looks like

Household income quintile grouping is the National Bureau of Statistics method of ranking all households by per-capita disposable income and dividing them into five equal groups, which makes it the most honest available picture of who can afford a premium price. In 2025 the five groups averaged RMB 10,150, 22,702, 35,536, 55,586 and 103,778 per person respectively, while the national median income was RMB 36,231 — only 83.5% of the mean, confirming a distribution pulled up by its top tail ([NBS via gov.cn, 2025 national economic performance](https://www.gov.cn/lianbo/fabu/202601/content_7055290.htm)).

Two implications follow. First, "the Chinese middle class" is a marketing abstraction, not a segment: the top two quintiles — around 40% of households — is the defensible proxy for imported-goods demand, and the top quintile alone is where luxury and premium beauty pricing becomes routine. Second, urban and rural income still differ by a factor of 2.31 (RMB 56,502 against RMB 24,456 in 2025, urban growth 4.3% versus rural 5.8%), so a single national price point is either too expensive for most of the country or too cheap for the buyers who matter.

## Lower-tier cities and rural demand are the faster-growing half of the market

County-level and rural consumer markets are the portion of Chinese consumption outside city districts, measured separately because their growth rate and channel mix now diverge from the urban core. In 2025 rural retail sales grew 4.1% against 3.6% in cities, and county and rural markets together accounted for 38.7% of all retail sales ([MOFCOM, Department of Circulation Development, 2025 wholesale and retail review](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/syxwfb/art/2026/art_f8416017c8e24d1f83160afcf0303e10.html)). Rural online retail passed RMB 3 trillion for the first time, up 6.7%, with agricultural products online up 9.9% ([gov.cn / Xinhua, Feb 2026](https://www.gov.cn/lianbo/202602/content_7057158.htm)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">38.7%</span><span class="l">Share of China's total retail sales coming from county-level and rural markets in 2025 — growing faster than the cities</span><span class="src">Source: MOFCOM Department of Circulation Development, 2025 review</span></div>

What made this reachable is infrastructure, not aspiration. Every county in China now has a logistics distribution centre, and 8,132 fifteen-minute convenience life circles have been built across 210 pilot cities, serving 168 million residents. For a foreign brand the consequence is straightforward: a cross-border or bonded e-commerce model can now serve tier-3 and tier-4 consumers directly, which removes the distributor requirement that used to gate those markets.

## Age is now a two-market split, not a demographic footnote

Age segmentation in China means separating a shrinking cohort of young, urban, globally oriented consumers from a rapidly expanding older cohort with very different spending priorities. At the end of 2025, 323.38 million people — 23.0% of the population — were aged 60 or above, and 223.65 million were 65 or above, while the 16–59 working-age group fell to 60.6% of the population. Urbanisation reached 67.89%, up 0.89 percentage points in a single year ([NBS statistical communiqué, 2025](https://www.stats.gov.cn/xxgk/sjfb/zxfb2020/202601/t20260119_1962330.html)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">323.38 million</span><span class="l">Chinese residents aged 60+ at the end of 2025 — 23.0% of the population and the core of the health and functional-food market</span><span class="src">Source: National Bureau of Statistics, 2025 statistical communiqué (Feb 2026)</span></div>

That split produces two different entry cases. The 25–40 urban cohort drives cross-border beauty, sports and outdoor, and premium packaged food, and is reached through content platforms. The 60+ cohort drives functional food, medical devices, health monitoring and senior-friendly personal care, and is reached through repeat purchase and channel trust rather than influencer discovery. A brand that has not chosen which of these it is selling to usually ends up under-spending on both.

## Which segments actually buy imported goods

An imported-goods buyer is a Chinese consumer who accepts a landed-cost premium in exchange for provenance, safety or category-specific expertise. Two filters govern access. The product must sit on the positive list for cross-border retail imports, and the tax framework sets the economics: within the RMB 5,000 per-order and RMB 26,000 per-person annual limits, tariff is zero and import VAT and consumption tax are levied at 70% of the statutory amount — 9.1% effective on a 13% VAT product, rising to roughly 23.1% for high-end cosmetics because the 15% consumption tax applies ([Cai Guan Shui [2018] No. 49, Shanghai Municipal Tax Service](https://shanghai.chinatax.gov.cn/zcfw/zcfgk/jckss/201812/t443050.html)).

Category growth shows where buyer willingness actually sits. In 2025, retail sales above designated size grew 15.7% for sports and recreational goods, 12.8% for gold and jewellery, 11.0% for household appliances, 5.1% for cosmetics and just 2.2% for clothing, while brand-exclusive stores shrank 0.6% ([NBS, December 2025 retail release](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202601/t20260120_1962354.html)). Offline brand exclusivity is no longer a proxy for premium demand — online physical-goods retail grew 5.2% to 26.1% of all retail, and food was the fastest-growing online category at 14.5%.

## How to build a segmentation-based entry case

A segmentation-based entry case is a short document that names two to four segments, sizes each in yuan rather than in national percentages, and states the channel and price point that reaches them. In practice it has five parts.

- **Cut by city tier first.** Determine whether your price point survives in tier-3 economics; if not, name the eight to twelve cities that matter and stop pretending the rest exist.
- **Confirm the income quintile.** Place your product against the RMB 55,586 and RMB 103,778 per-person benchmarks rather than the national average of RMB 43,377.
- **Pick the age cohort.** Cross-border beauty and the 60+ wellness market have almost nothing in common operationally.
- **Check the regulatory gate before the business case.** Category determines whether you need registration, filing or nothing at all, and that determines the calendar.
- **Size with channel data, not national statistics.** A category at 0.5% nationally can be viable in a beachhead, and unviable everywhere else.

## How GOODSINFINITE fits

GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED acts as importer of record and in-market operator for overseas brands testing China, which means the segmentation work above is normally the first thing we do with a new brand rather than a deliverable bolted onto a launch. We combine category retail data, city-tier distribution reality and bonded-warehouse reach across Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou and Qingdao to translate a segmentation choice into an SKU list, a channel plan and a landed cost. Start with our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) for the sequence, and the [glossary](https://www.goods-infinite.com/glossary.html) for the terminology you will meet in platform and customs documents.

## FAQ

**How many consumer segments does China actually have?** Most brands work with three overlapping cuts: geography (4 tier-1 cities, 15 new tier-1 cities, then 30 tier-2, 70 tier-3, 90 tier-4 and 128 tier-5 cities in the 2025 Yicai ranking), household income quintiles, and age cohort. Three to five target segments is normally enough for an entry case; more than that and the research stops informing decisions.

**Is the Chinese middle class really 400 million people?** Treat that figure with caution. The defensible 2025 anchor is the National Bureau of Statistics income quintile table: the upper-middle quintile averaged RMB 55,586 per person and the top quintile RMB 103,778, against a national median of RMB 36,231. In practice, the reliable buyer pool for imported goods is the top two quintiles — roughly 40% of households — concentrated in tier-1, new tier-1 and the stronger tier-2 cities.

**Are lower-tier Chinese cities worth targeting for a premium brand?** Yes, but for volume and first-time buyers rather than prestige. County and rural markets together reached 38.7% of total retail sales in 2025, rural retail grew 4.1% against 3.6% in cities, and rural online retail passed RMB 3 trillion. Brand-availability gaps have also narrowed — Yicai measures only about a 1.5-month lag between a brand launch in Shanghai and Chengdu.

**How do I size the imported-goods buyer for my category?** Combine three sources: NBS category retail growth for the category baseline, the cross-border retail import tax framework for landed cost, and platform search or sales data for the specific category. Then apply the city-tier cut, because imported-goods concentration is far higher in tier-1 and new tier-1 cities than the national population share implies. A category that looks small nationally can be a viable beachhead in eight cities.

**Should segmentation come before or after compliance work?** Before. Segmentation determines which product SKUs, price points and channels are worth registering at all, and China product registration is SKU-specific and slow. Brands that complete a segmentation exercise first typically register fewer, better-chosen SKUs — which shortens the registration calendar and reduces the cost of the first year.

## Medical Device in China: Which Class (I/II/III) and What Approval?
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-medical-device-classification
Published: 2026-10-07 · Cluster: Compliance & Registration

## Definition: what "medical device class" means in China

In China, **"which class" is the first question for any medical device — because the class determines the entire market-access path.** The country runs a **risk-based, three-tier system**: Class I (low risk), Class II (moderate risk) and Class III (higher risk). The class is fixed by law in the *Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Medical Devices* (医疗器械监督管理条例, State Council Order No. 739, as amended by Order No. 797 effective 20 January 2025), and the legal consequence is binary — **Class I is filed, Class II and Class III are registered.**

The single most useful thing to know: **classification is catalog-driven, not negotiable by brand.** You do not argue your way into a lower class; you find your product in the official Classification Catalog, and if it is not there, NMPA tells you the class.

## The legal baseline: three classes, one statute

Article 6 of the Regulations defines the three tiers by risk:

- **Class I** — low risk; routine management ensures safety and effectiveness (e.g. surgical scissors, bandages, examination gloves, medical X-ray film).
- **Class II** — moderate risk; strict control is required to ensure safety and effectiveness (e.g. blood pressure monitors, thermometers, ECG machines, infusion sets, hearing aids).
- **Class III** — higher risk; special measures are needed throughout the lifecycle (e.g. cardiac pacemakers, vascular stents, artificial joints, artificial cochleae, haemodialysis machines, implantable devices).

The risk level is judged on **intended purpose (预期目的), structural features (结构特征) and method of use (使用方法)** — the same factors NMPA applies when it issues a classification determination.

> The class is the gate. Everything else — dossier depth, review body, timeline, whether you need an in-China agent — flows from this one number.

## How to determine the class: the decision tree

China runs a **classification-rules-guided, catalog-first** system. The practical order is:

1. **Look it up in the Classification Catalog (医疗器械分类目录).** The 2017 version (NMPA Announcement No. 104) took effect on 1 August 2018 and remains the master list, organised into 22 sub-catalogs with product descriptions, intended-use statements and example product names. The catalog is kept current through a **dynamic adjustment mechanism** (NMPA Announcement No. 60 of 2021), so it changes over time — for example Announcement No. 101 of 2023 adjusted 58 catalog entries, including upgrading certain soft-tissue ultrasonic scalpel heads and breast-biopsy devices to Class III.
2. **If the catalog does not fit, use the Classification Rules (医疗器械分类规则, NMPA Order No. 15).** These rules set the principles — for instance, a device supplied sterile is classed no lower than Class II, and an absorbable device is managed as Class III.
3. **If still unclear, apply for a classification determination (分类界定).** For newly developed products not yet in the catalog, Article 23 of the Regulations lets you either apply directly for Class III registration or ask NMPA to confirm the class — NMPA must decide within **20 working days**. Where a product's attributes are genuinely ambiguous, this NMPA opinion is the authoritative answer.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">3 classes</span><span class="l">Every device in China falls into Class I, II or III under State Council Order No. 739; the class is set by risk (intended use + structure + method of use), not by the manufacturer's preference</span><span class="src">Source: Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Medical Devices, Art. 6 (nmpa.gov.cn)</span></div>

## What approval each class requires

Article 13 of the Regulations is the pivot: **Class I = product filing (备案); Class II and Class III = product registration (注册).** The filing/registration authority then depends on whether the device is made in China or imported.

| Class | Domestic (境内) | Imported (进口) | Mechanism |
|-------|-----------------|-----------------|-----------|
| **Class I** | Filing with **municipal** drug regulatory authority — effective on submission | Filing by the overseas filer's **designated China agent** with **NMPA** | Filing (备案) |
| **Class II** | Registration with **provincial** drug regulatory authority | Registration with **NMPA** | Registration (注册) |
| **Class III** | Registration with **NMPA** | Registration with **NMPA** | Registration (注册) |

These authority splits are codified in SAMR Order No. 47 (*Measures for the Registration and Filing of Medical Devices*, issued 26 August 2021, effective 1 October 2021), Article 8 — the implementing rule beneath the Regulations.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">5 years</span><span class="l">A medical device registration certificate (Class II/III) is valid for 5 years; renewal must be filed 6 months before expiry under Art. 22 of the Regulations</span><span class="src">Source: Regulations on the Supervision and Administration of Medical Devices, Art. 22 (nmpa.gov.cn)</span></div>

## Imported devices: the two hard requirements

If you are an overseas brand, registration is gated by two rules in SAMR Order No. 47 that foreign teams routinely miss:

- **You must appoint a China domestic agent.** Article 14 requires the overseas applicant/filer to designate a **China domestic enterprise legal person** as its agent. That agent, not your overseas company, files with NMPA and assists you in meeting your legal obligations.
- **You must show overseas marketing authorisation.** Article 18 requires the certificate of marketing authorisation issued by the competent authority in the country where the device is registered or manufactured (the proof it is lawfully sold there). An innovative device not yet marketed overseas can be exempted from this document.

This is why "no local company" does **not** mean "no China presence." You do not need to incorporate a WFOE to register a device — but you do need a licensed mainland agent. That is a different, lighter structure than a full entity, and it is exactly the slot a Hong Kong trading entity plus a mainland importer-of-record arrangement fills.

> Practical read: the device class decides the *depth* of approval; your entity structure decides *who files*. Most overseas brands register through a China agent while keeping the brand-owning layer offshore — see [importing into China without a local company](importing-into-china-without-a-local-company.html) and [using a Hong Kong entity to import](hong-kong-entity-china-import.html).

## Class II/III registration: what actually gets reviewed

Registration is a substantive review, not a notification. The dossier must demonstrate the device is safe, effective and quality-controlled, and typically includes: risk analysis, product technical requirements, test reports, clinical-evaluation data (with exemptions for mature products), labelling, and quality-system documentation. CMDE performs the technical review; the provincial or national authority then issues the administrative approval.

- **Clinical evaluation is the usual rule** (Art. 24), with exemptions for mature, well-understood products (e.g. devices with a long domestic track record and no serious adverse events).
- **Review timeframes** are set in working days at the CMDE level; real-world timelines stretch with supplementary-data rounds, so build buffer into any launch plan.
- **The agency that regulates devices is NMPA** (with provincial and municipal drug regulators handling Class II and Class I) — distinct from GACC (food), SAMR (non-device product standards) or CNCA (compulsory certification for some electronics). See our [agency-map guide](which-chinese-agency-regulates-my-product.html) for the full split.

## Where GOODSINFINITE fits the device path

For an overseas device maker, the bottleneck is rarely the science — it is the **China-side operational layer**: a licensed agent to file, the dossier in Chinese, and a compliant way to land and fulfil inventory. We run that layer so the class decision becomes a plan, not a blockage:

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">6,000㎡ + 8,000㎡</span><span class="l">Bonded warehouse (6,000㎡) plus temperature-controlled storage (8,000㎡), a self-operated AEO Advanced Certification with 15 partner AEOs, and a five-city fulfilment network for registered and filed devices</span><span class="src">Source: GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED operations</span></div>

- **China agent / importer of record.** GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED (Hong Kong) acts as your overseas trading counterparty; a mainland-licensed entity serves as the designated agent for filing/registration and clears customs as the importer of record.

Start by nailing the class: look up the catalog, and if it is ambiguous, get NMPA's determination early — because the class is what sets your clock, your cost and your authority.

## FAQ

**How do I know if my medical device is Class I, II or III in China?** China uses a risk-based, catalog-driven system. Look the product up in the NMPA Classification Catalog (2017 version, Announcement No. 104, updated via dynamic adjustments such as Announcement No. 101 of 2023). If it is listed, the catalog states the class. If not listed or unclear, apply to NMPA for a classification determination; for new products NMPA decides within 20 working days. Class is driven by intended use, structure and method of use.

**Does a Class I medical device need NMPA registration?** No. Class I (low risk) is subject to filing (备案), not registration. A domestic Class I device is filed with the municipal drug regulatory authority and takes effect on submission. An imported Class I device is filed by the overseas filer's designated China agent with NMPA. Filing is record-keeping, not substantive review.

**Who approves Class II and Class III registration?** Class II is registered with the provincial drug regulatory authority. Class III, and all imported Class II and Class III devices, are registered with NMPA; CMDE performs the technical review. The registration certificate is valid for 5 years.

**Can a foreign company register a device in China without a local entity?** Not directly. Under SAMR Order No. 47, an overseas applicant must designate a China domestic enterprise legal person as agent and submit the overseas marketing-authorisation certificate. The China agent files with NMPA. A Hong Kong trading entity plus a mainland agent/importer of record satisfies this without forming a WFOE.

**What is the difference between filing and registration?** Filing (备案) applies only to Class I and takes effect on submission — it is a notification. Registration (注册) applies to Class II/III and is a substantive review by the authority, issuing a 5-year certificate. Registration is the real market-access gate for moderate- and high-risk devices.

- NMPA — *Measures for the Registration and Filing of Medical Devices* (SAMR Order No. 47, issued 26 Aug 2021, effective 1 Oct 2021), Art. 8, 14, 18: [nmpa.gov.cn](https://www.nmpa.gov.cn/)
