## Tmall Global TP Partner: How Foreign Brands Choose a Tmall Partner (TP) Operator
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/tmall-global-tp-partner
Published: 2026-09-01 · Cluster: E-commerce Operations

## Why the TP question comes up before the store goes live

Most foreign brands discover the term "TP" the moment they get serious about Tmall Global. The store application is manageable, the [eligibility and cost picture is documented](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/tmall-global-store-setup.html), and then reality lands: the merchant back end is entirely in Chinese, customer enquiries must be answered in Mandarin within platform response targets, and the promotional calendar runs on mechanics no overseas team has seen before. That gap is what the TP ecosystem exists to fill. This guide explains what a Tmall Global TP partner actually does, how the commercial models work, how to vet one properly, and when hiring one is the wrong move.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 2.38 trillion</span><span class="l">China's cross-border e-commerce import and export value in 2023 — the channel a Tmall Global TP is hired to operate inside</span><span class="src">Source: General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) cross-border e-commerce statistics, 2023</span></div>

## A Tmall Global TP partner is an Alibaba-recognised service provider that operates a foreign brand's flagship store on the brand's behalf, supplying the local team for listings, customer service, campaigns and data

A Tmall Partner (天猫服务商, commonly shortened to TP) is an agency formally recognised within Alibaba's service-provider ecosystem and engaged to run a brand's store day to day. The brand remains the merchant of record and the store owner; the TP supplies the operating capability that sits behind the storefront. A typical scope covers six workstreams:

- **Store setup and visual design** — building the flagship shopfront, category navigation and campaign pages to Tmall's design conventions.
- **Listing and content localisation** — Chinese product titles, attribute fields, detail pages and search-relevant copy.
- **Customer service (客服)** — Mandarin pre-sales and after-sales response through Alibaba's Wangwang messaging tool, measured against platform service metrics.
- **Campaign and promotion management** — registering for 6.18, Double 11 and Double 12, structuring coupon and bundle mechanics, and negotiating platform traffic slots.
- **Paid traffic operation** — running Alibaba's in-platform advertising products against an agreed target return on ad spend.
- **Reporting and category analytics** — reading the store's data back into pricing, assortment and forecasting decisions.

The cross-border channel this sits inside is regulated rather than informal: retail imports through it are governed by the cross-border e-commerce retail import framework jointly administered by China's Ministry of Commerce, Customs and other agencies ([MOFCOM](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn)), which is why a competent TP also needs to understand the bonded fulfilment layer, not just marketing.

## What a TP does not do — and why that boundary matters

The most expensive misunderstanding in this market is assuming a TP replaces your entire China function. It does not. Three things almost always sit outside the scope:

1. **Product compliance and registration.** A TP is not a regulatory consultancy. Whether your goods need registration or filing before sale depends on category and channel, and it remains the brand's legal responsibility — see our [China product registration roadmap](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-product-registration-foreign-brands.html).
2. **Import of record and bonded fulfilment.** Physical movement of goods into a bonded warehouse, customs declaration and last-mile delivery are handled by an import agent or logistics partner. Some larger TPs bundle this through affiliates; many do not.
3. **Brand strategy and pricing authority.** A TP optimises within the strategy you set. If you outsource positioning and price architecture, you will typically get discount-led volume that is hard to unwind later.

## The three fee models, and what each one incentivises

TP commercial terms cluster into three shapes, and each creates a different behaviour:

- **Fixed monthly retainer.** Predictable, and appropriate when GMV is still small. Frequently quoted in the USD 3,000–10,000 per month range depending on headcount and scope. The weakness is that the TP earns the same whether the store grows or stagnates.
- **Commission on GMV.** Roughly 5–15% of store sales, sometimes tiered. Aligns the TP with growth, but pushes toward discounting because gross GMV — not margin — is the metric being paid on.
- **Hybrid (reduced retainer plus commission).** The most common structure for serious launches and usually the fairest: the retainer covers the fixed operating team, the commission rewards genuine growth.

Whichever shape you pick, treat **media spend as a separate, transparent pass-through** with monthly platform-side reporting. Advertising is often the largest first-year line item, and a TP that marks up media without disclosure is the most common source of disputes. The same open-book logic we apply to [transparent import pricing](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/transparent-import-pricing.html) should govern your TP relationship.

## How to vet a TP partner in five checks

Due diligence here is not complicated, but it is routinely skipped:

1. **Verify the legal entity, not the brochure.** Check the operating company's business licence and standing in the national enterprise credit information system maintained by China's market regulator ([SAMR](https://www.samr.gov.cn)). The entity signing your contract should be the entity with the track record.
2. **Confirm the service-provider grade.** Ask for the TP's listing and grade in Alibaba's official service marketplace, and confirm the categories it is authorised and experienced in. A TP that is excellent in home appliances is not automatically credible in skincare or infant nutrition.
3. **Demand category references you can call.** Two or three brands in your category, at comparable stage, contacted directly. Case-study decks are marketing collateral, not evidence.
4. **Interview the actual operating team.** Business development sells; a separate junior team often delivers. Ask who your store lead and customer-service staff will be, and how many other stores they carry.
5. **Read the exit clause first.** Confirm store account ownership, admin credential control, data and creative-asset handover, and a notice period of 60–90 days. If exit terms are vague, expect the handover to be painful.

## Store ownership: the structural point most brands get wrong

The Tmall Global store must be registered to **your** overseas entity, with your brand holding the master administrator account and granting the TP sub-account access only. Where a TP opens the store under its own entity "to speed things up", the brand ends up renting access to its own China customer base — and switching partners means starting again with zero review history and zero followers. This is not a hypothetical risk; it is the most common cause of stranded China operations. Note that operating through a Hong Kong or other offshore entity is entirely workable here and often preferable, as covered in our guide to [using a Hong Kong entity to import into China](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/hong-kong-entity-china-import.html).

## When to hire a TP — and when to skip one

**Hire a TP when** you are launching your first China store, have no Mandarin-speaking commercial team, need customer service coverage against platform SLAs from day one, and want to be live before a major shopping festival.

**Skip or in-source when** monthly GMV comfortably supports two or three dedicated hires, your assortment is narrow and stable, or your category is so technical that outside operators cannot represent the product credibly. Many brands run a sensible arc: TP for the first 12–24 months to buy speed and local knowledge, then a hybrid model where an in-house lead sets strategy and the TP executes customer service and campaigns.

Either way, sequence matters. Do not appoint a TP before your compliance route and fulfilment model are settled — a store that cannot legally receive and ship inventory is an expensive shopfront. Our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) sets out the order of operations, and the [glossary](https://www.goods-infinite.com/glossary.html) decodes the platform vocabulary your TP will use in every call.

## FAQ

**What is a TP partner on Tmall Global?** TP stands for Tmall Partner — an Alibaba-recognised service provider (代运营) that operates a brand's Tmall Global store on its behalf, covering store setup, listings, Mandarin customer service, campaigns such as 6.18 and Double 11, and reporting. The brand keeps ownership of the store and its data.

**Do I need a TP to sell on Tmall Global?** No. Tmall Global permits self-operation, but most foreign brands use a TP at launch because the back end is Chinese-language, customer service must respond in Mandarin within platform SLAs, and campaign mechanics shift every season. Brands often in-source once volume justifies a dedicated team.

**How much does a Tmall Global TP cost?** Typically a monthly retainer of roughly USD 3,000–10,000 depending on scope, a GMV commission of about 5–15%, or a hybrid of both. In-platform advertising spend is a separate pass-through cost and is frequently the largest first-year line item.

**How do I verify a TP is genuinely certified?** Request its profile and grade on Alibaba's official service marketplace, confirm its category track record, obtain two or three referenceable brands you can contact, and verify the operating entity's business licence through the SAMR national enterprise credit system.

**Who owns the store and the customer data if I use a TP?** The brand should. Register the store to your own overseas entity, retain master admin credentials, and contract explicitly for customer data, content and creative to remain with the brand on exit. A store held under the TP's own account is the biggest structural risk in this model.

## Sources

- [State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) — national enterprise credit information system](https://www.samr.gov.cn)
- [Tmall Global — official merchant onboarding portal](https://www.tmall.hk)
- [China market entry guide — GOODSINFINITE](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html)

## Finding a China Distributor for Foreign Brands: Agent, Partner, or Local Entity
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-distributor-for-foreign-brands
Published: 2026-08-31 · Cluster: Logistics & Distribution

## Why "find a China distributor" is the wrong question on its own

Every overseas brand eventually hears the same advice: "you need a China distributor." The problem is that "distributor" in China covers at least three structurally different arrangements — an import agent that clears and fulfills, a distribution partner that owns resale into retail, and a local entity you control outright. Picking the wrong one wastes margin, cedes brand control, or delays launch by months. This guide compares the three so you can choose reach without losing the upside. Our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) places distribution inside the full entry sequence.

## A China distributor is a local counterparty that takes your product to Chinese end buyers through retail, pharmacy, or platform channels, either as an agent, a reseller, or your own entity

A China distributor (经销商/渠道商) is any local party that moves your goods from the port to the Chinese consumer — but the legal and commercial shape varies enormously. At one end, an import agent simply lands and fulfills your product while you keep the customer relationship. At the other, a distributor buys or takes title and resells into supermarkets, pharmacies, specialty retail, or platform storefronts, owning the route to the buyer. Knowing which model you are negotiating is the first step to a sane contract. The distinction matters because China's cross-border e-commerce trade reached about RMB 2.38 trillion in 2023 per the General Administration of Customs, and much of that flow is routed through exactly these intermediaries ([GACC](https://www.customs.gov.cn)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">244,000+</span><span class="l">Overseas buyers attended the 135th Canton Fair (spring 2024) — the single largest venue for foreign brands to meet China distribution partners</span><span class="src">Source: China Foreign Trade Centre / MOFCOM, 135th Canton Fair, 2024</span></div>

## Model 1: The import agent (lowest commitment, fastest start)

An import agent helps you bring product INTO China without owning downstream resale. Services typically include:

- Customs clearance and declaration (general trade 0110 or cross-border 1210).
- Bonded warehousing in cities such as Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou, and Qingdao.
- 1210 bonded fulfillment for Tmall Global, JD Worldwide, or Douyin cross-border.
- China e-commerce operations support.

The flow is foreign brand → Chinese consumer, but the agent stays behind the scenes. Our [import agent vs. sourcing agent explainer](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-import-agent-vs-sourcing-agent.html) clarifies the direction of flow, since the two terms are constantly confused.

## Model 2: The distribution partner (real channel reach, shared control)

A distribution partner actually places product into retail and platform channels and often takes title. Choose this when you want physical or online shelf presence without building your own sales force. Trade fairs are the primary hunting ground: the Canton Fair drew over 244,000 overseas buyers at its 135th session in spring 2024, and country pavilions at CIIE (China International Import Expo) are purpose-built for exactly this matchmaking ([MOFCOM](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn)). Vet partners on category experience,现有 network, and whether they can carry the required registration.

## Model 3: Your own local entity (maximum control, maximum commitment)

A Wholly Foreign-Owned Enterprise (WFOE) lets you import, hold inventory, hire locally, and run domestic stores — full control of brand, pricing, and customer data. The cost is time and capital: registration under the PRC Company Law, a registered address, and months of setup. Our [WFOE setup guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/wfoe-china-import-setup.html) details the timeline. Most disciplined brands defer this until volume proves the market.

## How to choose: a decision frame

- **Prove demand first** → import agent + cross-border (1210). Lowest risk, fastest.
- **Enter retail/pharmacy** → distribution partner with category reach.
- **Scale and control** → WFOE once data justifies the spend.

The pattern that protects margin is to start upstream and move downstream only on evidence, rather than signing a multi-year distribution lock-in on day one.

## Compliance you cannot delegate away

A distributor cannot legally sell regulated product without the approvals in place, so registration is a prerequisite, not a nice-to-have:

- **Food** → GACC overseas-manufacturer registration (Decree 248) ([GACC](https://www.customs.gov.cn)).
- **Cosmetics** → NMPA filing (general) or registration (special) under CSAR ([NMPA](https://www.nmpa.gov.cn)).
- **Electronics / many consumer goods** → CCC certification where applicable ([SAMR](https://www.samr.gov.cn)).

Our [product registration roadmap](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-product-registration-foreign-brands.html) maps which authority owns your category before you sign any distributor.

## Protecting your brand through the relationship

The single most overlooked step is trademark registration: China is first-to-file, so whoever registers the mark owns it. Register before any distribution or platform activity. Then use a written agreement with clear territory, pricing, and termination clauses, keep control of e-commerce accounts where possible, and retain an importer of record for compliance. Our [trademark registration guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-trademark-registration-foreign-brand.html) covers the filing traps that have cost brands their own name.

## FAQ

**What is the difference between a China distributor and an import agent?** An import agent helps you bring product INTO China (customs, bonded warehousing, 1210 fulfillment, e-commerce operations) but does not usually own downstream resale. A distributor buys or takes title and resells into retail, pharmacy, or platform channels, owning the route to the end buyer.

**How do foreign brands find a China distributor?** Common routes are industry trade fairs (the Canton Fair drew over 244,000 overseas buyers at its 135th session in spring 2024), chambers of commerce and country desks, platform partner directories, and vetted import-agent networks. Verify track record, category experience, and registration capacity.

**Should a foreign brand use a distributor or set up its own local entity?** A distributor is faster and needs less capital, at the cost of margin and control. A WFOE gives full control but takes months and committed spend. Most brands prove demand through an agent or distributor first, then form a WFOE when volume justifies it.

**Do I need product registration before appointing a China distributor?** For regulated categories, yes. Food needs GACC registration, cosmetics need NMPA filing/registration, and many goods need CCC. A distributor cannot legally sell regulated product without these in place.

**How should a foreign brand protect its brand with a China distributor?** Register your trademark in China first (first-to-file rule), use a clear distribution agreement with territory and termination clauses, keep control of e-commerce accounts where possible, and retain an importer of record for compliance.

## Sources

- [Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) — trade fairs and distribution policy](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn)
- [General Administration of Customs (GACC) — import and registration](https://www.customs.gov.cn)
- [National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) — cosmetic registration](https://www.nmpa.gov.cn)
- [State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) — CCC and advertising](https://www.samr.gov.cn)
- [China market entry guide — GOODSINFINITE](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html)

## China Social Commerce Agency: What It Does and When a Foreign Brand Needs One
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-social-commerce-agency
Published: 2026-08-31 · Cluster: Marketing & New Media

## Why "social commerce" is one word in China, not two

In Western markets, "social media" and "e-commerce" are separate disciplines run by separate teams. In China they have collapsed into a single loop: a consumer discovers a product in a Xiaohongshu note or a Douyin livestream, taps a link, and buys without ever leaving the app. For a foreign brand, that means marketing and selling are the same motion — which is exactly what a China social commerce agency exists to run. This guide explains what such an agency does, how it differs from a plain KOL agency, and when bringing one in pays off. Our [China KOL agency guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-kol-agency.html) covers the creator-casting layer in depth.

## A China social commerce agency is a full-service operator that turns Chinese social-platform attention into store sales by combining KOL casting, content, live-streaming and store operations under one team

A China social commerce agency (社交电商代运营) is an agency that owns the entire path from discovery to purchase on Chinese platforms — not just the content. It casts and manages KOLs and KOCs (key opinion consumers), produces short-video and livestream content, books paid amplification, and operates the downstream store (Tmall Global, JD Worldwide, Douyin cross-border) so that traffic converts. The scale it plays in is enormous: China's live-streaming e-commerce GMV reached about RMB 4.9 trillion in 2023, much of it creator-driven, according to Ministry of Commerce data ([MOFCOM](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn)). For a foreign brand without a local team, this agency substitutes the entire China commercial function.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 4.9 trillion</span><span class="l">China's live-streaming e-commerce GMV in 2023 — the conversion scale a social-commerce agency is built to capture</span><span class="src">Source: Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) live-commerce market estimates, 2023</span></div>

## Social commerce agency vs. KOL agency: the commerce layer is the difference

The two terms overlap but are not the same:

- **KOL agency** — creator discovery, contracting, content briefing, booking, reporting. Stops at awareness and engagement.
- **Social commerce agency** — everything a KOL agency does, plus store operations, fulfillment coordination, promo planning, and sales attribution. Owns conversion.

If your objective is brand awareness, a [Xiaohongshu marketing approach](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/xiaohongshu-red-marketing-foreign-brand.html) through a KOL agency may suffice. If your objective is revenue, the social-commerce agency is the fuller fit because it closes the loop inside your store.

## What the agency actually runs, week to week

A typical engagement blends five workstreams:

1. **Casting and audience audit.** Proposing creators with follower-quality data and weeding out fake engagement.
2. **Content production.** Short videos for Douyin, seeding notes for Xiaohongshu, and livestream scripts.
3. **Live-commerce operation.** Running Douyin and Taobao Live sessions, including hosts and real-time promotion.
4. **Store and fulfillment coordination.** Linking creator traffic to your Tmall Global or Douyin cross-border store, with 1210 bonded fulfillment behind it ([bonded-to-consumer delivery](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-bonded-to-consumer-delivery.html)).
5. **Attribution and reporting.** Reconciling reach, engagement, and sales against trackable links or discount codes.

## How the engagement and fee model works

Compensation usually takes one of three shapes, often blended:

- **Retainer + media spend** — a monthly management fee plus pass-through budget for creators and ads.
- **Commission on sales (CPS)** — the agency earns a percentage of attributed sales, common on Douyin where links are trackable.
- **Project fee per campaign** — a fixed price for a launch or seeding sprint, sometimes with a top-creator seeding fee on top.

The negotiation principle is the same as with a KOL agency: tie a meaningful share of pay to measured outcomes, not vanity metrics, because reach without conversion wastes budget.

## Compliance you must build in from day one

Chinese advertising law is strict on efficacy and comparison claims, and "种草" (grass-planting) content can be deemed an advertisement. A competent social-commerce agency bakes in a content-compliance sign-off before anything goes live, because a single non-compliant claim can trigger a platform takedown and a regulator fine under SAMR's Internet Advertising Measures ([SAMR](https://www.samr.gov.cn)). Our [social-media advertising compliance guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-social-media-advertising-compliance.html) is the reference brands hand to their agency.

## When to bring one in — and when not to

Hire a China social commerce agency when:

- You are ready to convert attention into revenue on Chinese platforms.
- You lack a local team to run stores and live-commerce.
- You are launching or hitting a sales peak (6.18, Double 11).
- You need compliant content produced at platform speed.

Hold off if you are still in pure market-research mode or have not yet secured the required product registration — there is no point driving traffic to a store you cannot legally fulfill. Our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) shows where social commerce sits in the staged entry plan.

## FAQ

**What does a China social commerce agency actually do?** It combines influencer/KOL casting, short-video and live-stream content, paid amplification, and store operations so social traffic converts into sales inside your Tmall Global, JD Worldwide, or Douyin store — owning the conversion path end to end.

**How is a social commerce agency different from a KOL agency?** A KOL agency focuses on creator discovery, booking, and content; a social commerce agency adds the commerce layer — store setup, fulfillment coordination, promo planning, and attribution. For sales rather than awareness, it is the fuller fit.

**When should a foreign brand hire a China social commerce agency?** When you are ready to convert attention into revenue on Chinese platforms and lack a local team to run stores and live-commerce — most valuable at launch and during sales peaks, and when you need compliant content under China's advertising rules.

**How are China social commerce agencies paid?** Typically a retainer plus media spend, a commission on attributed sales (CPS), or a per-campaign project fee, often with a top-creator seeding fee. Tie pay to measured outcomes and trackable links, not follower counts.

**What are the main risks of using a social commerce agency in China?** Fake followers and inflated engagement, off-brand or non-compliant claims under SAMR rules, and weak attribution. Mitigate with audience audits, pre-approved scripts, and KPIs tied to trackable links or codes.

- [Douyin — official business platform](https://www.douyin.com)

## How to Sell on Tmall Global from Abroad Without a China Entity
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/sell-on-tmall-global-from-abroad
Published: 2026-08-31 · Cluster: E-commerce Operations

## Why Tmall Global is the default on-ramp for brands selling into China from abroad

For an overseas brand, the fastest way to reach Chinese consumers used to mean forming a Chinese company, renting office space, and building a local team — a 6–12 month commitment before the first sale. Tmall Global inverts that sequence: it is Alibaba's cross-border storefront where a foreign or Hong Kong entity sells directly to mainland shoppers, with goods cleared per order and delivered from a bonded zone. This guide walks through exactly how to sell on Tmall Global from abroad, what you do and do not need, and where a Tmall Partner fits. Our [cross-border e-commerce China guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/cross-border-ecommerce-china.html) covers the 1210 model that makes this possible.

## Tmall Global is Alibaba's cross-border retail platform that lets an overseas or Hong Kong entity sell directly to Chinese consumers without a mainland business licence

Tmall Global (天猫国际) is the cross-border arm of Tmall where foreign brands operate flagship stores aimed at Chinese buyers, with goods imported under cross-border e-commerce rules rather than general trade. The defining advantage for an overseas seller is the merchant of record: you can register as an overseas company — for example a Hong Kong trading entity such as GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED — and avoid forming a Wholly Foreign-Owned Enterprise (WFOE) in mainland China. China's cross-border e-commerce trade reached about RMB 2.38 trillion in 2023 according to the General Administration of Customs, and Tmall Global is one of the primary storefronts capturing that flow ([GACC](https://www.customs.gov.cn)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">~900 million</span><span class="l">Annual active consumers across Alibaba's China retail marketplaces — the demand base a Tmall Global storefront taps</span><span class="src">Source: Alibaba Group annual consumer disclosures</span></div>

## Cross-border vs. domestic Tmall: what "from abroad" actually means

The phrase "sell on Tmall Global from abroad" only makes sense once you separate the two Tmall routes:

- **Tmall Global (cross-border).** You are an overseas/HK entity. Goods sit in a bonded zone (1210) or ship by direct mail, cleared per order, with cross-border tax applied at checkout. No mainland licence required for the store itself.
- **Domestic Tmall / Tmall Flagship (general trade).** You need a China-incorporated entity, a Chinese business licence, and full product registration (NMPA, GACC, CCC, etc.) before listing. This is the "local company" route.

For a first entry, cross-border is lower risk: you prove demand on Tmall Global, then upgrade to a domestic store only once the data justifies the heavier regime. Our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) lays out this staged sequence.

## The entity and documents you need to register from abroad

To open a Tmall Global store as a foreign brand you typically prepare:

- **Overseas or Hong Kong business licence** proving the company is registered outside mainland China.
- **Brand ownership or authorisation** — trademark certificate or a licence from the rights holder.
- **Importer of record / fulfillment arrangement** — a bonded (1210) or direct-mail plan, often run through a China import agent or your HK trading company.
- **Category approvals where required** — special cosmetics need NMPA registration, imported food needs GACC manufacturer registration, under China's pre-market rules ([NMPA](https://www.nmpa.gov.cn), [GACC](https://www.customs.gov.cn)).

Crucially, you do not need a mainland WFOE to launch cross-border, which is why this route is the standard answer to "how do I sell on Tmall Global from abroad."

## The Tmall Partner (TP) model: running the store without a local team

A Tmall Partner (TP, 代运营) is an Alibaba-accredited agency that sets up and operates your flagship store end to end. For a foreign brand with no local staff, the TP is often the missing operational layer:

- Store design, listing, and pricing in line with Chinese shopping norms.
- Coordination with bonded warehousing and per-order customs clearance (1210).
- Promotion planning around Tmall's mega-sales (6.18, Double 11) and everyday traffic.
- Customer service and returns in Mandarin.

Most overseas brands run Tmall Global entirely through a TP, which removes the need to hire a China e-commerce team on day one. Our [JD Worldwide setup guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/jd-worldwide-store-setup.html) describes the parallel cross-border route if you want platform diversification.

## Fulfillment: how orders actually reach the buyer

Once a shopper orders, the goods are released from the bonded zone (if 1210) or dispatched via direct mail, cleared per order, and delivered by a domestic carrier (Cainiao, SF, JD Logistics) in 1–3 days from a well-positioned zone. GOODSINFINITE's five-city bonded network — Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou, Qingdao — covers most of China's addressable demand inside that window. The [bonded-to-consumer delivery guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-bonded-to-consumer-delivery.html) explains the last mile in detail.

## Compliance and tax you still cannot skip

Selling from abroad relaxes the entity requirement but not the rules. You remain subject to cross-border tax per order, product-specific registration for regulated categories, and China's strict advertising and labelling standards once you market on-platform. The [social-media advertising compliance guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-social-media-advertising-compliance.html) is the reference for claim and disclosure rules that also apply to store content. Plan these before launch, not after a takedown.

## FAQ

**Can a foreign brand sell on Tmall Global without a China company?** Yes. Tmall Global is Alibaba's cross-border channel and accepts an overseas or Hong Kong entity as the merchant of record. A China importer of record (or your Hong Kong trading company) handles customs and bonded fulfillment, so no mainland WFOE is required for the store.

**What is the difference between Tmall Global and a domestic Tmall store?** Tmall Global is cross-border: goods clear per order (often under 1210 bonded or direct mail) without a mainland business licence. A domestic Tmall store requires a China-incorporated entity, Chinese business licence, and full product registration before sale.

**What does a Tmall Partner (TP) do for a foreign brand?** A TP is an accredited agency that sets up and operates your flagship store — design, listing, pricing, bonded/fulfillment coordination, promotion, and customer service — letting many foreign brands run Tmall Global with no local operations team.

**How long does it take to open a Tmall Global store from abroad?** With documents ready, onboarding typically runs a few weeks to two months depending on category and whether product registration is required. Cross-border categories generally move faster than general-trade imports.

**Do I still need product registration to sell on Tmall Global?** It depends on the channel. Cross-border (1210) retail relaxes many pre-market rules for general cosmetics and supplements, while special cosmetics, food, and infant formula still need NMPA or GACC approvals.

## How Big Is the China FMCG Market and Who Buys Imported Goods
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-fmcg-market-size
Published: 2026-08-28 · Cluster: Market Research

## Why market size is the first question every brand asks

Before a brand commits budget to entering China, the board asks one practical question: how big is the prize, and is there a real audience for what we sell? "Entering China" is not a single market but a layered one — coastal megacities with Westernized tastes, a vast middle-income belt, and lower-tier cities catching up fast. This article sizes the FMCG opportunity with the figures decision-makers actually cite, and identifies the cohorts most likely to buy imported goods, so you can build a realistic entry case instead of a hope case.

## China FMCG market is the total annual retail value of fast-moving consumer goods bought by Chinese households, spanning food, beverage, personal care and home care

China FMCG market (快速消费品市场) is the aggregate annual retail value of fast-moving consumer goods — packaged food, beverages, personal care, and household products — purchased by Chinese households through all channels, from supermarkets to live-streaming apps. It is the most useful denominator for a foreign consumer brand because it strips out cars, appliances, and real estate and focuses on the repeat-purchase categories where imported positioning carries a premium. The market's scale is set by China's total consumption base, and even a single-digit share of a category can represent a multi-billion-yuan opportunity.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 47.1 trillion</span><span class="l">China's total retail sales of consumer goods in 2023 — the demand base behind every FMCG entry case</span><span class="src">Source: National Bureau of Statistics of China (NBS), 2023</span></div>

## How big the market actually is

China's total retail sales of consumer goods reached about RMB 47.1 trillion (roughly US$6.6 trillion) in 2023, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. FMCG is a substantial, steadily growing slice of that total, and crucially it is a consumption-led market: household spending rather than exports drives the bulk of demand. Urban households account for the majority of premium and imported purchases, while rural and lower-tier consumption is the fastest-rising segment as incomes converge. For a foreign brand, the implication is simple — the absolute top of the funnel is enormous, and the job is to find the category and city-tier where your specific offer fits.

## Who buys imported goods

Demand for imported consumer goods is concentrated in a few well-defined cohorts:

- **The middle-income belt.** Often cited at more than 400 million people, this group trades up on safety, quality, and provenance — the exact cues "imported" signals ([NBS](http://www.stats.gov.cn) / World Bank income estimates).
- **Women and younger households.** Beauty, maternal, and wellness imports skew heavily toward urban women aged 25–45, who are also the most active on Xiaohongshu and Douyin.
- **Health- and safety-conscious parents.** Infant formula and child products remain the clearest imported-wins category, where trust outweighs price.
- **Lower-tier cities as the frontier.** As logistics and cross-border delivery reach prefecture-level cities, first-time imported-goods buyers are appearing far beyond Beijing and Shanghai.

## Where imported goods win

"Imported" is not a uniform advantage — it over-indexes in specific categories where provenance equals trust:

- **Infant formula and maternal products** — the original imported-wins category.
- **Beauty and cosmetics** — where European, Japanese, and Korean brands command premiums.
- **Wine, spirits, and premium food** — gifting and self-reward occasions.
- **Health supplements** — driven by an aging and wellness-focused population.

In these segments a foreign brand can price above local equivalents and still grow, provided compliance and storytelling are handled correctly.

## The channel shift to cross-border and live commerce

The buying path has changed as fast as the size. China's cross-border e-commerce trade reached about RMB 2.38 trillion in 2023 (General Administration of Customs), and bonded import models such as 1210 now let foreign brands sell into China without incorporating locally. At the same time, live-commerce and social platforms — Douyin, Xiaohongshu, WeChat — have become primary discovery channels, meaning market entry is now as much about content and KOL strategy as about retail distribution. Our [cross-border e-commerce China guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/cross-border-ecommerce-china.html) explains the 1210 model that makes this low-friction entry possible.

## What this means for your entry timing

The size of the market argues for entry; the structure argues for a staged entry. Most disciplined foreign brands prove demand on cross-border first — using 1210 bonded fulfillment and platform storefronts — then upgrade to a domestic entity and wider distribution only once the data justifies the heavier regime. That sequence limits downside while preserving upside, and it is the pattern our [China market entry guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/guide-china-market-entry.html) recommends for first-time entrants.

## FAQ

**How big is the China FMCG market in dollar terms?** China's total retail sales of consumer goods reached about RMB 47.1 trillion (roughly US$6.6 trillion) in 2023 per the National Bureau of Statistics. The FMCG slice runs into the trillions of yuan annually.

**Who actually buys imported goods in China?** Demand is led by a middle-income cohort of more than 400 million, concentrated in tier-1 and tier-2 cities, skewed toward women and younger households, and driven by health, safety, and provenance cues.

**Which categories do imported goods win in?** Infant formula and maternal products, beauty and cosmetics, wine and spirits, health supplements, and premium packaged food — categories where "imported" is itself a trust signal.

**Is cross-border e-commerce still growing for imports?** Yes. China's cross-border e-commerce trade reached about RMB 2.38 trillion in 2023 (GACC), and 1210 bonded import lets foreign brands sell without a local entity.

## How China KOL Agencies Work for Foreign Brands
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-kol-agency
Published: 2026-08-28 · Cluster: Marketing & New Media

## Why foreign brands hire a KOL agency instead of going direct

A Western brand can usually book an influencer in its home market with a contract and a wire transfer. China is different: the creator economy is fragmented across Xiaohongshu, Douyin, Weibo, and Bilibili, each with its own norms, payment rails, and compliance rules, and the most effective creators are represented by multi-channel networks rather than managed directly. For a foreign brand without a local team, a KOL agency is the fastest way to turn intent into booked, compliant campaigns. This explainer covers what these agencies do, how they are paid, and how to keep control of your brand while you scale.

## A China KOL agency is an intermediary that connects foreign brands with vetted influencers across Xiaohongshu, Douyin, Weibo and Bilibili, handling casting, contracts, content and reporting

A China KOL agency (网红/达人代理机构) is a specialized intermediary that matches foreign brands with key opinion leaders — influencers with trusted audiences — and manages the full campaign lifecycle: creator discovery, contracting, content briefing and review, booking, payment, and performance reporting. Unlike a Western talent agency that may represent one creator, a China KOL agency typically represents or has direct relationships with many creators and sells access as a managed service. For a foreign brand it substitutes the local relationship graph you do not have and reduces selection risk by using platform data instead of guesswork ([Xiaohongshu marketing for foreign brands](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/xiaohongshu-red-marketing-foreign-brand.html) is where many beauty entries begin).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">RMB 4.9 trillion</span><span class="l">China's live-streaming e-commerce GMV in 2023, much of it KOL-driven — the scale that makes agency casting decisive</span><span class="src">Source: industry estimates / Ministry of Commerce live-commerce data, 2023</span></div>

## Types of agencies: MCN, boutique and platform partners

Not all KOL agencies are the same, and the right fit depends on your category and budget:

- **MCNs (multi-channel networks)** represent large rosters of creators and offer scale and reach, often with in-house live-streaming studios. Best for awareness pushes.
- **Boutique KOL agencies** focus on a niche — beauty, maternity, or tech — with deeper creator trust and higher content quality. Best for considered-purchase categories.
- **Platform-aligned partners** are accredited by Xiaohongshu or Douyin and can unlock official ad inventory and verification. Best when you also want paid media, not just organic seeding.
- **Full social-commerce agencies** combine KOL casting with store operations, so creator traffic converts inside your Tmall Global or Douyin store ([Douyin marketing for foreign brands](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/douyin-china-marketing-foreign-brand.html) covers the platform angle).

## How the engagement and fee model works

Agency compensation in China usually takes one of three shapes, and smart brands blend them:

- **Retainer + media spend.** A monthly fee to manage the program plus pass-through budget for creator fees and ads.
- **Commission on sales (CPS).** The agency earns a percentage of attributed sales, aligning incentives with outcomes — common on Douyin where links are trackable.
- **Project fee per campaign.** A fixed price for a defined seeding or launch sprint.

Top-tier KOLs may also command a flat seeding or appearance fee on top of any performance component. The key negotiation principle: tie a meaningful share of compensation to measured results, not follower counts, because reach without conversion wastes budget.

## How a foreign brand runs a campaign

A typical engagement runs in five stages:

1. **Briefing and goal-setting.** Define whether the objective is awareness, trial, or direct sales, and on which platform.
2. **Casting and audience audit.** The agency proposes creators and supplies follower-quality and engagement data; you audit for fake followers.
3. **Content briefing and compliance review.** Scripts are drafted and checked against China's strict advertising rules on efficacy and comparison claims ([social-media advertising compliance](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-social-media-advertising-compliance.html) is the reference).
4. **Booking, posting, and paid amplification.** Creators publish; the agency boosts winning content with platform ads.
5. **Reporting and attribution.** Reach, engagement, and sales are reconciled against trackable links or discount codes.

## Risks and how to avoid them

The model is powerful but has sharp edges. The biggest risks are inflated engagement from fake followers, off-brand or non-compliant claims, and weak sales attribution. Mitigate each with an audience-audit clause in the contract, pre-approved scripts, and KPIs tied to trackable links or unique codes. Insist on a content-compliance sign-off before anything goes live, because a single non-compliant efficacy claim can trigger a platform takedown and a regulator fine.

## FAQ

**What does a China KOL agency actually do for a foreign brand?** It casts and contracts vetted influencers, briefs and reviews content, books slots, handles payment and tax, and reports on reach and sales — replacing the local network a foreign brand lacks.

**How are China KOL agencies usually paid?** Typically a retainer plus media spend, a commission on attributed sales (CPS), or a per-campaign project fee, often with a top-KOL seeding fee on top. Tie pay to outcomes, not vanity metrics.

**Can a foreign brand work with KOLs without an agency?** Yes, by engaging creators directly, but you absorb contract, payment, tax, and compliance burden and lose benchmarking data. Most first-time entrants use an agency to start.

**What are the biggest risks when using a KOL agency?** Fake followers, off-brand or non-compliant claims under China's advertising law, and weak attribution. Mitigate with audience audits, pre-approved scripts, and trackable KPIs.

## China Product Registration for Foreign Brands: A Compliance Roadmap
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-product-registration-foreign-brands
Published: 2026-08-28 · Cluster: Compliance & Registration

## Why product registration decides whether you can sell at all

Most Western brands are used to a launch sequence where you build a listing, ship stock, and start selling. China does not always work that way. A large slice of consumer categories — from cosmetics and food to electrical goods and medical devices — cannot legally clear customs or appear on a shelf until a Chinese authority has pre-approved the product. For a foreign brand, "product registration" is therefore not a paperwork afterthought; it is the gate that determines whether your goods can enter the country at all. This roadmap shows which authority owns your category, how the registration-versus-filing split works, and how long the clock really runs.

## China product registration is the pre-market approval a foreign brand must obtain from a Chinese authority before its goods can be legally imported, marketed, or sold

China product registration (产品注册) is the mandatory pre-market approval issued by a designated Chinese regulator that authorizes a specific foreign product to be imported and sold in mainland China. It is distinct from customs clearance: clearance moves a shipment across the border, while registration confers the legal right for that product to be on the market in the first place. The single most common mistake foreign brands make is to confuse the two — they book freight and platform onboarding, then discover at the port that the product was never authorized to be sold. Registration is typically held by the overseas manufacturer as registrant of record, but in practice it is lodged and maintained through a China importer or qualified agent.

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">17 categories</span><span class="l">of products require China Compulsory Certification (CCC) before they can be sold, spanning electronics, vehicles and child-safety items</span><span class="src">Source: SAMR / CNCA compulsory-certification catalogue, 2024</span></div>

## Which authority owns your product category

Chinese product oversight is split by product type, and each category sits with a different regulator — so the first job is identifying who owns yours:

- **NMPA (National Medical Products Administration)** owns cosmetics, drugs, and medical devices. Under the Cosmetic Supervision and Administration Regulation (CSAR), special cosmetics need registration while ordinary cosmetics need only filing.
- **GACC (General Administration of Customs)** owns imported food through overseas-manufacturer registration (Decree 248) for the 18 higher-risk food categories — covered in detail in our [GACC food registration guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/gacc-food-registration.html).
- **SAMR / CNCA** own the CCC mark for about 17 categories of electrical, electronic, vehicle, and children's products that must carry compulsory certification before sale.
- **MIIT / SRRC** own radio-type approval (型号核准) for any device with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or cellular radio — a frequent surprise for consumer-electronics and IoT brands.
- Additional regimes exist for veterinary drugs, pesticides, and a handful of other controlled goods.

If your portfolio spans categories, expect to file with two or three of these bodies in parallel rather than one.

## Registration versus filing: the two speeds of market entry

Registration (注册) is a full pre-market review and approval where the regulator assesses safety, formula, and claims before granting market access — the slow lane. Filing (备案) is a lighter notification where the responsible party submits the dossier and can proceed once it is accepted — the fast lane. The same product family can sit in both: under CSAR, a sunscreen is a *special* cosmetic requiring NMPA registration, while a standard moisturizer is *ordinary* and only needs filing ([NMPA](https://www.nmpa.gov.cn)). Knowing which lane each SKU occupies is what turns a 12-month plan into a 6-week one, because filing-track products can go to market almost as soon as the dossier is complete.

## Timelines and validity you should plan around

Registration clocks vary enormously by authority and product risk:

- **NMPA special cosmetics:** typically 8–12 months including required safety and efficacy testing ([NMPA](https://www.nmpa.gov.cn), CSAR framework).
- **Ordinary cosmetics filing:** often weeks once the dossier and China responsible person are in place.
- **GACC 18-category food:** a few weeks to several months depending on category and home-country endorsement.
- **CCC certification:** commonly 1–3 months for testing and factory inspection ([SAMR](https://www.samr.gov.cn)).
- **SRRC radio approval:** roughly 4–8 weeks for model testing.

Registrations also carry validity and renewal obligations, and can be suspended if post-market surveillance finds non-compliance. Build the clock in at the planning stage and run it in parallel with your [Tmall Global or JD Worldwide store setup](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/tmall-global-store-setup.html), never after it.

## The importer of record is the bridge

For many categories the overseas manufacturer is the registrant, but the day-to-day lodgement and shipment accountability sit with a China import-record-filed entity (进口商备案). A Hong Kong or mainland importer of record — such as GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED — can act as that local anchor so a foreign brand does not need to incorporate in mainland China on day one. The importer's role includes holding the import qualification, matching each shipment to a valid registration, managing label review, and handling declaration and traceability. Our [Hong Kong entity explainer](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/hong-kong-entity-china-import.html) covers why a HK trading company is a common, low-friction structure for this.

## Common registration mistakes

- **Treating filing as registration.** Assuming a fast-lane filing covers a product that actually needs full registration leads to a refused shipment.
- **Starting registration after onboarding.** Because special-category clocks run 8–12 months, registration must start before — not after — platform and marketing work.
- **Assuming one approval covers the whole range.** A device can need both CCC and an NMPA medical-device filing; map every SKU separately.
- **Skipping label and claims review.** Chinese labelling and advertising rules are strict; fix them before production, not at the border.

## How GOODSINFINITE supports registration

We bundle the regulatory and logistics work so a brand enters cleanly:

- **Category mapping.** We confirm which authority and which lane (registration vs. filing) each SKU needs, and start the right process immediately.
- **Importer of record.** GOODSINFINITE holds the China import qualification and can anchor 1210 bonded shipments without you incorporating locally.
- **Dossier and label support.** We pre-review labels and assemble authority-ready dossiers so applications move fast.
- **Bonded fulfillment across five cities** (Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou, Qingdao) for rapid domestic delivery once clearance is granted.

> Enter China the way compliant brands do: map the category, secure the right registration or filing, and let a qualified importer carry the shipment across the border.

## FAQ

**Do all products need registration before entering China?** No. China gates specific high-risk or regulated categories behind pre-market registration or compulsory certification, while most general merchandise can be imported and sold once normal customs and labelling rules are met. The decisive question is which category your SKU falls into.

**Can a foreign brand complete registration without a China entity?** Often yes, but with help. The overseas manufacturer is usually the registrant of record and the application is lodged through a China importer or qualified agent, while a local import-record-filed entity is still required to lodge shipments and share accountability.

**How long does NMPA cosmetic registration take under CSAR?** Special cosmetics typically take 8–12 months including testing; ordinary cosmetics only require filing and can clear in weeks once the dossier and responsible-person requirements are met.

**What is the difference between CCC and NMPA registration?** CCC is a SAMR/CNCA safety-certification mark for about 17 hardware categories; NMPA registration governs cosmetics, drugs and medical devices at the product-and-claims level. A device can need both.

## Do You Need a China Import License Before Selling? A Foreign Brand Checklist
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/china-import-license
Published: 2026-08-27 · Cluster: Compliance & Registration

## The licence question that confuses every first-time exporter

Search "do I need a China import license" and you will find a fog of half-answers. The confusion is understandable: China does run an import-licence system, but it rarely applies to the branded consumer products most overseas businesses want to sell. This checklist clears the fog and tells you what you actually need — and what you do not.

## China's import licence system is a narrow control, not a blanket rule

China's import licence system is the MOFCOM-administered control that restricts entry of a narrow list of goods — it is not a requirement attached to every shipment crossing the border. The annual MOFCOM catalogue of licence-administered goods covers items such as certain grains, sugar, cotton, fertilizers, timber, and selected industrial inputs — not the化妆品, supplements, snacks, or apparel that make up most cross-border retail ([MOFCOM](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">1210</span><span class="l">the Customs bonded-import code that lets overseas brands sell into China without a local entity or per-shipment licence</span><span class="src">Source: General Administration of Customs cross-border e-commerce supervision rules</span></div>

If your product is a normal branded consumer good, the honest answer to "do I need an import licence?" is almost always no. The real question is whether your category needs a *product* approval — a different mechanism entirely.

## Product registration is the gate most brands actually face

Product registration is the category-specific approval — lodged with GACC, NMPA, or SAMR — that most regulated brands must clear instead of a generic import licence. The agency depends on what you sell:

- **Food** → GACC overseas-manufacturer registration (Decree 248) for the 18 high-risk categories; lighter information filing for the rest.
- **Cosmetics** → NMPA filing (general) or registration (special-use) under CSAR.
- **Medical devices / health food** → NMPA or SAMR approvals as applicable.

These approvals are the substantive compliance work. Treat "licence" and "registration" as different words for different gates, and you will plan correctly.

## The 1210 cross-border model removes the per-shipment burden

The 1210 bonded model is a Customs regime where goods are pre-stocked in a China free-trade zone and cleared per order, deferring tax until a unit actually sells. For most consumer goods sold this way, the per-shipment import-licence formalities that general trade would require are simplified, because the goods move under a dedicated cross-border e-commerce framework rather than the full general-trade (0110) regime ([GACC](https://www.customs.gov.cn)).

That is why a foreign brand can run a Tmall Global or JD Worldwide store as an overseas entity: the platform and the importer of record absorb the clearance mechanics, and you avoid both a mainland company and the heavier general-trade licence layer.

## An import record-filed entity is the local anchor you still need

An import record-filed entity (进口商备案) is the local party qualified to lodge declarations and hold food-safety and customs accountability — even when no licence is required. Under 1210, this role can be filled by a Hong Kong or mainland importer of record such as GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED, so you do not need a WFOE on day one. The entity:

- Holds the import record-filing with GACC
- Matches each shipment to valid product approvals
- Manages declaration, tax, and traceability
- Acts as the accountable party for compliance

## A practical pre-launch checklist

- **Step 1 — Classify your product.** Is it on the MOFCOM licence catalogue? For most branded consumer goods, no.
- **Step 2 — Identify the approval agency.** Food → GACC; cosmetics → NMPA; health/special foods → SAMR/NMPA.
- **Step 3 — Decide the channel.** 1210 cross-border for light compliance and no local entity; general trade for a domestic store.
- **Step 4 — Appoint an importer of record.** A qualified China entity or a Hong Kong importer such as GOODSINFINITE.
- **Step 5 — Pre-clear labels and claims.** Review against Chinese rules before production to avoid border rejection.

## Common mistakes brands make

- **Assuming "licence" and "registration" are the same.** They are not; chasing a licence you do not need wastes weeks.
- **Believing 1210 means zero compliance.** You still need product registration where the category demands it.
- **Shipping before the importer is filed.** Without a record-filed entity, nothing clears — licence or not.

## How GOODSINFINITE simplifies the path

- **Importer of record.** We hold the China import qualification so you can sell via 1210 with no WFOE.
- **Category triage.** We tell you, up front, whether you need GACC, NMPA, SAMR, or none — and start the right filing.
- **Bonded fulfillment** across Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou and Qingdao for fast domestic delivery.

> The smart move: stop asking "do I need a licence" and start asking "which approval fits my category" — then let a qualified importer carry the shipment.

## FAQ

**Do most foreign brands need a China import licence?** Usually not. China's import-licence system (administered by MOFCOM) covers a narrow catalogue of goods such as certain agricultural commodities, energy and chemicals — not ordinary branded consumer goods.

**What replaces the import licence for regulated products?** Category-specific approvals: GACC registration for imported food manufacturers, NMPA filing/registration for cosmetics and medical devices, and SAMR oversight for health food and special-dietary foods.

**Does the 1210 cross-border model remove the licence requirement?** For most consumer goods sold via 1210 bonded import, yes — per-shipment licence formalities are simplified because the goods enter under a dedicated CBEC regime. Product registration is still required where the category demands it.

**Who holds the import qualification?** A China import record-filed entity must lodge the declaration and hold accountability. GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED can act as that importer of record, so a brand can sell into China without a mainland company.

## Cross-Border E-commerce in China: The 1210 Model and How Foreign Brands Sell Without a Local Entity
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/cross-border-ecommerce-china
Published: 2026-08-27 · Cluster: E-commerce Operations

## The fastest legal way into the China consumer market

For an overseas brand, the hardest part of entering China used to be the entity, the licensing, and the warehouse. Cross-border e-commerce (CBEC) changed that. Instead of importing containers under general trade and building a mainland subsidiary, a brand can now sell directly to Chinese consumers while the goods sit in a bonded zone and clear per order. This guide explains how the model works and whether it is right for you.

## Cross-border e-commerce is the retail sale of imported goods under a dedicated Customs regime

Cross-border e-commerce (CBEC) in China is the retail sale of imported goods to Chinese consumers via bonded (1210) or direct-mail (9610) models that bypass the full general-trade regime. Rather than clearing a whole shipment as general trade (0110) with a mainland entity and full labelling, CBEC treats each consumer order as a separate, lightly-regulated import ([GACC](https://www.customs.gov.cn)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">¥2.38 trillion</span><span class="l">China's cross-border e-commerce import and export in 2023, up 15.6% year-on-year</span><span class="src">Source: General Administration of Customs of China, 2024</span></div>

That number signals a mature, policy-backed channel — not an experimental loophole. CBEC is explicitly supported by Chinese regulators as a way to give consumers access to imported goods while keeping compliance manageable.

## The 1210 bonded model is a Customs regime, not just a warehouse

The 1210 bonded model is a Customs regime where goods are pre-stocked in a China free-trade zone and cleared per order, deferring tax until a unit actually sells. You ship a bulk quantity into a bonded zone, and only when a consumer places an order does that single unit clear Customs, pay the consolidated cross-border tax, and ship domestically — typically arriving in 1–3 days.

This inverts the risk of general trade: instead of betting a full container before you know demand, you fund inventory in-bond and pay duty only on what sells. Unsold stock can usually be re-exported without the full tax hit.

## Tmall Global is the default first store for an overseas entity

Tmall Global is a CBEC platform that lets an overseas entity open a flagship store and sell into China without a mainland company. Alongside JD Worldwide and Douyin cross-border, it accepts foreign merchants — the merchant can be a Hong Kong, US, EU, or other overseas company ([MOFCOM](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn)). The essentials:

- An overseas business licence and brand ownership or authorisation
- Product compliance for the category (GACC/NMPA as needed)
- A bonded (1210) fulfillment arrangement

A Hong Kong trading company such as GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED can be the merchant of record, removing the entity hurdle entirely.

## Bonded fulfillment is what turns a stockpile into fast delivery

Bonded fulfillment is the warehousing-and-clearance operation inside a free-trade zone that turns a bonded stockpile into 1–3 day domestic delivery. Without it, 1210 does not work — the bonded zone is where the per-order clearance happens. GOODSINFINITE operates bonded fulfillment across five cities (Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo, Guangzhou, Qingdao) so brands can match delivery expectations that Chinese shoppers take for granted.

## Cross-border vs. general trade: the real trade-off

Cross-border e-commerce (CBEC) and general trade are two different paths into the same market; the right one depends on your stage:

- **CBEC (1210):** foreign entity OK, lighter compliance, tax per order, fast to launch, great for proving demand.
- **General trade (0110) / domestic store:** full Chinese labelling, a mainland entity, NMPA/filing for regulated goods, higher compliance — but deeper shelf presence and offline eligibility.

Most brands prove demand on CBEC first, then upgrade to a domestic store only when the data justifies the heavier regime. See our [Tmall Global setup guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/tmall-global-store-setup.html) and [JD Worldwide setup guide](https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/jd-worldwide-store-setup.html) for the store-level detail.

## Marketing is the missing half

Cross-border e-commerce discovery in China does not happen on Google. It happens on Douyin, RedNote (Xiaohongshu), and inside the platforms' own search. A bare listing underperforms; plan for ongoing content, livestream, and seeding from day one. Our [China marketing overview](https://www.goods-infinite.com/china-marketing.html) covers the ecosystem.

## Common mistakes brands make

- **Treating 1210 as zero-compliance.** Product registration (GACC/NMPA) is still required for regulated categories.
- **Under-investing in content.** Discovery is platform-native; a static store will not sell itself.
- **Ignoring the entity question until launch.** Appointing an importer of record and bonded fulfillment should happen before, not after, onboarding.

- **Bonded fulfillment.** Five-city bonded network for 1–3 day delivery under 1210.
- **Compliance triage.** We flag which SKUs need GACC/NMPA filings before you list.

## FAQ

**Can a foreign brand sell in China without a mainland company?** Yes. Under the 1210 cross-border model, the merchant can be an overseas entity (including a Hong Kong company such as GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED) with no mainland WFOE. You need bonded fulfillment, product compliance, and a record-filed importer — not a local company.

**What is the difference between 1210 bonded and 9610 direct mail?** 1210 means goods are pre-stocked in a China free-trade zone and cleared per order, enabling 1–3 day delivery. 9610 (direct mail) ships from overseas per order with longer delivery times. 1210 is better for proven demand; 9610 suits early testing.

**Which platforms let foreign entities sell into China?** Tmall Global, JD Worldwide, and Douyin cross-border all accept overseas merchants. Tmall Global and JD Worldwide are the established scale channels; Douyin cross-border adds livestream discovery.

**How is cross-border e-commerce taxed in China?** Cross-border retail imports are generally subject to a consolidated tax that is often lower than general trade, and duty is paid per order only when a unit sells. Confirm the current rates for your HS code.

## GACC Registration for Imported Food: A Step-by-Step Guide for Foreign Brands
Source: https://www.goods-infinite.com/insights/gacc-food-registration
Published: 2026-08-27 · Cluster: Compliance & Registration

## Why GACC registration is the first gate for imported food

China is one of the world's largest food-importing markets, and appetite for imported snacks, dairy, wine, and specialty foods keeps climbing. But food is handled differently from cosmetics or general merchandise: before a single carton reaches a Chinese port, the factory that made it usually has to be pre-approved by Chinese Customs. This guide explains exactly when that approval is required, how the system works, and how to plan around it.

## GACC registration is the pre-clearance that lets an overseas food factory export to China

GACC registration (境外生产企业注册) is the mandatory pre-clearance administered by the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) that authorizes an overseas manufacturer to export a covered food category to mainland China. Under GACC Decree 248 (《进口食品境外生产企业注册管理规定》), which took effect on 1 January 2022, overseas manufacturers of the 18 higher-risk categories of imported food must be registered before their products can clear Chinese customs ([GACC](https://www.customs.gov.cn)).

<div class="statcard"><span class="n">18 categories</span><span class="l">of imported food require overseas-manufacturer GACC registration before export to China</span><span class="src">Source: GACC Decree 248 《进口食品境外生产企业注册管理规定》, effective 2022</span></div>

The reform consolidated a patchwork of rules into one framework and shifted the burden onto the overseas manufacturer rather than the importer alone. If your plant is not on the GACC register, your goods will be refused at the border — regardless of how strong demand is on the Chinese side.

## Two tracks: registration vs. information filing

The GACC system splits imported food into two compliance tracks — a registration track for high-risk categories and an information-filing track for the rest — so the regulatory burden matches the risk profile rather than applying a blanket rule. Products on the registration track need a full GACC review and approval of the manufacturing site. Products on the information-filing track rely on the China importer recording the manufacturer's details and a self-declaration of compliance with Chinese food-safety standards ([SAMR](https://www.samr.gov.cn)).

This two-track design is the single most important thing for a new brand to understand: "Do I need GACC registration?" is the wrong question. The right question is "Which track does my product fall into?"

## Which products fall under the 18 categories

The 18 registered categories are the higher-risk imported foods — such as meat and poultry, aquatic products, dairy, bird's nest, edible oils, grains, canned food, health food, infant formula and food additives — that GACC screens before export. A representative set includes:

- Meat and meat products, poultry, and aquatic animals and their products
- Dairy products and bird's nest (燕窝)
- Edible vegetable oils, grains, canned goods, and aquatic plants
- Fruit, vegetables, nuts and seeds
- Health food (保健食品), foods for special medical purpose (FSMP), and infant formula
- Food additives

If your SKU sits in one of these, registration is non-negotiable. If it does not, your China importer can usually complete the lighter information-filing path. When in doubt, confirm the classification with a licensed broker before you ship, because mis-categorisation is a common cause of border rejections.

## The documents you actually need

A GACC registration dossier is the package of documents — legal entity proof, a HACCP or equivalent quality-management system, and product-category specifics — that proves an overseas plant meets Chinese food-safety equivalence. The core documents typically include:

- The manufacturer's business licence and legal entity proof
- A HACCP plan or equivalent food-safety management certificate
- A recommendation or attestation from the home-country competent authority (many categories require the national food-safety agency to endorse the application)
- Product specifications, labels, and a declaration of compliance with Chinese standards
- For category-specific items (e.g. health food), additional dossiers on function claims and safety

Applications are lodged through the GACC "Import Food Enterprises Registration System" (进口食品境外生产企业注册管理系统), almost always via the China importer or a qualified agent acting on the manufacturer's behalf.

## Timelines, validity and renewal

GACC registration validity is generally tied to the manufacturer's export licence and is subject to annual or category-specific renewal, so planning the clock in is critical. Many registrations complete in a few weeks once the dossier and the home-country recommendation are in place; first-time or complex categories can take several months. Registrations can also be suspended or revoked if a plant fails follow-up inspections or is linked to a food-safety incident — ongoing compliance, not just the initial approval, keeps you on the list.

## Where the China importer fits

A China import record-filed entity (进口商备案) is the local party that lodges shipments, holds the importer qualification, and is jointly accountable for food safety with the overseas manufacturer. Under the 1210 cross-border model, this role can be filled by a Hong Kong or mainland importer of record — such as GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED — so a foreign brand does not need to set up a mainland company on day one. The importer's responsibilities include:

- Holding the import record-filing with GACC
- Matching each shipment to a valid manufacturer registration
- Managing labelling review and the required Chinese-language information
- Handling customs declaration, tax, and traceability records

## Common mistakes food brands make

- **Assuming all food is treated equally.** Treating a high-risk category as a simple filing leads to a refused shipment at the port.
- **Starting registration after onboarding.** Because registration can take months, it must run in parallel with Tmall Global or JD Worldwide setup, not after it.
- **Skipping the home-country endorsement.** Many categories require your national food-safety authority to recommend the plant; brands that omit it stall.
- **Ignoring label review.** Chinese labelling rules (ingredients, nutrition, claims) are strict; fix the label before production, not at the border.

## How GOODSINFINITE supports a food entry

We bundle the compliance and logistics so a food brand can enter cleanly:

- **Importer of record.** GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED holds the China import qualification and can act as the registrant's local anchor for 1210 shipments.
- **Category mapping.** We confirm whether your SKUs sit on the registration or information-filing track and start the right process immediately.
- **Label and dossier support.** We pre-review labels and assemble the GACC dossier so applications move fast.
- **Bonded fulfillment across five cities** (Tianjin, Shanghai, Ningbo,
Guangzhou, Qingdao) for 1–3 day domestic delivery after clearance.

> Enter the China food market the way compliant brands do: confirm the track, register the manufacturer, and let a qualified importer carry the shipment across the border.

## FAQ

**Do all imported foods need GACC registration?** No. GACC Decree 248 requires overseas-manufacturer registration only for the 18 higher-risk categories of imported food. Everything else is handled through a lighter importer information-filing path.

**What is the difference between registration and information filing?** Registration is a GACC review and approval of the overseas manufacturer before export, required for the 18 high-risk categories. Information filing is the lighter path for remaining foods, where the China importer records the manufacturer's details in the GACC system.

**How long does GACC registration take?** Timelines vary by category and country. Many registrations complete in a few weeks once the dossier and the home-country recommendation are in place; complex or first-time categories can take several months.

**Can a foreign brand register itself, or does the importer do it?** The overseas manufacturer is the registrant of record, but the registration is lodged through the China importer or a qualified agent via the GACC Import Food Enterprises Registration System. A registered China import entity is also required to lodge shipments.

- [SAMR — State Administration for Market Regulation](https://www.samr.gov.cn)
- [MOFCOM — Ministry of Commerce (import/export regulation)](https://www.mofcom.gov.cn)
